1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot’s sensors and wheels are never exact, so one reading can fit many places and one move can end in several. The robot therefore keeps a probability for every place it could be, instead of a single guess.



Figure 1: A hallway of 10 cells of 1 m, numbered 0 to 9 and joined into a loop, with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7. The robot’s sensor says “door”. The robot could be at any of the three doors, so each of those cells gets probability 0.33
So far the kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model predicts where wheel commands take a robot: wheels at 12 and 8 rad/s drive it round a circle of radius 0.5 m. That prediction assumes wheels that never slip. Real wheels slip, so a command “move 2” can end 1, 2 or 3 cells on, and a robot that only counts such moves soon does not know where it is. This Note adds the answer: keep a probability for every place. We leave the floor for a hallway of cells, because one number per place keeps the counting small (Section 4.1 returns to the floor).
A delivery robot drives along the hallway of Figure 1, the hallway the belief and grid-filter Notes of this chapter return to. It has a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for: 10 cells of 1 m each, numbered 0 to 9, with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7. The hallway is a loop, so one step to the right of cell 9 is cell 0. The robot has a sensor that says “door” or “wall” for the cell beside it. Its sensor now says “door”. Where is it?
There is no single answer. Three cells fit that reading, and the robot has no reason to prefer one of them. A robot that picks one cell and forgets the rest is wrong two times out of three. A robot that keeps all three, each with probability 1/3, still has the true cell among them.
This Note builds that idea step by step:

why a robot can never be sure: five sources of uncertainty, and how errors pile up when the robot only counts its moves (Section 2);
why the robot keeps a probability for every place instead of one best guess (Section 3);
what the robot must keep track of, its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many., and when a state is complete (Section 4);
the two streams of data it receives, controls and measurements (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls., and their order in time (Section 5);
why moving makes the robot less sure and sensing makes it more sure (Section 6).

2. Why a robot is never sure


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A move of 2 cells can end 1, 2 or 3 cells on, and a reading can be wrong, because every part of a robot adds uncertainty: the world changes, sensors are limited and noisy, wheels slip, models are simplified and computers must answer in time. Errors in counted moves add up, so a robot that only counts its moves gets more and more lost: after 8 moves it is where it thinks only with probability 0.33.


2.1 Why counting moves is not enough: dead reckoning
The simplest way to know where we are is to start at a known place and add up our own moves: “I started at 0 m and moved 2 m eight times, so I am at 16 m.” The method is dead reckoning (G-2311)Dead reckoning: Working out a robot’s position from a known start by adding up its own moves, without looking at its surroundings; simple, but its error grows with every move, so it needs readings to correct it. Explained in §2.1 Why counting moves is not enough: dead reckoning.: working out the position from a known start plus the robot’s own motion, with no look at the surroundings. Facing north at 1 m/s for 3 s, a robot reckons it is 3 m north of where it started, without checking anything.
The trouble is that the moves themselves are not exact. Our hallway robot is told “move 2”, two cells of 1 m. Because its wheels sometimes slip or spin on, the real move is (Labbe ch.2):





















Real moveProbability1 cell (it falls short)0.12 cells0.83 cells (it runs on)0.1
We count positions in whole cells, so a move that falls well short counts as 1 cell and one that runs on counts as 3. The hallway robot moves this way throughout the chapter.
Figure 2 plays what happens to a robot that starts surely at 0 m on a long straight track (so that eight moves of 2 m do not wrap round the 10 m loop) and is told “move 2” eight times without looking around. The bars show the probability of each true position; the red dashed line is where the robot thinks it is.

Figure 2: Dead reckoning without readings: after 1, 2, 4 and 8 moves of 2 m the probability of each true position spreads wider; after 8 moves the robot is exactly where it thinks (16 m) with probability 0.33 only
The chance that the robot is exactly where it thinks shrinks with every move:



































MovesRobot thinksChance it is exactly thereStandard deviation12 m0.800.45 m24 m0.660.63 m48 m0.490.89 m816 m0.331.26 m
The last column is the standard deviation (G-1870)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term of the true position: the typical distance between the true position and the reckoned one, so it says how widely the robot may be off. Why does it grow? One move has variance 0.2 m², the average squared miss from the commanded 2 m:
0.1 \times (1 - 2)^2 = 0.1
0.8 \times (2 - 2)^2 = 0
0.1 \times (3 - 2)^2 = 0.1
\text{variance} = 0.1 + 0 + 0.1 = 0.2
The moves slip independently (G-934)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition, one move’s slip not changing the chances of the next, and for independent moves the variances addExplained in: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem, §4.2 Mean and variance of the sample means. After 8 moves:
\text{variance} = 8 \times 0.2 = 1.6
\text{standard deviation} = \sqrt{1.6}
= 1.26 \text{ m}
The standard deviation keeps growing, more slowly than the number of moves but without limit. Dead reckoning is good over short stretches; over longer ones its error grows until something outside the robot corrects it. The notebook RO-007-why-a-robot-is-never-sure.ipynb checks the table with 100 000 simulated robots.
2.2 Five sources of uncertainty
Slipping wheels are only one cause. The textbook on probabilistic robotics (G-2313)Probabilistic robotics: The approach in which a robot keeps a probability distribution over what might be the case (such as where it is) instead of one best guess, so it can handle ambiguous readings and recover from errors. Explained in §3.2 Why a single best guess gets lost., robotics that reasons with probabilities, lists five (Thrun et al. 2005 ch.1, as given in Khamis L5), shown in Figure 3:

Figure 3: Five sources of uncertainty around a robot: the environment, the sensors, the robot’s actuation, the models and the computation, each with an example

The environment. The world is not fully predictable: people walk past, doors open and close, chairs move. A person who steps between the robot and the wall makes a distance sensor read much less than the true distance to the wall.
The sensors. A sensor sees only so far and so finely; a camera cannot see through walls. Eight distance sensors around a robot tell it how far the nearest obstacle is in eight directions, which is usually not enough to say where it is in a room. And every reading carries sensor noise (G-2312)Sensor noise: Small random errors in a sensor’s readings, so the same quantity measured twice gives slightly different numbers (a wall 2 m away reads 1.92 to 2.07 m); it is one reason a robot cannot take a reading at face value. Explained in §2.2 Five sources of uncertainty.: small random errors, so the same wall measured again from the same spot gives slightly different numbers.
The robot’s actuation. Motors and wheels do not do exactly what they are told. A command to move 1 m gives 95 cm one time and 1.1 m the next; gears slip and wear.
The models. Every model simplifies. The kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model, the equations that turn wheel speeds into motion, assumes wheels that never slip.
The computation. A robot must decide in time, so its algorithms take shortcuts and approximate (Khamis L5).

In Figure 4, watch sensor noise and the environment at work on one wall: no two readings of the wall agree exactly, and while a person walks through the beam the readings fall far short of the wall. A distance sensor stands 2.00 m from a wall and takes 200 readings. The 190 readings of the wall itself spread from 1.92 m to 2.07 m, because of sensor noise. The 10 readings taken while a person walked past are between 0.61 m and 1.16 m, nowhere near the wall.

Figure 4: Animation: a distance sensor 2.00 m from a wall takes 200 readings (simulated), one at a time. Top: the beam and the distance the sensor reports (dot). Bottom: the histogram of the readings so far, one bar per 0.02 m, on the same metre scale. The wall’s readings pile up around 2.00 m; after the 100th reading a person walks through the beam, and the next 10 readings land where the person is. The last frame holds all 200: 190 readings of the wall between 1.92 and 2.07 m, and 10 readings of the person between 0.61 and 1.16 m
So no reading and no move can be taken at face value. Section 3 starts with the reading: “door” fits three cells, and the robot must still say where it is.
3. Keep a distribution, not one best guess


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

This section answers the opening question for one reading: “door” fits cells 1, 3 and 7. A robot that keeps one guess throws the other two away and gets lost when it guessed wrong; a robot that keeps a probability for every cell keeps the true one among its candidates.


3.1 Why one reading fits many places
Back to the hallway. For this section we make two simplifications: the moves are exact and the door sensor never errs. At the start the robot knows nothing, so each of the 10 cells has the same probability. We write:

n is a cell number, 0 to 9;
P(n) is the probability that the robot is in cell n, a number from 0 to 1; the ten cells’ probabilities add up to 1.

P(\text{each cell}) = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1
The sensor says “door”. Three cells have a door (1, 3 and 7) and nothing favours one of them, so each gets a third:
P(1) = P(3) = P(7) = \frac{1}{3} = 0.33
The other seven get 0, as Figure 1 shows. The same thing happens in two dimensions. A robot in a room whose laser scan shows “a flat wall 1 m straight ahead” could stand 1 m from any straight stretch of any wall, facing it (Figure 5). The reading rules out spots near a corner or facing the door, where the scan would look different, but it leaves many poses (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, positions together with a heading.

Figure 5: A room 7 m by 4 m with a door. The scan shows a flat wall 1 m ahead; every pose 1 m from a straight stretch of wall, facing it, fits the reading, so candidate poses line all four walls
Such a list of every possible value with its probability, adding up to 1, is a probability distribution (G-1571)Probability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tables. Ours has three separate peaks, so it is a multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode distribution: the robot is not in three places at once, it has narrowed its position down to one of three (Labbe ch.2).
3.2 Why a single best guess gets lost
A robot could instead keep only one value: its best guess, a point estimate (G-1507)Point estimate: A single number computed from sample data as the best guess for an unknown population parameter. Explained in: Estimating a Population Mean with the Central Limit Theorem, §1. Overview of its position. Figure 6 runs both robots side by side. The true robot is in cell 1 (red square).

Figure 6: Animation: after the reading “door” the distribution keeps cells 1, 3 and 7 while a best guess picks cell 7; after “move 2” the candidates become cells 3, 5 and 9; after a second “door” only cell 3 fits, while the best guess at cell 9 expected a wall and is lost
Step by step:

Reading “door”. The distribution keeps cells 1, 3 and 7. The best-guess robot must pick one and picks cell 7. With three equal candidates, a guess is right only one time in three.
Control “move 2”. Every candidate moves with the robot: cells 1, 3 and 7 become 3, 5 and 9. The best guess becomes cell 9.
Reading “door” again. Of cells 3, 5 and 9, only cell 3 has a door. Each other candidate would have read “wall”, which does not match. So the distribution is now certain: cell 3, with probability 1.

The best-guess robot expected a wall at cell 9 and read “door”. It now knows its guess was wrong, but it threw the other candidates away at step 1, so it has nothing to fall back on: it is lost. The robot that kept the whole distribution found its place, because it remembered every place the readings allowed (Labbe ch.2).
Keeping the whole distribution is the central idea of probabilistic robotics (G-2313)Probabilistic robotics: The approach in which a robot keeps a probability distribution over what might be the case (such as where it is) instead of one best guess, so it can handle ambiguous readings and recover from errors. Explained in §3.2 Why a single best guess gets lost.: the robot computes a probability distribution (G-1571)Probability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tables over what might be the case, instead of a single best guess, so it can handle ambiguous readings and recover from errors (Thrun 2000). The probability distribution a robot keeps over where it might be is its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, defined later in this chapter.
3.3 Why noisy sensors forbid crossing places out
Section 3.2 crossed out every cell that did not match a reading. Crossing out works only for a perfect sensor. A real door sensor errs. The sensor of our hallway robot, used throughout the chapter, behaves like this:




















Robot is atReads “door”Reads “wall”a door cell0.60.4a wall cell0.20.8
A robot that still crosses out non-matching cells throws away its true cell every time the reading is wrong. In Section 3.2 the true robot stood at a door both times (cells 1 and 3). The chance that both readings say “door” is:
0.6 \times 0.6 = 0.36
So the chance that at least one says “wall”, and the true cell is crossed out, is:
1 - 0.36 = 0.64
Nearly two times in three, the robot would delete the cell where it really is. (The two readings err independently (G-934), which is why their probabilities multiply.)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition
So with a noisy sensor the robot does not cross out; it weights. A reading of “door” makes each door cell 3 times as likely as each wall cell, because the sensor reads “door” 3 times as often at a door as at a wall (Labbe ch.2):
\frac{0.6}{0.2} = 3
Three door cells and seven wall cells make 16 equal shares, and the probability P of a cell (Section 3.1) is its shares out of 16:
3 \times 3 + 7 \times 1 = 16
P(\text{each door}) = \frac{3}{16} = 0.1875
P(\text{each wall}) = \frac{1}{16} = 0.0625
Check: the ten cells add up to 1.
3 \times 0.1875 + 7 \times 0.0625 = 1
Figure 7 plays the same reading on the cells, for the perfect sensor and the noisy one. Every cell starts at 0.1; watch each one be multiplied by the chance of reading “door” there, and then every cell be divided by the sum of the products, so that the ten add up to 1 again. The noisy sensor ends at the same 0.1875 and 0.0625 as the shares.

Figure 7: Animation of one reading “door” for a perfect sensor (top, blue) and the noisy sensor (bottom, purple). Every cell starts at 0.1 and is multiplied by the chance of reading “door” there: 1 at a door and 0 at a wall for the perfect sensor (products 0.1 and 0), 0.6 and 0.2 for the noisy sensor (products 0.06 and 0.02). The products add up to 0.3 and 0.32, and each cell is divided by its sensor’s sum. The last frame: the perfect sensor gives 0.33 to each door cell and 0 to each wall cell; the noisy sensor gives 0.1875 to each door cell and 0.0625 to each wall cell
The wall cells keep a small probability, so one wrong reading lowers the true cell but never deletes it; later readings can lift it again. How a reading turns into these numbers in general is Bayes’ theoremBayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4.1 From the counts to the formula, which this chapter later applies to the robot’s readingsExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §3.1 Why the robot needs Bayes’ theorem. So far the answer to “where is it?” has been one cell number; Section 4 asks what a robot must track in general.
4. The state: what the robot keeps track of


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

“Where is it?” asks for the robot’s state: in the hallway one number, its cell. In general the state is every quantity the robot needs to predict what happens next: its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, often its speeds, and the things around it that can change. A state is complete when knowing it now makes the past useless for predicting the future.


4.1 State: from one number to many
In the hallway the robot needs one number, its cell. A robot on a floor needs three, its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading: position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°).
The collection of quantities the robot keeps track of because they decide what happens next is its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many.. In the hallway run of Section 3.2 the robot is in cell 3 at time 2:

t is the time step, counted 0, 1, 2 and so on, here 2;
x_t is the whole state at time t, not only the position x of a pose; in the hallway it is the robot’s cell number, here 3.

x_2 = 3
Depending on the robot and the task, the state can also include:

the pose of the robot;
the speeds of the robot, when it does not stop the moment its motors stop (Section 4.2);
the positions of things around it: fixed things such as walls and doors are kept in a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for, while things that move, such as people, go into the state, often with their speeds.

4.2 Why the speed can belong to the state
Figure 8 plays two robots on a smooth floor with their motors switched off, from one second ago to one second from now: watch robot B roll to 2 m, where robot A stands, so that for a moment the two positions are the same, and then roll on. Both are at 2 m right now. Robot A has been standing still; robot B is rolling at 0.5 m/s.

Figure 8: Animation of two robots on a smooth floor with their motors off, from one second ago to one second from now. Robot A (blue) stands still at 2 m. Robot B (purple) rolls at 0.5 m/s: from 1.5 m up to 2 m, where now both robots are at 2 m and their positions look the same, then on to 2.5 m; dashed boxes mark where B was. The last frame: in one second A is still at 2 m and B is at 2.5 m
One second later:























RobotPosition nowSpeed nowPosition in 1 sA2 m0 m/s2 mB2 m0.5 m/s2.5 m
Their positions now are the same, but their futures differ. If the state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. were the position alone, we could not predict where each robot goes, while their positions one second ago (2 m and 1.5 m) would tell us. The past would carry information the state lacks. With the speed added, the state (2 \text{ m}, 0.5 \text{ m/s}) predicts robot B’s next position by itself, and the past adds nothing.
4.3 Complete state and the Markov property
That test gives the definition. A state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. is a complete state (G-2315)Complete state: A state that, once known, makes earlier states, controls and measurements useless for predicting the future (position plus speed for a coasting robot, not position alone); it lets the robot keep only its latest estimate. Explained in §4.3 Complete state and the Markov property. if knowing it now, the earlier states, commands and sensor readings, called controls and measurements (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls., tell us nothing more about the future (Thrun et al. 2005 §2.3.1). For robot B:

position only: not complete, because the position one second ago improves the prediction;
position and speed: complete, because nothing from the past improves it.

A sequence of states with this property, where the future depends on the past only through the present, has the Markov property (G-2316)Markov property: The property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone. Explained in §4.3 Complete state and the Markov property.. We want it because it lets the robot forget its history: to predict and to update its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, its probability for every place, it needs only the latest state, not every reading since it was switched on. The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm, which updates the belief after every move and every reading, is built on it.
In practice no robot’s state is truly complete: people move, gears wear, the floor changes. Robots still treat their state as complete, and the methods of this chapter work well when the leftover effects are small (Thrun 2000). The robot never sees its state directly; Section 5 names the two kinds of data it does receive.
5. Controls and measurements: two streams of data


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The robot answers “where is it?” from two kinds of data. Controls, such as “move 2”, change its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many., here its cell; measurements, such as “door”, only report on it. A control comes first, then the measurement in the new state.


5.1 Measurements and controls
The data that reaches a robot comes in two kinds (Thrun 2000; Khamis L5):


A measurement (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls. z_t is what the sensors report about the world at time t: our door sensor’s “door”, a laser scan of distances, a camera image. In the hallway at time 1:
z_1 = \text{door}


A control (G-2532)Control u_t: Information about how a robot’s state changed between two time steps, such as the command “move 2” or a count of how far the wheels turned; it changes the state, so a filter uses it to predict where the robot went, which spreads its probability distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls. is information about how the state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. changed: the command “move 2”, or a count of how far the wheels turned. We write it u_t, the same symbol as the control input (G-2298)Control input u: The numbers we choose to drive a robot, such as u = (v, \omega); the model turns them into motion. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model of a robot model. In the hallway at time 2:
u_2 = \text{move 2}


We keep them apart because they do opposite things to the robot’s knowledge (Section 6). A control causes the state to change; a measurement does not change the state, it only tells the robot something about it.
5.2 The order in time
The robot starts in some state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. x_0. Then each time step has two parts:

a control u_t moves the robot from x_{t-1} to x_t;
the robot takes a measurement (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls. z_t in the new state x_t.

Figure 9 builds this chain one event at a time on the hallway run: watch each control (green) carry the robot to its next state, and each measurement (orange) come out of the state it was read in.

Figure 9: Animation of the order of events, one at a time. Top: the chain of states x0, x1, x2, x3 (blue circles); each control u (green box) points into the state it produces, each measurement z (orange box) points out of the state it was read in. Under the chain, the hallway run: from x0 = cell 1, u1 stay gives x1 = cell 1 with z1 door; u2 move 2 gives x2 = cell 3 with z2 door; u3 move 2 gives x3 = cell 5 with z3 wall. Bottom: the hallway with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7; the red square, the robot’s true cell, moves with each control. The last frame holds the whole chain
Controls point into the states (green arrows), because they change them; measurements point out of the states (orange arrows), because each one is produced by the state the robot is in. The robot never sees the states themselves, only the controls it sent and the measurements it received. Working out the states from those two streams is localization (G-2318)Localization: Working out a robot’s pose in a known map from the controls it sent and the measurements it received; needed because the pose itself cannot be measured directly. Explained in §5.2 The order in time. when the state is the robot’s pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, its position and heading, in a known map (Thrun 2000).
How likely each next state is after a control, and each reading in a given state, are the two models every method in this chapter needs. The motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density is the first; the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid x, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose x in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model is the second. Before those models, Section 6 shows what each stream does to the hallway robot’s distribution.
6. Moving makes the robot less sure, sensing makes it more sure


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Here the whole opening problem comes back at once: moves that slip and a sensor that errs. Every uncertain move widens the robot’s distribution (its standard deviation (G-1870), the typical distance of a cell from the average, grows from 0 to 0.63 m in two moves)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term; every informative reading narrows it (to 0.42 m). Neither alone is enough: moves alone drift, readings alone are ambiguous, and together they pin the robot down.


Now we drop both simplifications: the moves are the noisy moves of Section 2.1, and the sensor is the noisy sensor of Section 3.3. Take a robot that knows it is in cell 3, as after Section 3.2. It drives two moves of 2 cells without a reading in between, and then reads its sensor. Figure 10 plays the four stages.

Figure 10: Animation: the robot is sure it is in cell 3; after one noisy move the probabilities are 0.1, 0.8, 0.1 at cells 4, 5, 6; after a second move 0.01, 0.16, 0.66, 0.16, 0.01 at cells 5 to 9; the noisy reading “door” lifts the door cell 7 to 0.853 and lowers cells 6 and 8 to 0.069
Control u_3 spreads the distribution. From cell 3 the robot ends in cell 4, 5 or 6 with the move probabilities of Section 2.1: 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1.
Control u_4 spreads it further. Each way of making two moves multiplies the two move probabilities, because the moves slip independently (G-934)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition: one slip does not change the chances of the other. Ending in cell 7, four cells on, happens in three ways, and the probability P(7) of ending in cell 7 is their sum:
\text{2 then 2}: 0.8 \times 0.8 = 0.64
\text{1 then 3}: 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01
\text{3 then 1}: 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01
P(7) = 0.64 + 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.66
The same counting gives the whole distribution:





















Cell56789Probability0.010.160.660.160.01
Measurement z_4 = “door” sharpens it. The robot weights each cell as in Section 3.3: it multiplies each probability by the chance of reading “door” there, 0.6 at the door cell 7 and 0.2 at the wall cells:
\text{cell 7}: 0.66 \times 0.6 = 0.396
\text{cells 6, 8}: 0.16 \times 0.2 = 0.032
\text{cells 5, 9}: 0.01 \times 0.2 = 0.002
What is left no longer adds up to 1:
0.396 + 2 \times 0.032 + 2 \times 0.002
= 0.464
Dividing each by that sum gives the probability of each cell given the reading, a conditional probability (G-444)Conditional probability: The probability of an event given that another event has happened: P(A \mid B); it updates a probability with what is now known, such as the chance of reading “door” once the robot is known to be at a door. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §2. The definition:

P(n \mid \text{door}) is the probability that the robot is in cell n, given that it read “door” (the bar reads “given”), a number from 0 to 1.

P(7 \mid \text{door}) = \frac{0.396}{0.464} = 0.853
P(6 \mid \text{door}) = \frac{0.032}{0.464} = 0.069
P(5 \mid \text{door}) = \frac{0.002}{0.464} = 0.004
Cells 8 and 9 get the same as cells 6 and 5. The standard deviation of the distribution after each stage tells the story in one number:

























StageStandard deviationsure in cell 30 mafter u_30.45 mafter u_40.63 mafter z_40.42 m
Moves add uncertainty because the robot cannot tell which of the possible outcomes happened; readings remove it because they make places that do not fit less likely, or rule them out (Thrun 2000). So a robot needs both streams of data:

with moves alone it drifts, as in Section 2.1;
with readings alone it stays ambiguous, as the three doors of Section 3.1 show;
with both, each reading is checked against where the moves say the robot can be, and the places that fit everything gain probability, as in Section 3.2 and here.

“Where is it?” after the reading “door” has no single answer: cells 1, 3 and 7 each get 0.33, because all three fit the reading equally, so a single guess would be right only one time in three. A move and a second “door” then leave only cell 3; with slipping moves and the noisy sensor, two moves and a “door” give cell 7 probability 0.853.

Uncertainty comes from five places, so a robot must plan for imperfect readings and moves rather than hope for perfect ones.
A single best guess, once contradicted, has nothing left, so the robot keeps every candidate.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-009-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot finds where it is by comparing what it senses with a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for.. A map can list a few landmarks or mark every cell as free or occupied; obstacles can be stored exactly as polygons built from half-planes, as triangles, or as a grid of cells; and landmarks are pulled out of raw sensor data as range, bearing and signature.



Figure 1: A room 7 m by 4 m with a door in the top wall, a four-sided table, an L-shaped cabinet in the top right corner, a pink pole at (1, 3) and a green pole at (6, 0.8); the robot stands at (2, 1) facing 30 degrees
So far the robot can say how a move blurs its pose: the motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density turns a drive from (2 m, 1 m, 30°) into a cloud of end poses (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, positions with headings. What still breaks: a reading can shrink that cloud only if the robot knows where the sensed thing stands. “The pink pole is 2.236 m away” means nothing until a map says the pink pole is at (1, 3). A robot compares each reading with a mapExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §3.1 Why one reading fits many places: “door” fits only the places where the map has a door. This Note adds the map, for the same robot at (2 m, 1 m) facing 30°, now placed in the room of Figure 1 so that there is something to map:

what a map is, and the main families of maps: feature-based and grid (Sections 2 and 3);
how to store an obstacle exactly, as a polygon made of half-planes (G-2336)Half-plane: All points on one side of a line, together with the line: the points where a x + b y + c \le 0; one sign test, used as a building block for polygon obstacles. Explained in §4.2 Half-plane: one side of a line., and test whether a point is inside it (Section 4);
two other common models, triangle meshes (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in §5.1 Triangle meshes. and bitmaps, and what each costs (Section 5);
how a robot pulls landmarks (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. out of a laser scan and describes each by its range, bearing and signature (Section 6).

2. Why a robot needs a map


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for. is the robot’s model of its surroundings: a list of the objects that matter, with where they are. Localization compares readings with it, and planning searches it for routes.


2.1 What a map is for
A reading such as “the pink pole is 2.236 m away, to the left” says where things are relative to the robot. To turn it into “where am I?”, the robot needs to know where those things are in the room. A map gives exactly that: the robot compares what it sees with the map and keeps the poses where the two agree. Planning needs the map too: a route to the door must go round the table.
A map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for. is a list of the objects in the environment that matter to the robot, with their positions and properties (Thrun et al. 2005 §6.2). We write it as a list of objects:

m_i is object number i of the map, such as the pink pole at (1 m, 3 m);
N is the number of objects, 2 when the map holds only the two poles (Section 3);
m is the whole map, the list of all N objects.

m = \lbrace m_1,\ m_2,\ \dots,\ m_N \rbrace
Fixed things, such as walls and furniture, belong in the map; things that move, such as people, belong in the robot’s state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many, the quantities it keeps track of, instead. What goes in the map is settled; how much of the room it records is not.
3. Feature-based and grid maps


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A feature-based map lists only landmarks and where they are; a grid map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for. gives every cell of space a value, free or occupied. The first is tiny but says nothing about free space; the second is large but answers “can the robot be here?” at once.


What should the map of Figure 1’s room hold: only the two poles, or every spot of floor? Maps come in two kinds (Thrun et al. 2005 §6.2). Figure 2 draws our room both ways.
Make interactive
Figure 2: The room as a feature-based map, only the pink pole at (1, 3) and the green pole at (6, 0.8): 6 numbers; and as a grid map of 0.1 m cells, black where the walls, table, cabinet and poles are: 70 by 40 = 2800 cells
A feature-based map (G-2334)Feature-based map: A map that stores only landmarks, each with its coordinates and signature, such as (1, 3, pink); very compact, but it says nothing about which space is free. Explained in §3. Feature-based and grid maps. is a list of landmarks (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features., distinctive objects such as the two poles, each with its coordinates and a label that tells landmarks apart. Our room needs two entries, each a pole’s x and y in metres and its colour. The map m, the list of the room’s objects, is then:
m = \lbrace(1,\ 3,\ \text{pink}),\ (6,\ 0.8,\ \text{green}) \rbrace
The map holds 6 numbers for the whole room (Brown CS148 tutorial). A feature-based map is cheap to store and to search, but it says nothing about the rest of the room: from it the robot cannot tell that the table is there.

4. Obstacles as polygons made of half-planes


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A line splits the floor into two half-planes, told apart by the sign of one formula. A convex obstacle is the overlap of a few half-planes, so a point is inside exactly when every formula is at most 0; any other obstacle is a union (G-2045)Union (A ∪ B): The set of elements in A or B (or both), such as the points inside either of two convex pieces of an obstacle; for events, the event that A or B (or both) happens. 4.1 Why store obstacles exactly

Collision checks in route planning often need the exact shape: does the robot’s path clip the table’s corner or not? The table in Figure 1 is a four-sided polygon, given by its corners in counter-clockwise order (LaValle §3.1.1):
(3,\ 1),\ (5,\ 1),\ (5.5,\ 2.5),\ (3.5,\ 3)
The list draws the table’s outline, but it does not answer the question a planner asks a million times: is the point (4, 2) inside the table? 4.2 Half-plane: one side of a line
Every edge of the table lies on a line, which we can write in the general form of a lineExplained in: The Equation of a Hyperplane, §3.1 The general form of a line. For a point on the floor:

x is the point’s x coordinate, in m;
y is its y coordinate, in m;
a is the number that multiplies x, set by the line’s direction (1.5 for the table’s right edge below);
b is the number that multiplies y (−0.5 for the right edge);
c is the constant that shifts the line into place (−7 for the right edge);
f(x, y) is the line’s function: 0 on the line, negative on one side and positive on the other.

f(x, y) = a x + b y + c = 0
The vector (a, b) is the line’s normal vector (G-1346)Normal vector: A vector perpendicular to a line, plane or hyperplane; for w^{\mathsf T}x + w_0 = 0 it is w. Explained in: The Equation of a Hyperplane, §6.1 The argument, a direction square to the line, and points towards the positive side. All the points on one side of a line, together with the line, form a half-plane (G-2336)Half-plane: All points on one side of a line, together with the line: the points where a x + b y + c \le 0; one sign test, used as a building block for polygon obstacles. Explained in §4.2 Half-plane: one side of a line. (LaValle §3.1.1):

H is the half-plane on the negative side: the set of floor points (x, y) where f is 0 or less; in the braces below, the colon reads “such that”.

H = \lbrace(x, y) : f(x, y) \le 0 \rbrace
Worked example: the right edge of the table. It runs from (5, 1) to (5.5, 2.5), so its direction is (0.5, 1.5). The corners run counter-clockwise, so the table always lies on the left of each edge as we walk along it. Turning the direction a quarter turn clockwise therefore gives a normal that points to the right of the edge, out of the table:
(a, b) = (1.5,\ -0.5)
The line passes through (5, 1), where f must be 0:
1.5 \times 5 - 0.5 \times 1 + c = 0
c = -7
Doubling every number gives whole numbers and the same line, with the same signs. We call this right-edge function f_2:
f_2(x, y) = 3x - y - 14
One edge gives one half-plane; the table has four edges.

5. Triangle meshes and bitmaps


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

In 3D, obstacles are often stored as many triangles, which graphics hardware draws fast but which do not say what is inside. A bitmap (G-2339)Bitmap (obstacle bitmap): A grid of cells marked 1 if the cell contains any obstacle point and 0 otherwise, like a black-and-white image; simple and natural for sensor data, but it overstates obstacles, and finer cells cost many more cells. Explained in §5.2 Bitmaps and occupancy grids. marks every cell that touches an obstacle; it is simple and fits sensor data, but finer cells cost many more cells.


5.1 Triangle meshes
Half-planes (G-2336)Half-plane: All points on one side of a line, together with the line: the points where a x + b y + c \le 0; one sign test, used as a building block for polygon obstacles. Explained in §4.2 Half-plane: one side of a line., the regions on one side of a line, describe the table’s outline on the floor plan, but the room’s table and cabinet are really 3D, and the common 3D model is a set of triangles, each given by its three corner points in space. A set of triangles that together cover an object’s surface is a triangle mesh (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in §5.1 Triangle meshes. (LaValle §3.1.3). Figure 5 builds our table, 0.75 m high, from 8 corner points and 12 triangles: 2 for the top, 2 for the bottom and 2 for each of the 4 sides.

Triangles are popular because graphics hardware is built to draw them (LaValle §3.1.3). Neighbouring triangles share corners, so meshes often store each corner once and list triangles by corner numbers, as the table’s 12 triangles share 8 corners. The drawback: a mesh is only a surface. Nothing in a loose set of triangles says which side is inside, and meshes made from scans or design files often have holes, so a planner cannot always tell whether a point is inside an object (LaValle §3.1.3).

6. Landmarks and feature extraction


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A scan of 360 distances is mostly wall. Feature extraction (G-2341)Feature extraction (from sensor data): Pulling a few distinctive objects out of raw sensor data, such as two poles out of a 360-beam laser scan; it shrinks hundreds of numbers to a short list that is easy to match with a map. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. finds the few objects in it that are easy to spot and tell apart, the landmarks, and reports each as a range, a bearing and a signature.


6.1 Why extract features
The other half of the comparison is the reading itself. A laser scanner on our robot at (2, 1) measures 360 distances, one per degree. Comparing all 360 with a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for., the robot’s model of the room, is possible (the range-sensor Notes later in this chapter do it), but most of the numbers describe plain wall, which looks the same all along the room. A few distinctive objects carry most of the information about where the robot is. Pulling such objects out of raw sensor data, so that a scan of hundreds of numbers becomes a short list of objects, is feature extraction (G-2341)Feature extraction (from sensor data): Pulling a few distinctive objects out of raw sensor data, such as two poles out of a 360-beam laser scan; it shrinks hundreds of numbers to a short list that is easy to match with a map. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. (Thrun et al. 2005 §6.6, as in the Freiburg sensor-model slides).
An object makes a good landmark (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in §6.1 Why extract features. when two things hold:

the robot can detect it reliably, such as a pole that stands out in a laser scan or a coloured marker in a camera image;
the robot can tell it apart from the other landmarks: tree 1 from tree 2, the pink pole from the green one.

Landmarks can be natural objects (trees, doors, road signs) or artificial ones put there for the robot (coloured markers, reflectors). Some are passive, only seen; others are active and send a signal, such as a radio beacon (Freiburg sensor-model slides). The two poles of our room are passive landmarks; the next step finds them in the scan.
6.2 Finding the poles in a scan
Our robot at (2, 1) facing 30° takes a simulated scan: 360 beams, one per degree, each with 1 cm of range noise. The beams hit the walls, the near side of the table, and two small clusters.
A pole shows up as a few neighbouring beams that are much shorter than the beams on both sides, which pass it and hit the wall behind. So the extraction rule, applied to the scan in order, is:

cut the scan wherever the range jumps by more than 0.3 m between neighbouring beams;
keep a piece that is narrower than 0.35 m and nearer than the beams on both sides of it;
report its bearing (G-2344)Bearing: The angle from the robot’s heading to a sensed landmark, positive to the left, such as 86.6 degrees; together with the range it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in §6.3 Range, bearing and signature., its direction measured from the robot’s heading, as the average direction of its beams, and its range (G-2343)Range (of a landmark reading): The distance from the robot to a sensed landmark, such as 2.236 m; together with the bearing it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in §6.3 Range, bearing and signature., its distance, as its nearest beam’s range plus the pole’s radius of 0.1 m, so that the range is to the pole’s centre.

Why each of the three numbers is needed:

Range and bearing fix where the landmark is relative to the robot. Range alone puts it anywhere on a circle around the robot; bearing alone, anywhere along a ray from it.
The signature says which landmark of the map the reading belongs to. Without it, two identical poles would leave the robot with two explanations of every reading, like the three identical doors of the hallwayExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §3.1 Why one reading fits many places; with it, the reading “pink” can only be the pole at (1, 3).

In localization the map is known and the pose is not. Then a single landmark reading cannot fix the pose; with the range alone it only says the robot stands somewhere on a circle of radius r around the landmark, and two or three landmarks together pin it down. Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-010-.title: Range Sensors: the Beam Model
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-010-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot judges a guess about its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, where it stands and which way it faces, by asking how likely its laser readings would be from there. The beam model gives that number for one reading as a mix of four causes, so that a person walking past does not make the right pose look impossible.


So far the robot has a grid map (G-2335)Location-based map (grid map): A map that splits space into cells and stores a value for every cell, occupied or free, free space included (2800 cells for a 7 m by 4 m room at 0.1 m); larger, but it answers at once whether a pose is free. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §3. Feature-based and grid maps of its room: the room split into small cells, each marked free or occupied. The map does not say where the robot is on it; the robot can only guess poses and test each guess against what its sensors report. Figure 1 shows where that test breaks: watch the four beams leave the robot one by one, and see which one stops short of the wall.

Figure 1: Animation: a 5 m by 4 m room seen from above. The robot at (2, 2), facing along x, fires four laser beams one by one, at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° from its heading. Each beam travels out and stops at the first surface it meets: the forward beam at a person 1.00 m ahead, although the wall is 3 m away (dashed blue line); the other three at the walls, after 1.97, 2.04 and 1.99 m. The readings fill in beside the room, and the last frame holds the whole scan
The robot stands at pose (2, 2, 0) in a 5 m by 4 m room; its laser measures the distance to the nearest surface in four directions. A person stands 1 m in front of it, so the forward beam reads 1.00 m, although the map says the wall is 3 m away. Is the robot at (2, 2, 0), or one metre further along at (3, 2, 0)? This Note adds the rule that answers it.
The room is smaller and emptier than the 7 m by 4 m room with poles and furnitureExplained in: Maps and Landmarks, §1. Overview used for maps: a laser needs only walls, and bare walls keep every expected range (G-2375)Expected range z^{\ast}: The distance a beam would read with a perfect sensor, if the robot were at a given pose in the map; the measurement model compares each real reading with it. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., the distance a beam should read according to the map, a round number we can check by hand.
A sensor reading is a measurement (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §5.1 Measurements and controls: what the sensors report about the world at one moment. To test a guessed pose we need a rule that answers one question: how likely are these four readings if the robot stood at that pose? This Note builds the standard rule for range sensors:

what a range sensor reports, and why the question above is the one to ask (Section 2);
why a Gaussian around the expected range is not enough (Section 3);
the four causes of a reading and the shape each one gives, with the reason for every shape (Section 4);
how the four shapes combine into one model, and what the model says about Figure 1 (Section 5);
how to learn the model’s numbers from recorded readings, by maximum likelihood and the EM algorithm (G-675)EM algorithm (expectation maximization): A method for finding the maximum likelihood when some variables are hidden (latent): it repeats two steps, an E-step and an M-step, until the fit settles. Explained in: The Expectation Maximization (EM) Algorithm, §3. The two steps and the algorithm (Section 6);
the other kinds of sensor models a robot uses (Section 7).

2. What a range sensor measures


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A range sensor reports, for each direction, the distance to the first surface the beam meets. A measurement model scores a guessed pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, a position and heading, by how likely those distances are from there.


2.1 Range finders and scans
The four numbers of Figure 1 come from a range finder (G-2371)Range finder: A sensor that measures the distance to the nearest surface in one direction, for example by timing a laser or sound pulse; robots use it to compare what they see with a map. Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans., which measures the distance to the nearest surface in one direction. A laser range finder, or LiDAR (G-1083)LiDAR: A sensor that measures distances to nearby objects with laser light. Explained in: Types of Neural Networks, History and Applications of Deep Learning, §4.1 Mainstream applications, sends a short pulse of light and times its return. The pulse travels to the surface and back, so the time of flight multiplied by the speed of light is twice the distance; halved, it is the distance. A sonar does the same with a sound pulse (LaValle §11.5.1).
A scanning laser turns, so one sweep gives many readings, for example one every half degree. The list of readings from one sweep is a range scan (G-2372)Range scan: The list of readings from one sweep of a scanning range finder, one distance per beam direction, such as z = (1.00, 1.97, 2.04, 1.99); it is the measurement a laser-based robot tests poses against. Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans.. Figure 2 plays both steps in our room: first watch one pulse of the forward beam go out to the person and back while a clock runs, and the round trip turn into the reading 1.00 m; then watch the head turn and the readings outline the room.

Figure 2: Animation in the room of Figure 1. First, one reading: the forward beam’s pulse travels out to the person and back while a clock runs; the echo is back after 6.67 nanoseconds (ns, billionths of a second). Light covers about 0.3 m per ns, so in 6.67 ns the pulse travelled 2.00 m, out and back, and the reading is half of that, 1.00 m. Then the laser head turns and fires one beam every 0.5°; each red dot marks where a beam stopped, and after a full turn 720 dots outline the walls and the person, scattered by a few centimetres of sensor noise. Beams that leave through the glass pane in the top wall meet nothing within 5 m, no echo comes back in time, and each reports 5 m (purple dots)
For one scan:

z^k is the reading of beam k, in m (1.00 m for the forward beam of Figure 1);
K is the number of beams, 4 in Figure 1;
z is the whole scan, the list of all K readings.

z = (z^1, z^2, \dots, z^K)
Figure 1’s four beams point at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° from the robot’s heading:
z = (1.00,\ 1.97,\ 2.04,\ 1.99)
Every sensor has a longest distance it can report. When no surface returns the pulse in time, as for the beams through the glass in Figure 2, the sensor reports that longest distance itself. That longest distance is the maximum range (G-2373)Maximum range z_{\max}: The longest distance a range sensor can report, such as 5 m; when no pulse returns, the sensor reports this value, so a reading of z_{\max} usually means a failure, not a wall. Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans. z_{\max}; our laser has:
z_{\max} = 5 \text{ m}
2.2 Why we need a measurement model
Suppose the robot is unsure whether it is at pose A, (2, 2, 0), or at pose B, (3, 2, 0): one metre further along the room. To decide, it compares its readings with what each pose would predict. The map predicts, for each pose and each beam, the distance the beam should travel before it meets a wall: the expected range (G-2375)Expected range z^{\ast}: The distance a beam would read with a perfect sensor, if the robot were at a given pose in the map; the measurement model compares each real reading with it. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., written z^{\ast}.
We find it by ray casting (G-2376)Ray casting: Finding the expected range by walking along a beam’s direction through the map until the first occupied cell; it turns a guessed pose and a map into the readings the robot should see. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model.: start at the robot, walk along the beam’s direction in small steps, and stop at the first occupied cell of the grid map (Figure 3). The distance walked is z^{\ast}. For the forward beam:

z_{A}^{\ast} is its expected range from pose A, in m;
z_{B}^{\ast} is its expected range from pose B, in m.

z_{A}^{\ast} = 3.0 \text{ m}
z_{B}^{\ast} = 2.0 \text{ m}
In Figure 3, watch the counter as each ray checks one cell after another: the walk ends when the ray enters a wall cell, after 3.0 m from pose A and after 2.0 m from pose B.

Figure 3: Animation of ray casting in the grid map of the room, drawn with 0.5 m cells (the notebook walks in 1 mm steps); the dark ring of cells is the wall. From pose A at (2, 2) the forward ray checks one cell at a time (orange box): six free cells, then it enters a wall cell and stops after 3.0 m. Then from pose B at (3, 2): four free cells, then a wall cell, stop after 2.0 m. The counter shows the distance walked; both rays start at y = 2 and are drawn in different rows so both show
The reading was 1.00 m, which matches neither 3.0 nor 2.0. We need a number for “how well does a reading of 1.00 m fit an expected range of 3.0 m?”, one that tolerates small sensor errors and an odd reading now and then. That number is the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid x, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose x in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., also called the sensor model or observation model (Thrun §6.1). For one scan and one guessed pose:

z is the scan, the four readings (1.00, 1.97, 2.04, 1.99) m;
\mathbf{x} (bold) is the guessed pose, the three numbers (x, y, \theta), such as A; plain x is its first number;
m is the map, the grid map of the room;
the bar \mid reads “given”.

p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m)
In words: the density of getting the readings z, given that the robot is at pose \mathbf{x} and the world looks like map m. The pose \mathbf{x} is the pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading of a floor robot, position and heading:

its first entry x is the position along the room, in m (2 m at pose A);
y is the position across the room, in m (2 m at pose A);
\theta is the heading, in degrees (0° at pose A, facing along x).

\mathbf{x} = (x,\ y,\ \theta)
For a fixed set of readings, p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) read as a function of the pose is the likelihood (G-1086)Likelihood: How probable the observed data is under given parameter values; read as a function of the parameters with the data fixed. Explained in: Probability vs Likelihood, §2.2 Likelihood: from the event back to the parameter of that pose: the poses under which the readings are more likely score higher. A localization filter uses the model this way: the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm multiplies its belief by this likelihood in its correction step.
A range reading is a continuous quantity, so p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) is a probability density (G-1569)Probability density: The height of a continuous distribution’s curve; compares how likely nearby values are. Explained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §5. What the density at a point means, not a probability: per metre for one reading, per m⁴ for our scan of four readings. A density can be larger than 1; only areas under it are probabilities.
2.3 Why a whole scan is a product of beams
A scan has many beams, and writing one density for all of them at once is hard. We split it into one density per beam and multiply. With the symbols of Section 2.1 and Section 2.2:

z^k is the reading of beam k, in m;
K is the number of beams, 4;
\mathbf{x} is the guessed pose, such as A;
m is the map;
\prod means “multiply the terms for k = 1 to K“.

p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m) = \prod_{k=1}^{K} p(z^k \mid \mathbf{x}, m)
Multiplying is allowed when the beams are independent: knowing one beam’s error tells us nothing about another’s. Independence does not hold in general, but it nearly holds once the pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading and the map are known (Thrun §6.3.1):

Without a map, beams are linked: if one beam hits something at 2 m, the beam half a degree away probably hits the same object at about 2 m.
With the map and the pose given, that shared object is already in the map, so each beam’s remaining error is its own sensor noise, and the beams are close to independent.

Independence that holds only once a third thing is known is conditional independence (G-443)Conditional independence: Independence that holds once a third variable is known: given the class, knowing one feature tells nothing more about another. Naive Bayes assumes it so it can multiply one probability per feature. Explained in: Naive Bayes: The Mathematics, §5. Step 3: the naive assumption, the same assumption Naive Bayes makes for features given the class.


                  
                  Extra 
                  
                

The assumption is not exact. A person blocks several neighbouring beams at once, and their errors are then linked. The product then counts that one person several times, which makes the model overconfident (Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Summary beam-based model”). Implementations therefore use only a subset of the beams of each scan: the ROS localization package AMCL uses 30 evenly spaced beams per scan by default (ROS amcl, laser_max_beams).


So scoring a pose comes down to one density per beam; what is still missing is the shape of that density.
3. Why a Gaussian alone fails


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A narrow Gaussian around the expected range gives a reading caused by a passer-by a density of practically zero, and the product then rejects the true pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, the robot’s real position and heading, outright.


The first rule that comes to mind fails on the person’s 1.00 m reading of Figure 1. The rule says the reading should be the expected range (G-2375)Expected range z^{\ast}: The distance a beam would read with a perfect sensor, if the robot were at a given pose in the map; the measurement model compares each real reading with it. Explained in §2.2 Why we need a measurement model., the distance the map predicts, plus a small sensor error, and small errors follow a Gaussian distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is. A good laser’s readings typically lie about 0.05 m from the true distance: its standard deviation (G-1870)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term is \sigma = 0.05 m. For one beam:

z is the beam’s reading, in m (1.00 m for the forward beam);
z^{\ast} is its expected range, 3 m for the forward beam at pose A;
\sigma is the sensor’s standard deviation, 0.05 m;
\mathcal{N}(z;\ z^{\ast}, \sigma^2) is the Gaussian density of the reading, with mean z^{\ast} and variance \sigma^2, in per m.

\mathcal{N}(z;\ z^{\ast}, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\ e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{z - z^{\ast}}{\sigma}\right)^2}
Figure 4 draws it for the forward beam at the true pose A, where z^{\ast} = 3 m. Now put the person’s reading, 1.00 m, into it. The distance from the expected range, in units of \sigma:
\frac{1.00 - 3.00}{0.05} = -40
The exponent:
-\tfrac{1}{2} \times 40^2 = -800
The factor in front of the exponential:
\frac{1}{0.05 \times \sqrt{2\pi}} = 7.98
The density:
7.98 \times e^{-800}
\approx 0
The number e^{-800} is so small that a computer stores it as exactly 0 (the notebook checks). In Figure 4, the reading of 1.00 m sits 40 standard deviations left of the peak, where the curve lies flat on the axis.

Because the scan density is a product, one zero beam makes the whole scan density zero, whatever the other beams say. So the true pose A gets 0. The wrong pose B fits the backward beam far worse but escapes the zero: its forward beam expects 2 m, and its backward beam expects 3 m but reads 2.04 m. Those two densities are tiny but not zero, and B ends up with a scan density of about 4 \times 10^{-164}. A Gaussian alone would prefer the wrong pose, only because a person stepped in front of the robot.
The cure is not a wider Gaussian: that would make every reading near the wall less informative too. Instead we list the other ways a reading can come about, and give each its own shape.
4. The four causes of a reading

Explained in §2.1 Range finders and scans.; or a random reading with no modelled cause. Each cause has its own density shape, and each shape follows from how that cause works.

4.2 Unexpected objects: why the curve falls off, and why it stops
A person, a chair or an open door that is not in the map can block the beam first. The reading is then shorter than z^{\ast}. Explained in §4.2 Unexpected objects: why the curve falls off, and why it stops., and its reading a short reading. Figure 5 shows its shape: high at 0, falling off, and zero after z^{\ast}. Both features have a reason.
Why it stops at the expected range. An object behind the wall cannot block the beam: the wall is hit first. So a short reading is always shorter than z^{\ast}, and the density is 0 beyond it.
Why it falls off. Only the first object along the beam matters; anything behind it is hidden. Cut the beam into 4 equal cells and let each cell be either blocked (1) or free (0), all 16 patterns equally likely. Figure 8 sorts the 16 patterns by the first blocked cell:

The first cell is blocked in 8 of the 16 patterns, more than all the patterns that first stop further out:
1 + 2 + 4 = 7
The count halves with each cell, because each extra free cell in front is one more condition the pattern must meet.
The same holds for any blocking chance. Let each cell be blocked independently of the others:

b is the chance that one cell is blocked, a number from 0 to 1 (0.2 below);
j is a cell’s number along the beam, counted from the robot (1, 2, 3, …);
P(\text{first stop at cell } j) is the probability that the beam stops at cell j and not before.

For the beam to stop at cell j, the j - 1 cells before it must be free and cell j blocked:
P(\text{first stop at cell } j) = (1 - b)^{j - 1}\ b
Each further cell multiplies the chance by the same factor 1 - b. With cells of 0.1 m and b = 0.2:
P(\text{cell } 1) = 0.2
P(\text{cell } 2) = 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.16
P(\text{cell } 3) = 0.8^2 \times 0.2 = 0.128

Record many readings of a wall at a known distance and choose the weights and widths that make those readings most likely. The causes are hidden, so EM finds them by alternating “which cause made each reading?” with “refit each cause”.

6.2 Maximum likelihood, and why it needs a search
The principle is maximum likelihood estimation (G-1191)Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): Fitting parameters by making the likelihood of the observed data as large as possible. Explained in: Maximum Likelihood Estimation, §7.2 The maximum likelihood estimate: choose the six numbers that make the 1000 recorded readings most likely. With the log-likelihood (G-1113)Log-likelihood: The logarithm of the likelihood, which turns the product of probabilities into a sum of log probabilities; it peaks at the same parameters as the likelihood and is easier to compute and maximise. Explained in: Logistic Regression: Maximum Likelihood and the Log Loss, §4.2 Taking logs, we maximise a sum over the readings:

z_i is recorded reading number i, in m;
n is the number of readings, 1000;
z^{\ast} is the expected range, the wall’s distance, 3 m;
p(z_i \mid z^{\ast}) is the mixture of Section 5 at reading z_i, in per m;
\ell is the log-likelihood, the sum of the logs of those densities.

\ell = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p(z_i \mid z^{\ast})
The log of a sum of four parts does not split into simple pieces, so setting the derivative to zero gives no closed formula, exactly as for a Gaussian mixtureExplained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §9. Why maximum likelihood has no closed form. The standard way out for mixtures is EM, which guesses which cause made each reading, refits each cause to its readings, and repeats; each of its steps has a simple formula (UW CSE 571 slides; Thrun §6.3.4; De Laet et al. 2008, Algorithm 1).
6.3 EM for the beam model
The hidden piece of information is the cause of each reading, a latent variable (G-1050)Latent variable: A variable in a model that is never observed, such as the component that produced a point. Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §5.2 The latent variable. The EM algorithm (G-675)EM algorithm (expectation maximization): A method for finding the maximum likelihood when some variables are hidden (latent): it repeats two steps, an E-step and an M-step, until the fit settles. Explained in: The Expectation Maximization (EM) Algorithm, §3. The two steps and the algorithm repeats two steps from a starting guess. We start from equal weights 0.25, a standard deviation of the hits \sigma_{\text{hit}} of 0.3 m and a rate of short readings \lambda_{\text{short}} of 0.5 per m.
E-step: share each reading among the causes. For each reading, compute each weighted part and divide by their sum.
