7. A catalogue of sensor models


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Every sensor needs its own measurement model p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m), the density of its reading z given the pose \mathbf{x} (position and heading) and the map m, because each reports a different kind of number. Four kinds cover most mobile robots: landmark, range, boundary and odometry sensors.


The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in §5.1 The mixture. answers the question of Figure 1 for a laser; it is one entry in a family. A model is needed for every sensor the robot uses, and its shape follows from what the sensor reports. LaValle collects the common kinds (LaValle §11.5.1); Figure 17 draws four of them in our room.

Explained in: Probability vs Likelihood, §2.2 Likelihood: from the event back to the parameter that a localization filter multiplies into its belief.
A scan’s density is the product of its beams’ densities, because once the pose and map are known the beams are nearly independent; the leftover dependence makes the product overconfident, so implementations use a subset of beams.
A Gaussian alone fails, because one reading caused by a passer-by gets density 0 and the product then rejects the true pose.
The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in §5.1 The mixture. mixes four causes with weights that add up to 1, so a short reading costs a pose a factor instead of everything; in our scan the readings are 215 times more likely from the true pose than from the wrong one.
The short-reading curve is exponential because the beam stops at the first of many evenly spread blockers, which halves (or shrinks by a fixed factor) the chance with every extra stretch of beam.
The weights and widths are learned by maximum likelihood from recorded readings; the causes are hidden, so EM alternates responsibilities and weighted refits, and it never lowers the log-likelihood (G-1113)Log-likelihood: The logarithm of the likelihood, which turns the product of probabilities into a sum of log probabilities; it peaks at the same parameters as the likelihood and is easier to compute and maximise. Explained in: Logistic Regression: Maximum Likelihood and the Log Loss, §4.2 Taking logs.
Each sensor kind (landmark, range, boundary, odometry) needs its own model, because each reports a different kind of number.

Now the robot can score a guessed pose from a laser scan on a grid map, even with a person in the way. Still missing is speed: every guessed pose needs a ray cast per beam, and a filter tries hundreds of poses per scan, so the next step is a score that looks only at where each beam endsExplained in: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching, §1. Naive Bayes assumes it so it can multiply one probability per feature. Explained in: Naive Bayes: The Mathematics, §5. Step 3: the naive assumptionIndependence that holds once a third variable is known: given the class, knowing one feature tells nothing more about another. Naive Bayes assumes it so it can multiply one probability per feature.Gaussian distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution isAnother name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements.Standard deviation of a random variable (G-1870)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by termThe square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value.Truncated normal (G-2023)Truncated normal: A normal distribution restricted to a range and rescaled so its area is 1; it keeps its bell shape inside the range. Keras’ normal initialisers cut at two standard deviations: values beyond are redrawn. Explained in: Xavier (Glorot) and He Initialisation, §6.2 With Keras’ initialisersA normal distribution restricted to a range and rescaled so its area is 1; it keeps its bell shape inside the range. Keras’ normal initialisers cut at two standard deviations: values beyond are redrawn.Exponential distribution (G-733)Exponential distribution: The pattern of waiting times between random events: short waits are common and long waits rare (a right-skewed continuous distribution). Explained in: MLE for the Binomial, Exponential and Normal Distributions, §3.1 The distribution of waiting timesThe pattern of waiting times between random events: short waits are common and long waits rare (a right-skewed continuous distribution).Uniform distribution (G-2043)Uniform distribution: A distribution in which every outcome in a range is equally likely. Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distributionA distribution in which every outcome in a range is equally likely.Mixture weight \pi_k (G-1238)Mixture weight \pi_k: How big a share of a mixture one component k gets; the weights are non-negative and add up to 1. Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §6.1 The formulaHow big a share of a mixture one component k gets; the weights are non-negative and add up to 1.MLE of a normal distribution (G-1242)MLE of a normal distribution: The normal curve that makes the data most likely: its mean is the sample mean and its variance the average squared distance from that mean (dividing by n), \hat\mu = \bar{x} and \hat\sigma^2 = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2/n. Explained in: MLE for the Binomial, Exponential and Normal Distributions, §4.4 The MLE of the standard deviationThe normal curve that makes the data most likely: its mean is the sample mean and its variance the average squared distance from that mean (dividing by n), \hat\mu = \bar{x} and \hat\sigma^2 = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2/n.Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) (G-1191)Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): Fitting parameters by making the likelihood of the observed data as large as possible. Explained in: Maximum Likelihood Estimation, §7.2 The maximum likelihood estimateFitting parameters by making the likelihood of the observed data as large as possible.Log-likelihood (G-1113)Log-likelihood: The logarithm of the likelihood, which turns the product of probabilities into a sum of log probabilities; it peaks at the same parameters as the likelihood and is easier to compute and maximise. Explained in: Logistic Regression: Maximum Likelihood and the Log Loss, §4.2 Taking logsThe logarithm of the likelihood, which turns the product of probabilities into a sum of log probabilities; it peaks at the same parameters as the likelihood and is easier to compute and maximise.Latent variable (G-1050)Latent variable: A variable in a model that is never observed, such as the component that produced a point. Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §5.2 The latent variableA variable in a model that is never observed, such as the component that produced a point.Responsibility r_{nk} (G-1687)Responsibility r_{nk}: In a mixture model, how likely it is that component k produced point n, given that point (the posterior probability). Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §3.2 The standard termsIn a mixture model, how likely it is that component k produced point n, given that point (the posterior probability).E-step (G-654)E-step: The expectation step of the EM algorithm: using the current parameters, give every point its responsibilities (the probability that it came from each component), a soft assignment that the M-step then uses. Explained in: The Expectation Maximization (EM) Algorithm, §3.1 The two stepsThe expectation step of the EM algorithm: using the current parameters, give every point its responsibilities (the probability that it came from each component), a soft assignment that the M-step then uses.M-step (G-1139)M-step: The second step of each EM round (maximisation): with the responsibilities held fixed, re-estimate each component’s mean, covariance and weight as responsibility-weighted averages, so the fit to the data improves. Explained in: The Expectation Maximization (EM) Algorithm, §2.1 One round, recalledThe second step of each EM round (maximisation): with the responsibilities held fixed, re-estimate each component’s mean, covariance and weight as responsibility-weighted averages, so the fit to the data improves.MLE of an exponential rate (G-1243)MLE of an exponential rate: The rate of an exponential distribution that makes the observed waiting times most likely: one over their mean, \hat\lambda = n/\sum x_i = 1/\bar{x}. Explained in: MLE for the Binomial, Exponential and Normal Distributions, §3.3 The derivationThe rate of an exponential distribution that makes the observed waiting times most likely: one over their mean, \hat\lambda = n/\sum x_i = 1/\bar{x}.Landmark measurement model (G-2401)Landmark measurement model: The density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw. Explained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §4.1 Two Gaussians, multipliedThe density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw.Likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching, §4.2 From distances to the likelihood fieldA grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam.Odometry motion model (G-2323)Odometry motion model: A motion model that splits the pose change reported by odometry into a first turn, a straight drive and a second turn, and adds independent noise to each, with a standard deviation that grows with the motion; used when wheel encoders exist. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §4. The odometry motion modelA motion model that splits the pose change reported by odometry into a first turn, a straight drive and a second turn, and adds independent noise to each, with a standard deviation that grows with the motion; used when wheel encoders exist.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-011-.title: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-011-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in §3.2 From distance to density. scores a laser reading by one look-up: how close does the beam’s end point land to an obstacle in the map? The model gives up some physics for a large gain in speed and smoothness, and the same idea lets a robot match one scan against another to measure how far it moved.


Make interactive
Figure 1: The 5 m by 4 m room with a box in the lower right. The robot at pose A (2, 2, 0) sends 12 laser beams, one every 30 degrees; each beam ends at a red dot on a wall or on the box, except the forward one, which stops at a person 1 m ahead
So far the robot can score a guessed pose from a laser scan with the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture: it casts every beam through the map and compares each reading with the distance it should have read, and in this room it rated the true pose A 215 times above a pose 1 m off, even with a person in front. What still breaks is that it is slow and jumpy. A localization filter may try hundreds of guessed poses for every scan, and each guess needs a ray cast per beam: 15 million small steps per scan for 1000 poses (Section 2.1). And a 1 cm move can make one beam slip past an edge and change its score 270-fold (Section 2.2). This Note adds a score that looks only at where each beam ends.
We keep the 5 m by 4 m room, pose A and person of the beam model, and add one box (Figure 1) so that a beam has an edge to slip past. The Note covers:

why the beam model is too slow and too jumpy for some uses (Section 2);
the likelihood field model: look only at where each beam ends (Section 3);
how the whole map is turned into a look-up picture once, in advance, and what that picture gives up (Section 4);
scan matching: using a likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. built from one scan to find how far the robot moved before the next (Section 5);
correlation-based map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan.: comparing a small map built from a scan with the global map (Section 6).

2. Why the beam model is not enough


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture needs a ray cast for every beam of every guessed pose, and a tiny change of pose can make a beam slip past an edge and change its score 270-fold.


2.1 It is slow
For each guessed pose, the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture walks every beam through the map until it meets an obstacle (ray casting (G-2376))Ray casting: Finding the expected range by walking along a beam’s direction through the map until the first occupied cell; it turns a guessed pose and a map into the readings the robot should see. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model. A particle filter, which tries many poses at once, multiplies that work. With 1000 guessed poses, 30 beams each, and up to 500 steps of 1 cm per beam:
1000 \times 30 \times 500
= 15\ 000\ 000 \text{ steps per scan}
In the notebook, scoring the 12-beam scan of Figure 1 at one pose takes about 11 ms with the beam model and 0.045 ms with the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. of Section 3: about 250 times faster (plain Python; the exact ratio depends on the machine). The Freiburg slides list “not very efficient” as a weakness of the beam model and “highly efficient, uses 2D tables only” as a strength of the endpoint model of Section 3 (Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model” and “Properties of endpoint model”).
2.2 It jumps at edges
The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture is “not smooth for small obstacles and at edges” (Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model”). Figure 2 shows why. Take one beam, at 330° (pointing down to the right), with the reading 1.86 m, and slide the robot down the room a centimetre at a time, so that its y coordinate y falls; the table gives the beam’s expected range z^{\ast} at each y:




















Robot at yExpected range z^{\ast}Beam model (per m)1.53 m1.85 m (hits the box)5.881.52 m3.04 m (misses the box)0.0218
One centimetre of movement lets the beam slip under the box’s corner. Its expected range jumps from 1.85 m to 3.04 m, and the density of the same reading drops by a factor of:
5.88 / 0.0218 = 270
Figure 2 plays the slide, with the robot’s y going from 1.70 m down to 1.40 m. Watch the red curve, the beam model’s density of the reading: it holds at 5.88 and then drops to 0.0218 in a single centimetre, while the green curve only bends gently.

Figure 2: Animation: the robot slides down the room 1 cm at a time, its y coordinate falling from 1.70 m to 1.40 m, and one beam at 330 degrees reads 1.86 m. Left: the ray cast from the robot, blue while it meets the box after an expected range z* of 1.85 m, orange from y = 1.52 m, when it slips under the box’s corner and meets the bottom wall after 3.04 m; the green dot is where the reading 1.86 m ends. Right: the density of that reading as y falls: the beam model (red) jumps from 5.88 to 0.0218 per m between y = 1.53 and 1.52 m, while the likelihood field (green) changes smoothly. The last frame shows both beams and both full curves
A score that jumps like this is hard to search: a method that improves a guess by small steps, such as gradient descent (G-862)Gradient descent: Finding the lowest point of a function by repeated small steps downhill. Explained in: Gradient Descent from Scratch, §1. Overview, finds no slope to follow on the flat parts and a cliff at the edge. The green curve in Figure 2 is the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. of the next section. The field changes smoothly with the pose, which is the second thing we gain (Freiburg slides, “Properties of endpoint model”).
3. The likelihood field model


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Turn each reading into the point where the beam ended. A reading is likely if that end point lies close to an obstacle in the map; the density is a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is of the distance to the nearest obstacle, plus a small uniform part.


3.1 Look only at where the beam ends
Both problems of Section 2, the ray cast per beam and the jump at the box’s edge, come from following the beam through the map. A correct reading ends on a surface. So instead of following the beam, we can ask a simpler question: does the beam’s end point lie on, or near, a surface in the map (Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model”: “instead of following along the beam, just check the endpoint”)? The point where a beam ends is the beam endpoint (G-2392)Beam endpoint: The point where a beam ends: the robot’s position plus the reading along the beam’s direction, (x + z\cos(\theta + \theta_k),\ y + z\sin(\theta + \theta_k)); the likelihood field model looks only at this point. Explained in §3.1 Look only at where the beam ends.. For beam k:

x is the robot’s x coordinate, in m (2 m at pose A);
y is its y coordinate, in m (2 m at pose A);
\theta is its heading, in degrees (0° at pose A);
\theta_k is the beam’s angle from the heading, in degrees (90° in the worked example below);
z^k is the beam’s reading, in m (1.97 m for the 90° beam);
x_{\text{end}} is the x coordinate of the beam’s end point, in m;
y_{\text{end}} is its y coordinate, in m.

The beam ends at:
x_{\text{end}} = x + z^k \cos(\theta + \theta_k)
y_{\text{end}} = y + z^k \sin(\theta + \theta_k)
The two lines are the cosine and sine shares of a length along a direction, as in the kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model. The laser sits at the robot’s centre here; a laser mounted elsewhere adds its offset (UChicago class 05).
Worked example. At pose A, the beam at 90° reads 1.97 m:
x_{\text{end}} = 2 + 1.97 \cos 90^\circ = 2
y_{\text{end}} = 2 + 1.97 \sin 90^\circ = 3.97
The forward beam reads 1.00 m, so it ends at (3, 2). Figure 3 marks both end points and how far each lies from the map’s obstacles:

d is the distance from an end point to the nearest obstacle in the map, in m.

d(2, 3.97) = 0.03 \text{ m (top wall)}
d(3, 2) = 1.0 \text{ m (box corner)}

Figure 3: Two beams of the scan at pose A. The 90-degree beam ends at (2, 3.97), 0.03 m from the top wall. The forward beam ends at the person, (3, 2), 1.0 m from the nearest obstacle, the corner of the box
3.2 From distance to density
An end point 3 cm from a wall is what a good reading looks like; one 1 m away from everything is not. We turn the distance into a density with two parts (Thrun §6.4; Freiburg slides, “Endpoint model”; UChicago class 05):

a Gaussian of the distance: sensor noise scatters end points a little around the surface, so we use a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is of d with mean 0 and standard deviation (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum \sigma, the typical distance of an end point from the surface;
a uniform part: readings with no modelled cause, such as the person, must not get density 0, so every reading from 0 to z_{\max} gets the same small density, the random measurement part p_{\text{rand}} (G-2381)Random measurement (p_{\text{rand}}): A reading with no modelled cause, such as cross-talk or a stray reflection; modelled as a uniform density 1/z_{\max} (the uniform part p_{\text{rand}}) so that no reading ever has density 0. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.4 Random readings: the uniform part of the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture.

With our numbers:

d is the distance from the beam’s end point to the nearest obstacle, in m;
\sigma is the standard deviation of that distance, 0.1 m;
z_{\max} is the laser’s maximum range, 5 m;
w_{\text{hit}} is the share of readings that end on a surface, 0.9;
w_{\text{rand}} is the share of random readings, 0.1;
\mathcal{N}(d;\ 0, \sigma^2) is the Gaussian density of d with mean 0 and variance \sigma^2, in per m;
p(z^k \mid x, m) is the density of beam k‘s reading z^k, given the guessed pose x and the map m, in per m.

p(z^k \mid x, m) = w_{\text{hit}}\ \mathcal{N}(d;\ 0, \sigma^2) + \frac{w_{\text{rand}}}{z_{\max}}
The standard deviation is wider than the beam model’s 0.05 m, because d also absorbs small errors in the map and the pose. The ROS localization package uses 0.2 m by default (ROS amcl, laser_sigma_hit).
Worked example: the 90° beam, d = 0.03 m. The Gaussian at d = 0 has height 3.989 per m:
\mathcal{N}(0.03;\ 0, 0.1^2) = 3.989 \times e^{-0.045}
= 3.8135
0.9 \times 3.8135 = 3.432
3.432 + 0.1 / 5 = 3.452 \text{ per m}
The person’s beam, d = 1.0 m, ten standard deviations away. The Gaussian part is about e^{-50}, so only the uniform part is left:
0.9 \times 3.989 \times e^{-50} \approx 0
p = 0 + 0.02 = 0.02 \text{ per m}
Two kinds of reading need a rule of their own:

Max-range readings are skipped. Their end point is not on any surface; it only says nothing came back (UChicago class 05; Thrun §6.4).
The whole scan is the product of its beams, as for the beam model, because the beams are close to conditionally independentExplained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.3 Why a whole scan is a product of beams given the pose and the map. In practice we add logs instead of multiplying, which gives the same ranking without very small numbers.

This mixture, evaluated at beam end points, is the likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in §3.2 From distance to density., also called the endpoint model (Thrun §6.4; Freiburg slides).
3.3 The scan at pose A
The notebook scores all 12 beams of Figure 1; d is each end point’s distance to the nearest obstacle:















































BeamReading (m)End pointd (m)Density (per m)0°1.00(3.00, 2.00)1.010.02090°1.97(2.00, 3.97)0.033.452270°1.99(2.00, 0.01)0.023.539330°1.86(3.61, 1.07)0.003.6108 others2.04 to 3.48on a wall0.003.610
The distances come from a grid of 1 cm cells, so they are rounded to the grid: an end point inside a wall cell has d = 0, and the 270° end point, 1 cm above the bottom wall, gets d = 0.02 m. Figure 4 scores the beams one at a time: watch each end point’s distance d set its density, and the logs of the densities add up to the scan’s score at pose A, 10.15.

Figure 4: Animation: the room of Figure 1 with the robot at pose A (2, 2, 0). Its 12 beams are taken one at a time: the dashed line is the beam, which the model does not use, and the red dot is its end point. The table fills in each end point’s distance d to the nearest obstacle (in m), its density (per m) and the natural log of that density, and the running sum of the logs grows below the table. The person’s beam ends 1.01 m from the box corner (purple arrow) and gets only the uniform part, 0.020 per m; the 90° and 270° beams end next to a wall, d = 0.03 and 0.02 m on the grid (3.452 and 3.539 per m); the other nine end inside a wall or the box, d = 0 (3.610 per m). The last frame holds the whole scan: the 12 logs add up to 10.147, which is 10.15 to two decimals
Adding the logs of all 12 densities gives the scan’s log-likelihood at each guessed pose:





























Guessed poseLog-likelihood of the scanA, (2, 2, 0)10.15(2.1, 2, 0): 10 cm off8.91(2, 2, 5°): turned 5°8.49(2, 2.3, 0): 30 cm off−19.29B, (3, 2, 0): 1 m off−15.75
The true pose scores highest, and poses a few centimetres or degrees away score only a little lower: the smooth fall-off of Section 2.2. The person’s beam costs every pose the same, because its end point is far from every obstacle at all of them.

Python: the likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in §3.2 From distance to density. for one scan.
def field_loglik(F, pose, z, angles):
    x, y, th = pose
    keep = z < ZMAX                    # skip max-range readings
    ex = x + z[keep] * np.cos(th + angles[keep])
    ey = y + z[keep] * np.sin(th + angles[keep])
    return np.log(lookup(F, ex, ey)).sum()
F is the precomputed field of Section 4 and lookup reads the grid cell under each end point; both are in RO-011-likelihood-fields-and-scan-matching.ipynb.

Every score still needs the distance d from each end point to the nearest obstacle, and finding it at every guessed pose would bring back the slowness of Section 2.1. Section 4 computes it once, for the whole map.
4. Precomputing the field


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The density depends only on where the end point lands, not on the pose, so we compute it once for every cell of the map and store it. That stored picture is the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field..


4.1 The distance transform
The ray casts that made the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture slow (Section 2.1) are replaced here by a table built once. The density of Section 3.2 needs one number per end point: the distance to the nearest obstacle. That number depends only on the end point’s position, never on the pose the beam came from. So we can work it out for every cell of the map once, before the robot moves, and store it.
The stored grid of “distance from this cell to the nearest occupied cell” is the distance transform (G-2394)Distance transform: A grid that stores, for every cell of a map, the distance to the nearest occupied cell (with straight-line distances, the Euclidean distance transform); it lets a likelihood field be built in one pass. Explained in §4.1 The distance transform. of the map, and with straight-line distances the Euclidean distance transform. Image-processing libraries compute it in one pass over a grid of marked and unmarked cells, for example scipy.ndimage.distance_transform_edt (SciPy docs). Figure 5 shows it on a coarse grid of 0.5 m cells, with the box rounded to whole cells. Read it like a table: each number is the distance in metres from that cell’s centre to the nearest grey cell. The numbers grow by about one cell size (0.5 m) per step away from any wall, and the cells between the box and the right wall stay small because two obstacles are near.

Figure 5: The distance transform on a grid of 0.5 m cells: the walls form a grey ring and the box is two grey cells by two. Each free cell shows its distance in metres to the nearest grey cell: 0.5 next to the walls, rising to 2.0 in the middle of the room; greener cells are closer to an obstacle
4.2 From distances to the likelihood field
Putting each cell’s distance into the density of Section 3.2 gives the density an end point would have in that cell. The grid of these densities is the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. of the map (Thrun §6.4; Freiburg slides, “Example”). We build it in three views, from the familiar to the compact.
A line through the room. Figure 6 walks along the line y = 0.9 m, which crosses the left wall, the box and the right wall. The top panel is the distance to the nearest obstacle: zero at each obstacle and rising in a straight line away from it, until it levels off at 0.9 m in the middle, where the nearest obstacle is the bottom wall 0.9 m below the line. The bottom panel is the field: a peak of 3.61 per m on every obstacle, falling to the uniform part’s 0.02 within about 0.3 m (three standard deviations (G-1871) of 0.1 m)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). The field is computed once per map, so its cost does not grow with the number of poses tried. Scoring a pose then costs one look-up per beam, with no ray casting (G-2376)Ray casting: Finding the expected range by walking along a beam’s direction through the map until the first occupied cell; it turns a guessed pose and a map into the readings the robot should see. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model, the walk along each beam: this is where the speed-up of Section 2.1, about 250 times, comes from (Freiburg slides: “highly efficient, uses 2D tables only”). The ROS localization package AMCL uses this model by default (ROS amcl, laser_model_type).
4.3 What the field gives up
The model “ignores physical properties of beams” (Freiburg slides, “Properties of endpoint model”): it looks at the end point and ignores what lies between the robot and it. Two consequences follow.
The field sees through walls. Figure 9 shows a guessed pose C, (3.9, 2, −90°), above the box, facing down. Suppose a reading of 1.98 m. Its end point, (3.9, 0.02), lies next to the bottom wall, so the field scores it 3.45 per m, a near-perfect reading. But from C the beam would meet the box after 0.8 m; it could never reach the wall. The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture knows this and gives the reading 0.016 per m (Thrun §6.4 lists the same drawback).

Figure 9: A guessed pose C above the box, facing down. A reading of 1.98 m would end next to the bottom wall, which the likelihood field scores 3.45 per m; the beam model knows the box blocks the beam after 0.8 m and gives 0.016 per m
The field does not model people. The field has no short-reading part. A person’s reading is scored only by the uniform part of Section 3.2, 0.02 per m, wherever it lands. The cost is mild in practice, because the uniform part still keeps the scan’s product from reaching 0, and the person costs every guessed pose the same.
So the trade is: physics for speed and smoothness. The trade pays when many poses must be scored, as in a particle filter, and when the score is searched by small steps, as in scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts., lining up two scans to measure the robot’s motion (Section 5) (Freiburg slides, “Properties of endpoint model”).
5. Scan matching: how far did the robot move?


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Build a likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field., the look-up grid of end-point densities, from the first scan’s end points, then slide the second scan over it. The shift that puts the second scan’s end points on the brightest places is the robot’s motion between the two scans.


5.1 The problem: odometry drifts
The smooth score of Section 3, with no 270-fold jump, lets a search slide one scan over another to measure how far the robot moved. Wheel odometry estimates motion by counting wheel turns, and wheels slip, so its estimate drifts (wheel odometry (G-2321): motion measured from wheel turns, with errors that grow as the robot drives)Wheel odometry: Working out a robot’s pose by adding up the wheel motion its encoders measure: ticks to wheel distances, to the robot’s move and turn, to a new pose; accurate over short distances but it drifts, because every error stays in the sum. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §3.1 From encoder ticks to a new pose. A laser sees the same walls before and after a move, and they shift in its view by exactly the robot’s motion. Finding that shift is scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts.: aligning two scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from (Olson 2009).
Our test: the robot takes scan 1 at (2, 2, 0), then drives to (2.3, 2.1, 5°). Odometry claims it reached (2.3, 2.0, 0): it missed the 0.1 m sideways slip and the 5° turn. Each scan has 360 beams, one per degree.
5.2 A likelihood field from the first scan
Scan matching needs no map. We treat the end points of scan 1 as the occupied cells of a little map and build its likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field. exactly as in Section 4 (Freiburg slides, “Scan matching (G-2395): extract likelihood field from first scan and use it to match second scan”)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts.. Scan 2’s end points, placed at the right motion, must then land on the bright ridges of that field.
5.3 Search the candidate motions
A candidate motion is a shift and a turn:

\Delta x is the shift along x, in m (0.3 m for the true motion);
\Delta y is the shift along y, in m (0.1 m for the true motion);
\Delta\theta is the turn, in degrees (5° for the true motion).

To test one, we turn scan 2’s end points by \Delta\theta, shift them by (\Delta x, \Delta y), look up the field of scan 1 under each, and add the logs. That sum is the score of the candidate. We try every candidate on a grid:

\Delta x from −0.1 to 0.7 m and \Delta y from −0.3 to 0.3 m, in steps of 0.02 m;
\Delta\theta from −10° to 10°, in steps of 1°.

The grid holds:
41 \times 31 \times 21
= 26\ 691 \text{ candidates}
The notebook scores them in about one second. Searching a whole grid of candidates and keeping the best is correlative scan matching (G-2396)Correlative scan matching: Scan matching that scores every candidate motion on a grid of shifts and turns and keeps the best, so it needs no good first guess. Explained in §5.3 Search the candidate motions. (Olson 2009). The grid search does not need a good first guess, unlike methods that improve one guess step by step.
Figure 10 plays a few candidates. At the odometry guess, scan 2’s end points sit beside the ridges: the score is 169. The best candidate is the true motion, (0.3, 0.1, 5^\circ), where the points lie along the ridges and the score is 447.

Figure 10: Animation over the likelihood field built from scan 1 (bright = near a scan-1 end point). Red dots are scan 2’s end points placed by a candidate motion. At the odometry guess (0.3, 0, 0) they sit beside the bright ridges, score 169; at the best candidate (0.3, 0.1, 5 degrees) they lie on the ridges, score 447
Because the field is smooth, the score also rises smoothly towards the best candidate, so the search can be refined by small steps, for example by gradient ascent from the best grid point (Freiburg slides: the distance grid “is smooth w.r.t. to small changes in robot position”; Olson 2009).


                  
                  Extra 
                  
                

The field must be dense enough. With 72 beams per scan (one every 5°), scan 1’s end points 3 m away lie about 0.26 m apart, more than twice the field’s standard deviation \sigma of 0.1 m. The field then has dark gaps between the points, and the same search picks (0.28, 0.1, 7^\circ) instead of the true motion (the notebook shows it). Denser scans, a wider \sigma, or a field built from several scans fix it.


Scan matching measures how far the robot moved between two scans, not where it stands in the map; Section 6 compares a scan with the map itself.
6. Correlation-based map matching


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Turn the scan into a small map of marked cells, place it on the global map at a candidate pose, and measure how well the two agree with a correlation coefficient. The placement with the highest correlation is the best pose.


6.1 A local map from the scan
Scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts. compared one scan with another. A third way to score a pose compares the scan with the global map, again without a ray cast per beam: it compares maps instead of points. We mark, on cells of 0.1 m, every cell that holds an end point of scan 2. This small grid built from the robot’s own readings is a local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan.. Placed at a candidate pose, it should line up with the global map’s occupied cells (Freiburg slides, “Map matching: generate small, local maps from sensor data and match local maps against global model”). Comparing the two grids cell by cell to score the placement is map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. (Thrun §6.5).
6.2 Multiply and add
The simplest comparison places the local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. on the global map, multiplies matching cells and adds the products (Konolige and Chou 1999: “places the sensor patch on the map, multiplies the corresponding values, and sums them”). A cell adds 1 only where both maps are marked. Take a strip of 8 cells across a corridor, small enough to work by hand, with walls in cells 3 and 7 of the global map:

















































Cell12345678global map g00100010local map, placed off by one01000100local map, placed right00100010
Placed off by one, no marked cells meet, so the sum is 0; placed right, two meet, so the sum is 2. Larger is better.
The raw sum has a flaw: it rewards a local map for marking many cells. In the room of Figure 1, the right placement of scan 2 scores 175, but a local map with every cell marked scores 224, the global map’s whole count. A comparison must not prefer “everything is a wall”.
6.3 Why we normalise: the correlation coefficient
The fix is the Pearson correlation coefficient (G-1474)Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson’s r): A number from −1 to +1 that measures how closely two numerical columns follow a straight-line relationship (+1: they rise together exactly; 0: no straight-line link), written r; it is the one df.corr() computes. Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §9.1 Correlation of the two maps, read cell by cell as two lists of numbers. The coefficient subtracts each map’s mean before multiplying, so cells marked everywhere earn nothing, and divides by the two maps’ standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, their typical spread about the mean, so the result lies between −1 and +1. For the two maps, read cell by cell:

g_i is cell i of the global map, 1 if marked and 0 if not;
l_i is cell i of the local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan., 1 or 0 in the same way;
\bar g is the global map’s mean, the share of its cells that are marked;
\bar l is the local map’s mean;
\sum_i adds the terms over all cells i;
r is the correlation, a number from −1 to +1.

r = \frac{\sum_i (g_i - \bar g)(l_i - \bar l)}{\sqrt{\sum_i (g_i - \bar g)^2\ \sum_i (l_i - \bar l)^2}}
Thrun §6.5 uses this correlation for map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan..
Worked example: the strip placed off by one. Both maps mark 2 of 8 cells:
\bar g = \bar l = 2 / 8 = 0.25
Each cell’s product (g_i - 0.25)(l_i - 0.25) is one of three values:


both 0 (4 cells):
(-0.25) \times (-0.25) = 0.0625


one marked, one not (4 cells):
0.75 \times (-0.25) = -0.1875


both marked: no such cell.


The top of the fraction:
4 \times 0.0625 = 0.25
4 \times (-0.1875) = -0.75
0.25 - 0.75 = -0.5
Each map’s sum of squares, 2 marked and 6 unmarked cells:
2 \times 0.75^2 + 6 \times 0.25^2 = 1.5
The correlation:
r = \frac{-0.5}{\sqrt{1.5 \times 1.5}}
= -0.5 / 1.5 = -0.333
Placed right, the two lists are identical, so r = 1. A local map with half its cells marked at random gets r = 0.001 against the room, although its raw sum is 113: the correlation sees that it agrees with the walls no better than chance.
The score is used as the likelihood of the reading at that pose, a weight for the pose, and a likelihood cannot be negative. The correlation can be, as the placement off by one shows. Only a positive correlation counts as evidence for a pose; a negative one is treated the same as no correlation at all. So the score of a placement is the correlation cut at zero (Thrun §6.5; Omr et al. 2024):
\text{score} = \max(r,\ 0)
For the strip placed off by one:
\max(-0.333,\ 0) = 0
6.4 Matching scan 2 against the room
Figure 11 slides scan 2’s local map (G-2398)Local map: A small grid map built from the robot’s current readings alone, such as the cells holding a scan’s endpoints; map matching compares it with the global map. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. along x over the room’s map, 2 cm at a time: watch the red cells line up with the grey walls as the correlation climbs to a flat top, then drift off again as it falls. With the turn fixed at 5° and the sideways shift at 0.1 m, the correlation rises from about 0.6 to a flat top of 0.86 to 0.875 for a shift along x, \Delta x, between 0.24 and 0.36 m. Its best value is at 0.28 m, next to the true 0.3 m. Searching all candidates of Section 5.3, the best placement is (0.30, 0.08, 6^\circ) with correlation r = 0.877, against r = 0.872 at the true motion and 0.617 at the odometry guess.

Figure 11: Animation of map matching on 0.1 m cells. Left: the global map (grey cells along the walls and around the box) and the local map of scan 2 (red cells, the cells that hold an end point), placed at a candidate shift along x, dx, with the sideways shift fixed at 0.1 m and the turn at 5°; end points that fall beyond the map’s edge are counted in its edge cells. Right: the correlation r of the two maps, drawn point by point as dx slides from −0.1 to 0.7 m in steps of 0.02 m: about 0.6 at both ends and a flat top near 0.87 between 0.24 and 0.36 m. The last frame keeps the best placement, dx = 0.28 m with r = 0.875, where the red cells cover the walls and the two box faces the robot can see
So map matching found the motion to within one cell (0.1 m) and one degree. The flat top shows its limit: on 0.1 m cells, placements a few centimetres apart mark the same cells, so they cannot be told apart. Smaller cells sharpen it at a higher cost. Map matching is cheap and needs only a grid comparison, but its score is a measure of agreement, not a density derived from how the sensor works; like the likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field., it ignores what lies along each beam (Konolige and Chou 1999: correlation “violates the visibility constraint”).

ModelLooks atCost per guessed poseSmooth in the poseKnows what blocks a beambeam modelthe whole beam, by ray castinga ray cast per beamno: jumps at edgesyeslikelihood fieldeach beam’s end pointone look-up per beamyesno: sees through wallsmap matchinga local map of the scana grid comparisonin steps of a cellno

The likelihood field fixes both problems of the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture: scoring the 12-beam scan takes about 0.045 ms instead of 11 ms, and the score of a beam rises smoothly as the robot slides past the box’s edge instead of jumping 270-fold, because each pose needs only one look-up per beam on a field computed once in advance.
The likelihood field model (G-2391)Likelihood field model: A measurement model for range finders that scores each reading by how close its beam endpoint lands to an obstacle in the map (a Gaussian of that distance plus a small uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0); it is fast and smooth because it skips ray casting, but it ignores what lies along the beam. Explained in §3.2 From distance to density. scores a reading by the distance from its end point to the nearest obstacle, because a correct reading ends on a surface; the density is a Gaussian of that distance plus a uniform part p_{\text{rand}}, so no reading scores 0.
The distances depend only on where the end point lands, not on the pose, so the whole field is computed once with a distance transform (G-2394)Distance transform: A grid that stores, for every cell of a map, the distance to the nearest occupied cell (with straight-line distances, the Euclidean distance transform); it lets a likelihood field be built in one pass. Explained in §4.1 The distance transform. and every later score is a look-up: about 250 times faster than the beam model in our test.
The field changes smoothly with the pose, because moving the robot moves each end point only a little, so a search by small steps can climb it; the beam model jumps when a beam slips past an edge.
The price is physics: the field ignores what lies along the beam, so it can score a reading that would have to pass through a wall, and it has no part for people.
Scan matching (G-2395)Scan matching: Aligning two range scans to find the motion between the poses they were taken from, for example by sliding the second scan over a likelihood field built from the first; it corrects drifting odometry. Explained in §5.1 The problem: odometry drifts. builds a field from one scan and slides the next scan over it; the best shift, here (0.3 m, 0.1 m, 5°), is the motion the odometry got wrong.
Map matching (G-2397)Map matching (correlation-based): Scoring a guessed pose by placing a local map built from the scan on the global map there and computing their correlation, cut at zero; it is cheap but coarse, limited by the cell size. Explained in §6.1 A local map from the scan. compares a local map of the scan with the global map by their correlation, cut at zero, because the raw sum of products would reward a local map that marks everything.

Now the robot can score hundreds of guessed poses per scan quickly, and measure its own motion by matching one scan against the last. Still missing: one laser end point looks like any other, so a score says how well the scan fits the walls but not which object each beam hit; a landmark readingExplained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §1. Overview, such as the range and bearing to a known pole, says which object it saw.
