Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic modelEquations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed.Standard deviation (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximumHow far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default).Random measurement (p_{\text{rand}}) (G-2381)Random measurement (p_{\text{rand}}): A reading with no modelled cause, such as cross-talk or a stray reflection; modelled as a uniform density 1/z_{\max} (the uniform part p_{\text{rand}}) so that no reading ever has density 0. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.4 Random readings: the uniform partA reading with no modelled cause, such as cross-talk or a stray reflection; modelled as a uniform density 1/z_{\max} (the uniform part p_{\text{rand}}) so that no reading ever has density 0.Wheel odometry (G-2321)Wheel odometry: Working out a robot’s pose by adding up the wheel motion its encoders measure: ticks to wheel distances, to the robot’s move and turn, to a new pose; accurate over short distances but it drifts, because every error stays in the sum. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §3.1 From encoder ticks to a new poseWorking out a robot’s pose by adding up the wheel motion its encoders measure: ticks to wheel distances, to the robot’s move and turn, to a new pose; accurate over short distances but it drifts, because every error stays in the sum.Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson’s r) (G-1474)Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson’s r): A number from −1 to +1 that measures how closely two numerical columns follow a straight-line relationship (+1: they rise together exactly; 0: no straight-line link), written r; it is the one df.corr() computes. Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §9.1 CorrelationA number from −1 to +1 that measures how closely two numerical columns follow a straight-line relationship (+1: they rise together exactly; 0: no straight-line link), written r; it is the one df.corr() computes.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-012-.title: Landmark Measurement Model
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-012-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A landmark reading is a range and a bearing to a known point, and the model scores a guessed pose with two Gaussians (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is around the range and bearing that pose predicts. One reading puts the robot on a ring, three readings pin it to one spot, and a reading can also be turned around to propose poses.



Figure 1: The 5 m by 4 m room with three coloured poles: pink at (4.4, 3.8), green at (0.4, 3.2), blue at (3.2, 0.4). The robot at A = (2, 2, 0) reads each one as a range and a bearing: pink 3.10 m at 40 degrees, green 1.95 m at 141 degrees, blue 2.05 m at −55 degrees
The likelihood field (G-2393)Likelihood field: A grid over the map that stores, for each cell, the density of a beam endpoint landing there; computed once from the distance transform, so scoring a pose becomes one look-up per beam. Explained in: Likelihood Fields and Scan Matching, §4.2 From distances to the likelihood field lets the robot score a laser scan about 250 times faster than the beam model. What still breaks: a scan gives hundreds of distances, all of which look alike: wall, wall, wall. This Note adds readings that say which object was seen. A camera that spots a pink pole gives far less data, but the data says exactly which object it saw, and the map says exactly where that object stands. Such a recognisable object at a known place is a landmark. Robots pull landmarks (G-2342)Landmark: An object the robot can detect reliably and tell apart from the others, such as a coloured pole or a door; its known position in the map lets readings of it fix the robot’s pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.1 Why extract features out of sensor dataExplained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.2 Finding the poles in a scan, and each one is seen as a range (how far), a bearing (at what angle from the robot’s heading (G-2284))Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading and a signature (what it looks like, here its colour).
Figure 1 shows the test case of this Note: the same 5 m by 4 m room and pose A = (2, 2, 0) as the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture, now with three coloured poles that the robot sees. To use these readings, the robot needs the same thing the beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture gave it for a laser: a measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid x, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose x in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model, the density of the readings p(z \mid x, m) for any guessed pose x in the map m. The question is: how well does a guessed pose, such as A or a pose B 1 m to its right, explain these three readings? This Note builds the model that answers it:

what range and bearing a pole should show from a guessed pose, and the two pitfalls in computing the angle (Section 3);
the density of a reading, and why it is a product of two Gaussians (Section 4);
why one reading puts the robot on a ring, and several readings pin it down (Section 5);
how to turn one reading around and draw poses that fit it (Section 6).

2. A landmark reading


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each reading is a range, a bearing and a signature; the signature tells us which landmark of the map was seen.


First, what the robot at A gets from each pole of Figure 1. We write one landmark reading as a list of three entries, the range, bearing and signature (G-2343, G-2344, G-2345)Range (of a landmark reading): The distance from the robot to a sensed landmark, such as 2.236 m; together with the bearing it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signatureBearing: The angle from the robot’s heading to a sensed landmark, positive to the left, such as 86.6 degrees; together with the range it fixes where the landmark is relative to the robot. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signatureSignature (of a landmark): A label that says what kind of landmark was sensed, such as its colour or ID number; it tells the robot which landmark in the map a reading belongs to. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signature:

r is the range: the distance from the robot to the landmark, in m (3.10 m for the pink pole);
\varphi (phi) is the bearing: the angle from the robot’s heading to the landmark, counter-clockwise positive, as for the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading itself, in degrees (40° for the pink pole);
s is the signature: what identifies the landmark, here its colour (pink);
z is the whole reading, the three entries together.

z = (r,\ \varphi,\ s)
The three readings of Figure 1:





























PoleRange rBearing \varphiSignature spink3.10 m40°pinkgreen1.95 m141°greenblue2.05 m−55°blue
A sensor that gives both numbers, such as a laser that picks poles out of its scan or a calibrated camera that also judges size, is a range-bearing sensor (Brown CS148 tutorial; Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Landmarks”). The signature solves a problem the laser scan never had to face: which landmark of the map is this? Knowing which map landmark a reading belongs to is known correspondence (G-2405)Known correspondence: Knowing which landmark of the map a reading belongs to, for example from a unique colour (its signature); with it the model can predict that one landmark’s range and bearing. Explained in §2. A landmark reading.. Here each colour appears once, so the colour gives the correspondence directly (Brown CS148 tutorial, §3). For the landmark a reading belongs to:

c is its index, the number of that landmark in the map’s list;
m_{c,x} is its x coordinate in the map, in m (4.4 m for the pink pole);
m_{c,y} is its y coordinate in the map, in m (3.8 m for the pink pole).

For the pink pole:
(m_{c,x},\ m_{c,y}) = (4.4,\ 3.8)
When colours repeat, the correspondence is unknown and must be worked out too. Here each pole is known, so for any guessed pose the robot can ask what that pole should read.
3. What a guessed pose predicts


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

From a guessed pose, position (x, y) and heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading \theta, a landmark should appear at the straight-line distance and at its direction minus the heading. Compute the direction with atan2, and wrap every angle difference into −180° to 180°.


3.1 Expected range and bearing
To score a guessed pose against the three readings of Figure 1, we first ask what the robot would read from there. The steps are those that turn a known pose and the map into a readingExplained in: Maps and Landmarks, §6.3 Range, bearing and signature, now done from a guessed pose. Figure 2 draws the pink pole seen from (2, 2), with the robot turned 15° so that the direction to the pole (green) and the bearing (pink) can be told apart; at pose A the heading is 0° and the two are equal. The pole lies 2.4 m further along x and 1.8 m further along y:

\Delta x is how far the pole lies beyond the robot along x, in m;
\Delta y is how far it lies beyond the robot along y, in m.

\Delta x = 4.4 - 2 = 2.4
\Delta y = 3.8 - 2 = 1.8

Figure 2: The pink pole seen from a robot at (2, 2): a right-angled triangle with sides 2.4 along x and 1.8 along y and long side 3.0 m. The direction to the pole is 36.87 degrees from the x-axis; the bearing is that direction minus the robot’s heading
Expected range. The straight-line distance is the long side of the triangle (Pythagoras), the Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance. A hat marks a predicted value:

\hat r is the expected range, the distance the robot should read, in m.

\hat r = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}
= \sqrt{5.76 + 3.24} = 3.0 \text{ m}
Expected bearing. The direction from the robot to the pole, measured from the world x-axis, is the angle whose tangent is \Delta y / \Delta x:
\text{direction} = \operatorname{atan2}(1.8,\ 2.4) = 36.87^\circ
The bearing is measured from the robot’s heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, not from the x-axis, so we subtract the heading (Figure 2):

\theta is the robot’s heading, in degrees (0° at pose A);
\hat\varphi is the expected bearing, in degrees.

\hat\varphi = 36.87^\circ - \theta
= 36.87^\circ - 0^\circ = 36.87^\circ
In general, for landmark c and any guessed pose:

x is the guessed position’s x coordinate, in m (2 m at A);
y is its y coordinate, in m (2 m at A);
m_{c,x} is landmark c‘s x coordinate in the map, in m (4.4 m for the pink pole);
m_{c,y} is its y coordinate in the map, in m (3.8 m for the pink pole).

Together, the expected range and bearing (G-2402)Expected range and bearing (\hat r, \hat\varphi): The range and bearing a landmark would show from a guessed pose: the straight-line distance to its place in the map, and its direction (by atan2) minus the robot’s heading; the model compares the real reading with them. Explained in §3.1 Expected range and bearing. of landmark c from pose (x, y, \theta) are (Thrun §6.6; Brown CS148 tutorial, Eq. 5–6):
\hat r = \sqrt{(m_{c,x} - x)^2 + (m_{c,y} - y)^2}
\hat\varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(m_{c,y} - y,\ m_{c,x} - x) - \theta
3.2 Why atan2 and not arctan
The expected bearing of Section 3.1 takes the direction from atan2, not from the plain arctangent of the ratio. The green pole of Figure 1, at (0.4, 3.2), shows why. From A, how far it lies beyond the robot along x, \Delta x, and along y, \Delta y:
\Delta x = 0.4 - 2 = -1.6
\Delta y = 3.2 - 2 = 1.2
The plain arctangent of the ratio:
\arctan(1.2 / {-1.6}) = \arctan(-0.75)
= -36.87^\circ
That direction points down and to the right, away from the pole (Figure 3). The ratio has lost the signs: a point at (1.6, −1.2) gives the same ratio −0.75. So the formula uses atan2 (G-2325)atan2: A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §4.2 Turn, drive, turn, which takes \Delta y and \Delta x separately, so it knows which quarter of the plane the point lies in, and returns the angle in the right quarter, between −180° and 180° (Brown CS148 tutorial, §3):
\operatorname{atan2}(1.2,\ -1.6) = 143.13^\circ

Figure 3: The green pole, at (−1.6, 1.2) as seen from the robot. atan2 gives 143.13 degrees, pointing up and left at the pole; arctan of the ratio 1.2 / −1.6 gives −36.87 degrees, pointing down and right, the opposite way
3.3 Why angle differences must be wrapped
Scoring a reading means comparing it with the prediction. For range, the difference is a plain subtraction. For bearings it is not. None of the three poles sits near the ±180° line, where the trouble shows, so take a made-up case: the bearing reads 175° and the prediction is −178°. The two directions are only 7° apart, across the ±180° line, but the plain difference is:
175 - (-178) = 353^\circ
A bell-shaped error curve around the prediction, a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, would call that a wild miss. The fix is to add or subtract 360° until the difference lies between −180° and 180°:
353^\circ - 360^\circ = -7^\circ
Adding or subtracting full turns in this way is angle wrapping (G-2404)Angle wrapping: Adding or subtracting full turns until an angle or angle difference lies between −180° and 180°, so that 175° and −178° count as 7° apart, not 353°; needed whenever bearings or headings are compared. Explained in §3.3 Why angle differences must be wrapped., the wrap-around of headings (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading on a dial, where 350° and 10° are 20° apart. Every bearing difference and every heading in this Note is wrapped (Brown CS148 tutorial, §3, which uses the angle between two unit vectors to the same effect). With the prediction and a fair way to subtract angles, the robot can now score how far each reading lies from what pose A predicts.
4. The landmark measurement model


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The density of a reading is a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, because the two errors are taken as independent. Several landmarks multiply in the same way.


4.1 Two Gaussians, multiplied
The pink pole reads 3.10 m and 40°, but from pose A it should read 3.00 m and 36.87°: the real reading differs from the prediction by sensor noise. As for the measurement noise of a laserExplained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range, small errors follow a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is centred on 0. Our sensor has these standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, the typical size of each error:

\sigma_r is the standard deviation of the range error, 0.1 m;
\sigma_\varphi is the standard deviation of the bearing error, 5°, which is 0.0873 rad.

We treat the range error and the bearing error as independent: knowing that the range came out 10 cm long says nothing about the bearing (Brown CS148 tutorial, Eq. 13). For independent events (G-934)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition the probabilities multiply, and so do the densities. So the density of one reading is the product of two Gaussians. For one reading and one guessed pose:

r is the measured range, in m (3.10 m for the pink pole);
\hat r is the expected range from the guessed pose, in m (3.00 m from A);
\varphi is the measured bearing (40° for the pink pole);
\hat\varphi is the expected bearing (36.87° from A);
\mathcal{N}(e;\ 0, \sigma^2) is the Gaussian density of an error e, with mean 0 and standard deviation \sigma;
p(z \mid x, m) is the density of the reading z given the guessed pose x and the map m, in per m per rad.

p(z \mid x, m) = \mathcal{N}(r - \hat r;\ 0, \sigma_r^2)
\qquad \times\ \mathcal{N}(\varphi - \hat\varphi;\ 0, \sigma_\varphi^2)
with the bearing difference wrapped. A camera can confuse colours, so Thrun adds a third Gaussian for the signature; with known correspondence (G-2405)Known correspondence: Knowing which landmark of the map a reading belongs to, for example from a unique colour (its signature); with it the model can predict that one landmark’s range and bearing. Explained in §2. A landmark reading. that factor is the same for every pose and can be left out (Thrun §6.6; Brown CS148 tutorial, Eq. 16–17). The product of the two Gaussians is the landmark measurement model (G-2401)Landmark measurement model: The density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw. Explained in §4.1 Two Gaussians, multiplied. with known correspondence (Thrun §6.6, Table 6.4; Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Probabilistic Model”).
Worked example: the pink pole at pose A. The errors:
r - \hat r = 3.10 - 3.00 = 0.10 \text{ m}
\varphi - \hat\varphi = 40^\circ - 36.87^\circ = 3.13^\circ
3.13^\circ = 0.05463 \text{ rad}
The range Gaussian. Its peak height:
\frac{1}{\sigma_r \sqrt{2\pi}} = \frac{1}{0.1 \times 2.5066}
= 3.9895 \text{ per m}
The error is one standard deviation, so:
3.9895 \times e^{-\frac{1}{2} \times 1^2}
= 3.9895 \times 0.6065 = 2.420 \text{ per m}
The bearing Gaussian. Its peak height:
\frac{1}{\sigma_\varphi \sqrt{2\pi}} = \frac{1}{0.08727 \times 2.5066}
= 4.5714 \text{ per rad}
The error, in standard deviations:
\frac{0.05463}{0.08727} = 0.626
4.5714 \times e^{-\frac{1}{2} \times 0.626^2}
= 4.5714 \times 0.822 = 3.758 \text{ per rad}
The product:
2.420 \times 3.758 = 9.09
The result is a density, per metre per radian, so it can be larger than 1; only areas under it are probabilities (what a density meansExplained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §5. What the density at a point means, G-1569)Probability density: The height of a continuous distribution’s curve; compares how likely nearby values are. Explained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §5. What the density at a point means. It is easy to call such a number “the probability of the reading”, and wrong.
4.2 Several landmarks
Readings of different landmarks come from separate detections, so their errors are taken as independent too, and their densities multiply (Brown CS148 tutorial, Eq. 11). The three readings at pose A, with each pole’s expected range \hat r and expected bearing \hat\varphi:





































Pole\hat r (m)\hat\varphiRange errorBearing errorDensitypink3.0036.87°0.10 m3.13°9.09green2.00143.13°−0.05 m−2.13°14.70blue2.00−53.13°0.05 m−1.87°15.01
The density of all three readings at A is the product of the three:
9.09 \times 14.70 \times 15.01 = 2006
At the wrong pose B = (3, 2, 0), one metre to the right, the pink pole should appear at 2.28 m and 52°, the green at 2.86 m and 155°, the blue at 1.61 m and −83°. Every reading misses by several standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, and the product is about 10^{-43}. The readings say A, overwhelmingly.

Python: the model for one reading (Brown CS148 tutorial, Table 2).
def landmark_density(pose, m, r, phi):
    x, y, th = pose
    r_hat = np.hypot(m[0] - x, m[1] - y)
    phi_hat = np.arctan2(m[1] - y, m[0] - x) - th
    return gauss(r - r_hat, 0.1) * gauss(wrap(phi - phi_hat), np.radians(5))
landmark_density((2, 2, 0), (4.4, 3.8), 3.10, np.radians(40))   # 9.09
gauss is the Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is density and wrap wraps an angle to (−π, π]; both are in RO-012-landmark-measurement-model.ipynb.

These scores judge poses the robot already guessed. The next section asks the reverse: which positions fit the readings at all?
5. Where can the robot be?


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

One range reading allows every position on a ring around the landmark. Two rings meet in at most two points, and a third ring, or the map, picks one.


5.1 One landmark: a ring
Section 4 scored two guessed poses, A and B. Now turn the question around: the readings of Figure 1 are fixed, and we ask which robot positions fit them, starting with one. Take the pink pole’s range, 3.10 m, alone. Every position 3.10 m from the pole predicts that range exactly, whatever its direction from the pole. So the positions that fit form a ring of radius 3.10 m around the pole, blurred by the 0.1 m noise (Freiburg sensor-model slides, “Distances only”).
Figure 4 draws the range Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is over every position of the room as a surface: a curved ridge of height 3.99 per m along the ring, falling to zero on either side. The true position A sits on the ridge, and so does every other point of it.
Make interactive
Figure 4: The density of the pink pole’s range reading over every robot position in the room, drawn as a surface: a curved ridge of radius 3.10 m around the pink pole, about 0.2 m wide, with the true position A on its crest
5.2 Two and three landmarks: rings meet
The green pole’s range, 1.95 m, gives a second ring. A position that fits both readings must lie on both rings. Two circles cross in at most two points, and here one of the two lies outside the room. Finding a position from distances to known points is trilateration (G-2406)Trilateration: Finding a position from measured distances to points at known places: each distance puts the robot on a circle, and the circles meet at the position; GPS works this way. Explained in §5.2 Two and three landmarks: rings meet., the principle GPS uses with satellites.
Figure 5 multiplies the range densities in, one pole at a time; the product of densities is how readings combine, as in Section 4.2. Each frame is a surface like that of Figure 4 seen from above: darker colour means higher density, and each frame is divided by its own highest point, so its scale runs from 0 to 1. With pink alone the whole ring fits. With pink and green, only the spot near (1.9, 2.0) is left inside the room. With all three, the highest point is (1.90, 1.98), 10 cm from the true position, because each reading carries its own noise.

Figure 5: Animation over the room: first the density of the pink range reading, a ring around the pink pole; then pink times green, which leaves one bright spot near (1.9, 2.0); then pink times green times blue, one sharp spot at (1.90, 1.98) next to the true position (2, 2), marked by a black cross
The bearings add the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading. Once the position is known, a bearing says which way the robot faces: the pole must appear at the measured angle from the heading. Rings and bearings say where the robot could be; Section 6 turns them into poses the robot can try.
6. Sampling poses from a landmark reading


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To propose poses that fit one reading, pick a random angle around the landmark, step out by the measured range, and turn the robot so the landmark appears at the measured bearing.


6.1 Why turn a reading around
The scores of Section 4 can only judge guesses the robot already has; they cannot help when no guess lies near A. A particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step keeps a cloud of guessed poses and moves them with the motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density, the distribution of where a move ends. If the robot is carried somewhere else, or starts with no idea where it is, none of its guesses may lie near the truth, and weighting them by the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid x, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose x in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model cannot fix that. A remedy is to add guesses drawn from the reading itself: poses where the robot could be, given what it just saw. Lenser and Veloso used exactly this on soccer-playing legged robots, adding poses drawn from the landmark readings whenever the filter was lost (“sensor resetting localization”, Lenser and Veloso 2000). Drawing poses that fit a reading is sampling poses from a measurement (G-2408)Sampling poses from a measurement: Drawing poses that fit one reading: for a landmark, a random angle around it, the measured range plus noise, and the heading that makes the landmark appear at the measured bearing; used to add good guesses to a particle filter that is lost. Explained in §6.1 Why turn a reading around. (Thrun §6.6.3). The particle filter loopExplained in: Particle Filter, §4.6 The algorithm runs the filter itself; drawing random values from a distribution is sampling (G-2326)Sampling (from a distribution): Drawing random values so that, over many draws, each value comes up as often as a given distribution says; it turns a motion model into a cloud of possible poses for particle filters. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §5.1 Why sample instead of scoring.
6.2 The recipe, and where the heading comes from
Section 5.1 says the robot lies on a ring around the pole, at any angle. So we pick that angle at random, and add noise to the reading so the samples spread as the sensor’s errors do (Thrun §6.6.3, Table 6.5). For one reading of the pink pole:

r is the measured range, 3.10 m;
\varphi is the measured bearing, 40°;
\sigma_r is the standard deviation of the range noise, 0.1 m;
\sigma_\varphi is the standard deviation of the bearing noise, 5°;
m_{c,x} is the pole’s x coordinate in the map, 4.4 m;
m_{c,y} is its y coordinate in the map, 3.8 m;
\gamma (gamma) is the direction from the pole to the robot, in degrees, drawn at random;
\tilde r is the range with noise added, in m;
\tilde\varphi is the bearing with noise added, in degrees;
x is the sampled robot’s x coordinate, in m;
y is its y coordinate, in m;
\theta is the direction the sampled robot faces, in degrees.

The recipe:


Draw an angle \gamma (gamma) around the pole, uniformly from 0° to 360°.


Draw a noisy range and bearing:
\tilde r = r + \text{noise of std. dev. } \sigma_r
\tilde\varphi = \varphi + \text{noise of std. dev. } \sigma_\varphi


Place the robot at distance \tilde r from the pole, in direction \gamma:
x = m_{c,x} + \tilde r \cos\gamma
y = m_{c,y} + \tilde r \sin\gamma


Set the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading (wrapped):
\theta = \gamma + 180^\circ - \tilde\varphi


Step 4 needs a reason. The robot sits in direction \gamma from the pole, so seen from the robot the pole lies the opposite way, half a turn further:
\text{direction to the pole} = \gamma + 180^\circ
The bearing is that direction minus the heading (Section 3.1):
\tilde\varphi = \gamma + 180^\circ - \theta
Solving for the heading gives step 4. Thrun writes the same step in radians, where \pi rad is 180°:
\theta = \gamma - \pi - \tilde\varphi
Both give the same heading, since adding 180° and subtracting 180° differ by a full turn.
Figure 6 runs the recipe on the noise-free reading of A, range 3.0 m and bearing 36.87°, one step at a time. Watch the angle \gamma swing round the pole to 216.87°, the robot step out 3.0 m to (2, 2), and its heading turn from the pole until the pole sits 36.87° to its left: the heading ends at 0°, so the recipe gives back pose A. The animation then runs the same four steps with the real reading and noise, 200 times (Section 6.3).

Figure 6: Animation in two parts. Part 1, one pose from the noise-free reading of A (range 3.0 m, bearing 36.87 degrees): the angle gamma around the pink pole swings from the grey 0-degree line to 216.87 degrees; the robot steps out 3.0 m along it to (2, 2), on the dashed circle of radius 3.0 m; seen from the robot the pole lies at 216.87 − 180 = 36.87 degrees, and the heading theta turns from there down to 0 degrees, so that the pole appears at the bearing phi = 36.87 degrees to its left; theta = 216.87 + 180 − 36.87 = 360, which is 0 after wrapping. Part 2, the real reading (3.10 m, 40 degrees) with noise of 0.1 m and 5 degrees: pose 1 with its numbers, then 5, 20, 50, 100 and 200 poses fill a ring of radius about 3.1 m around the pole, each arrow turned so that the pole appears about 40 degrees to its left; the black arrow is the true pose A. The last frame shows all 200 poses, 64 of them inside the room
Check with the noise-free reading. From the pink pole, A lies in the direction:
\gamma = \operatorname{atan2}(2 - 3.8,\ 2 - 4.4)
= -143.13^\circ
Step 1 draws \gamma from 0° to 360°, so we add a full turn:
-143.13^\circ + 360^\circ = 216.87^\circ
With the predicted range 3.0 m and bearing 36.87°:
x = 4.4 + 3.0 \cos 216.87^\circ
= 4.4 - 2.4 = 2.0
y = 3.8 + 3.0 \sin 216.87^\circ
= 3.8 - 1.8 = 2.0
\theta = 216.87^\circ + 180^\circ - 36.87^\circ = 360^\circ
= 0^\circ \text{ after wrapping}
The recipe gives back pose A exactly. With the real reading (3.10 m, 40°) it gives (1.92, 1.94, −3.13°): close to A, off by the reading’s own noise.
6.3 The samples
The second part of Figure 6 draws 200 poses from the pink reading, with noise. They form a ring of radius about 3.1 m around the pole, and each arrow is turned so that the pole appears about 40° to its left. Seen from the 200 samples, the pole’s range averages 3.10 m with standard deviation (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum 0.10 m and its bearing averages 39.8° with standard deviation 4.9°: the samples reproduce the reading and its noise, as they should.
Only 64 of the 200 samples lie inside the room. One reading does not know about walls; the map does. Samples outside the free space are thrown away, as the motion model does for poses inside wallsExplained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §7. Ruling out poses inside walls, and readings of the other poles, through the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid x, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose x in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model of Section 4, then weight the rest.
7. Summary
The symbols in the table are listed in Section 3.1 (expected range and bearing), Section 4.1 (the density) and Section 6.2 (a pose from a reading).






























StepFormulaWhyexpected range\hat r = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}straight-line distance to the landmark’s place in the mapexpected bearing\hat\varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta y, \Delta x) - \thetathe direction to the landmark, measured from the headingdensity of a reading\mathcal{N}(r - \hat r) \times \mathcal{N}(\varphi - \hat\varphi)range and bearing errors taken as independenta pose from a reading(m_{c,x}, m_{c,y}) + \tilde r(\cos\gamma, \sin\gamma), \theta = \gamma + 180^\circ - \tilde\varphithe robot lies on a ring; the bearing fixes its heading

The opening question has its answer: the three readings of Figure 1 score the true pose A at 2006 and the pose B one metre away at about 10^{-43}, because each pole, reduced to a range and a bearing, misses by several standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum from the wrong pose.
A landmark reading is a range, a bearing and a signature; the signature gives the correspondence, so the robot knows which map landmark to predict.
The expected bearing uses atan2 (G-2325)atan2: A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §4.2 Turn, drive, turn, because the plain arctangent of the ratio of the offsets, \Delta y / \Delta x, loses the signs and can point the opposite way (−36.87° instead of 143.13° for the green pole).
Bearing differences are wrapped into −180° to 180°, because 175° and −178° are 7° apart, not 353°.
The density of a reading is the product of a range Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is and a bearing Gaussian, because the two errors are taken as independent; readings of several landmarks multiply for the same reason. The product is a density, so it can exceed 1 (9.09 for the pink pole).
One range reading fits a whole ring of positions, because every position at the measured distance predicts that range; two rings cross in at most two points, and a third reading or the map picks one; here the three poles put the robot within 10 cm of the truth.
A reading can be turned around to draw poses that fit it: a random angle \gamma around the landmark, the measured range, and the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading that makes the landmark appear at the measured bearing, so that a lost particle filter can put guesses where the robot could really be.

The robot now has a motion model and sensor models for a laser and for landmarks, so it can score any guessed pose. Still missing: what it should keep in memory between steps, the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-013-.title: Belief: What the Robot Knows
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-013-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot never sees its own position. What it can keep is a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in §4.2 The definition.: a probability for every place it might be, computed from the commands it gave and the readings it got.



Figure 1: A hallway of 10 cells, numbered 0 to 9 and joined into a loop, with doors in front of cells 1, 3 and 7; a robot stands in cell 1 and does not know it
With the landmark modelExplained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §4. The landmark measurement model, the robot has a motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density and sensor models, so it can score any guessed pose for one command or one reading. What still breaks: each score covers one moment, and nothing says what the robot should carry from one step to the next. This Note adds that memory, the belief.
Figure 1 shows the world of this Note: the same hallway of 10 cellsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §1. Overview as before, with the same layout and numbers, because a belief over 10 cells is 10 numbers we can draw and check by hand. A robot stands in a hallway of 10 cells, each 1 m long. The hallway is a loop: one step to the right of cell 9 is cell 0. There are doors in front of cells 1, 3 and 7, and all three look the same.
The robot has two things to go on:

a door sensor that reads “door” or “wall”, and is sometimes wrong;
its commands, such as “move 2 cells to the right”, which its wheels carry out only roughly.

The robot stands in cell 1, but nothing tells it so. A reading of “door” fits three cells. A move of “2 cells” may really be 1 or 3. So the question of this Note is: what should the robot keep in memory about where it is, so that it can act sensibly?
We answer it in steps:

what the robot really knows: the list of its commands and readings (Section 2);
a first summary of that list: the set of cells it could be in, and why a set is not enough (Section 3);
a better summary: a probability for every cell, the belief (Section 4);
the two probability tables that tell the robot how commands and readings change the belief (Section 5);
one picture of how states, commands and readings depend on each other, the hidden Markov model (G-2439)Hidden Markov model (HMM): A Markov chain whose states cannot be seen, where each state produces an observation that can, such as hidden robot cells producing “door” or “wall” readings; it is the model behind robot state estimation, speech recognition and many trackers. Explained in §6.3 Hidden Markov model. (Section 6).

The state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many is what the robot keeps track of, and the commands and readingsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §5.1 Measurements and controls are the two streams of data it receives. In symbols:

t is the time step, counted 1, 2, 3;
x_t is the state, the robot’s cell at time t, a cell number from 0 to 9 (cell 1 at t = 1);
u_t is the command at time t, such as “move 2”;
z_t is the reading at time t, “door” or “wall”.

2. What the robot knows: its history


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The robot cannot know its true cell. It can only know the commands it gave and the readings it got; that list is its information state (G-2431)Information state (history): Everything a robot knows at time t: its starting knowledge plus every command and every reading so far, such as (stay, door, move 2, door); every decision must be based on it, because the true state is never seen. Explained in §2.2 The information state: everything the robot knows..


2.1 Why the true cell is out of reach
The robot stands in cell 1, but its sensor reads “door” in front of three different cells, and it is sometimes wrong. The wheels slip, so the command “move 2” does not say exactly how far the robot went. Nothing the robot has ever received names its cell. Figure 2 sorts the pieces into what the robot cannot see (the top row) and what it can (the framed rows).

Figure 2: Top row, hidden: the true cells x1 = 1, x2 = 3, x3 = 5. Framed rows, known: the commands stay, move 2, move 2 and the readings door, door, wall. The frame is the history the robot knows at t = 3
The robot’s run in Figure 2 is the running example of this Note:





























Time tCommand u_tReading z_tTrue cell x_t (hidden)1staydoor12move 2door33move 2wall5
2.2 The information state: everything the robot knows
The framed part of Figure 2 is everything the robot knows at time t: what it knew at the start, followed by every command and every reading so far. This list is the information state (G-2431)Information state (history): Everything a robot knows at time t: its starting knowledge plus every command and every reading so far, such as (stay, door, move 2, door); every decision must be based on it, because the true state is never seen. Explained in §2.2 The information state: everything the robot knows., also called the history information state (LaValle §11.1.2). At time 2 it is the list (stay, door, move 2, door). Each new step adds one command and one reading.
Why give the list a name? Because it is the only thing a robot’s decisions can be based on. A rule such as “if you think you are at the second door, open it” has to be a rule on what the robot knows, not on its true cell, which it never sees (LaValle §11.1.3).
The trouble with the list is its length. The list grows by two entries every step and never shrinks. A robot that reads its sensor 10 times a second has, after one hour:
10 \times 3600 = 36{,}000 \text{ readings}
Storing and searching that whole list at every step is not practical. So we look for a short summary of the history that keeps everything the robot needs and throws away the rest (LaValle §11.2). Sections 3 and 4 give two such summaries.
3. Summary 1: the set of cells the robot could be in


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

We can keep the set of cells that agree with every command and reading: a move turns each cell into all the cells it can reach, and a reading keeps only the cells that agree with it. With a sensor that can be wrong, the set stops shrinking.


3.1 The set, step by step
A first thing to keep in memory, shorter than the history: the cells the robot could be in. Suppose for a moment that the sensor is never wrong. The reading “door” then means “one of the door cells”. So after the first reading the robot can be in:
\lbrace1, 3, 7 \rbrace
Next, the command “move 2” moves the robot 1, 2 or 3 cells. Every cell of the set becomes all the cells it can reach, and we collect them together (the move stage of Figure 3). The symbol \cup (union) means “all cells in either set”:
\lbrace2,3,4\rbrace\cup \lbrace4,5,6\rbrace\cup \lbrace8,9,0\rbrace
= \lbrace0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 \rbrace
The second reading “door” keeps only the cells of this set that are doors. The symbol \cap (intersection) means “cells in both sets”:
\lbrace0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 \rbrace\cap \lbrace1, 3, 7 \rbrace
= \lbrace3 \rbrace
Figure 3 plays these steps, one set per row. Watch the reading cross out the wall cells, each door cell fan out to the three cells the move can reach, and the second reading cross out every cell but cell 3. Its last stages replay the second reading with a sensor that can be wrong (Section 3.2).

3.2 Why a set is not enough
Now use the real sensor, which reads “door” at a wall 20 percent of the time. A reading of “door” is then possible in every cell. In symbols:

S is the set of cells the robot could be in before the reading, such as \lbrace0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 \rbrace after the move of Section 3.1;
\lbrace0, 1, \ldots, 9 \rbrace is the set of cells where “door” can be read, which is now all 10 cells.

So the intersection \cap removes nothing:
S \cap \lbrace0, 1, \ldots, 9 \rbrace= S
The set never shrinks, however many readings arrive (the last stages of Figure 3). Crossing places out only works for a perfect sensor, for the reason shown in why noisy sensors forbid crossing places outExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §3.3 Why noisy sensors forbid crossing places out: a wrong reading would cross out the true cell. The set also cannot say that cell 3 fits the readings much better than cell 9: both are simply “possible”. We need a summary that keeps a number for every cell, saying how strongly the readings point to it. Probabilities are that number.

Explained in §4.2 The definition. gives every cell the probability that the robot is there, given its whole history. A reading sharpens it; a move shifts it and blurs it.

4.3 A belief is not a position
The robot is always in exactly one cell. A belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in §4.2 The definition. of 0.19 on three cells does not mean the robot is spread over three places; it means the robot does not know which of the three it is in (Labbe ch.2). The belief describes the robot’s knowledge, not the world. For the same reason, the arrow for the true cell and the bars in Figure 4 are drawn separately: the bars can be wrong, and the true cell does not care.
4.4 Why the whole history appears in the definition
The definition conditions on every command and reading since the start, which looks like the long list we wanted to avoid. The history is there because the robot does not know its earlier cells either: if it knew its previous cell x_{t-1}, that one cell plus the latest command and reading would be enough, but it only has the history (PR §2.3.4). RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-014-.title: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-014-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. updates a robot’s belief one step at a time: a prediction step pushes the belief through the motion model after each command, and a correction step multiplies it by the measurement probability after each reading. The robot never needs to store its history.


So far the robot keeps a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition: a probability for every possible state, given every command and every reading since it started. That list is what still breaks. The list grows by one command and one reading at every step: a robot that reads its sensor 10 times a second holds 36,000 readings after an hour, and by its definition the belief must be recomputed from all of them. This Note adds the Bayes filter, which keeps only the last belief, and answers the question: how can a robot keep its belief up to date at every step, using only the newest command and the newest reading?

Figure 1: Thrun’s door world: a door that is open (left) or closed (right); a robot in front of it with an arm that can push the door and a sensor that reads open or closed
We leave the hallway, where the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition was a probability for each of 10 cells, for Thrun’s door world (Figure 1): 2 states instead of 10 cells, so every sum can be done by hand (PR §2.4.2). The grid filtersExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §1. Overview bring the filter back to the hallway. This Note covers:

one reading at a time, with Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof that remembers earlier readings (Section 3);
the filter itself, a prediction step (G-2447)Prediction step (motion update): The Bayes-filter step after a command: for each state, add up the probability of reaching it from every previous state, weighted by the belief in that state, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1}); it moves the belief with the robot and usually widens it, because the motion is uncertain; a near-certain command, such as a push that opens a door, can make the belief sharper. Explained in §4.2 The prediction step. and a correction step, worked on the door (Section 4);
why the two steps give the exact belief, and which three assumptions that needs (Section 5);
the same two steps on a continuous position, where sums become integrals (G-957)Integration: Finding the area under a curve by adding up infinitely many thin strips. Explained in: Probability Density Function and the CDF of a Continuous Variable, §3. Area under the curve is probability (Section 6);
why the belief is all the robot needs to keep (Section 7), and which later filters are this one in disguise (Section 8).

2. The door world


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

One state (the door, open or closed), two commands (push, do nothing), one noisy sensor. Its two probability tables are all the filter needs.


The robot does not know whether the door is open. The two tables that drive the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition describe the robot (PR §2.4.2); with them and its last belief, the filter never needs the list of past readings. At step t:

x_t is the state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many, the door at time t: open or closed;
x_{t-1} is the door one step earlier;
x_0 is the door at the start, before any command;
u_t is the command: push or do nothing (do nothing at t = 1, push at t = 2);
z_t is the reading: “sense open” or “sense closed” (“sense open” at both steps);
\text{bel}(x_t) is the robot’s belief, its probability for each door state at time t, a number from 0 to 1 (0.5 for open at the start).

The measurement probability (G-2435)Measurement probability: The probability of a sensor reading given the true state, p(z_t \mid x_t), such as 0.6 for reading “door” in front of a door; it tells the robot how well each state explains a reading. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §5.2 What the sensor reads in each place: the measurement probability p(z_t \mid x_t): the sensor reads “open” or “closed”, and is sometimes wrong.




















True doorp(sense open)p(sense closed)open0.60.4closed0.20.8
The numbers are the same as for the door sensor of the hallway.
The state transition probability (G-2434)State transition probability: The probability of the next state given the command and the previous state, p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}), such as 0.8 for “move 2” taking the robot from cell 1 to cell 3; it tells the robot how a command changes where it is. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §5.1 How a command moves the robot: the state transition probability p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}): the robot can push the door or do nothing.



































CommandDoor beforep(open after)p(closed after)pushopen10pushclosed0.80.2do nothingopen10do nothingclosed01
A push on a closed door fails one time in five, because the door is heavy. Doing nothing changes nothing.
The start. The robot has no idea, so its first belief is:
\text{bel}(x_0 = \text{open}) = 0.5
\text{bel}(x_0 = \text{closed}) = 0.5
The run. At t = 1 the robot does nothing and senses “open”. At t = 2 it pushes and senses “open” again. We want its belief after each step.
3. One reading at a time: Bayes’ theorem with past readings


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof turns “how likely is this reading in each state” into “how likely is each state given the reading”. Applied again with the first answer as the new prior, it adds a second reading, provided the readings are independent once the state is known.


3.1 Why the robot needs Bayes’ theorem
First the readings alone: can the robot take in a new reading without going back to the old ones? For now, nobody touches the door; the robot only reads. Its table tells it p(z \mid x): how often the sensor reads “open” for each kind of door. The robot needs the other direction, p(x \mid z): given the reading, how likely is each kind of door? For one reading:

x is the door, open or closed;
z is the reading, here “sense open”;
p(x) is the prior (G-1565)Prior: The probability of an event before any evidence is seen. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §3. The names of the four parts, the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition in each door before the reading, 0.5 for open and 0.5 for closed;
p(z \mid x) is the chance of the reading given the door, from the table (0.6 for an open door, 0.2 for a closed one);
p(z) is the overall chance of the reading, 0.4 for “sense open” (found below);
p(x \mid z) is the posterior (G-1536)Posterior: The probability of an event after the evidence is taken into account. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §3. The names of the four parts, the belief in each door after the reading (0.75 for open, found below).

Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof turns one into the other:
p(x \mid z) = \frac{p(z \mid x)\ p(x)}{p(z)}
First reading, “sense open”. Multiply each prior by how well that door explains the reading:
\text{open: } 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.3
\text{closed: } 0.2 \times 0.5 = 0.1
The two products are not yet probabilities, because they add to 0.4, not 1. Their sum is the evidence (G-718)Evidence: The overall chance of seeing what we observed, counted over every possible hypothesis, written P(E). Bayes’ theorem divides by it: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §3. The names of the four parts p(z), the overall chance of the reading, by the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview. Divide by it:
p(\text{open} \mid z_1) = 0.3 / 0.4 = 0.75
p(\text{closed} \mid z_1) = 0.1 / 0.4 = 0.25
Dividing by the sum is the same as multiplying by its inverse, written \eta (eta):
\eta = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5
This number is the normaliser (G-2382)Normalizer \eta: The factor that rescales a set of numbers, or a density, so that they add up (or integrate) to 1; it is always one over the current total: the sum of the products in the Bayes filter (1/0.4 = 2.5 after a reading in the door world), the area under the cut curve in the beam model (1/0.655 = 1.53). Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range: whatever factor makes the products add to 1, the same job it does for the cut Gaussian of the beam modelExplained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range. We never need p(z) from anywhere else, because it is always the sum of the products (PR §2.2).
3.2 A second reading: Bayes’ theorem with background knowledge
One reading leaves a 0.25 chance of a closed door. To be surer, the robot reads again and again gets “open”. Now the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition must depend on both readings. For the second reading:

x is the door, open or closed;
z is the new reading, here the second reading z_2, “sense open”;
C is the background knowledge, everything known before z, here the first reading z_1, “sense open”.

Bayes’ theorem still works if every term also carries the earlier readings C behind the bar:
p(x \mid z, C) = \frac{p(z \mid x, C)\ p(x \mid C)}{p(z \mid C)}
The formula is Bayes’ rule with background knowledge (G-2452)Bayes’ rule with background knowledge: Bayes’ theorem with an extra condition C in every term, p(x \mid z, C) = p(z \mid x, C)\ p(x \mid C) / p(z \mid C), such as earlier readings; it lets the posterior after one reading serve as the prior for the next. Explained in §3.2 A second reading: Bayes’ theorem with background knowledge. (PR §2.2). The rule holds for the same reason as the plain rule: the joint probability of x and z given C can be split two ways by the multiplication rule (G-2212)Multiplication rule: The chance that both A and B happen is the chance of B times the chance of A given B: P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) \times P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §5. The multiplication rule, and setting the two equal gives the formula.
With z_2 in place of z and z_1 in place of C, two of the terms are known:

p(x \mid z_1) is the answer of Section 3.1: the old posterior becomes the new prior;
p(z_2 \mid x, z_1) asks how likely the second reading is, given the door and the first reading.

Here the robot makes an assumption: once the state of the door is known, the first reading tells nothing more about the second. Each reading is the door plus its own independent sensor noise. So:
p(z_2 \mid x, z_1) = p(z_2 \mid x)
The assumption is conditional independence (G-443)Conditional independence: Independence that holds once a third variable is known: given the class, knowing one feature tells nothing more about another. Naive Bayes assumes it so it can multiply one probability per feature. Explained in: Naive Bayes: The Mathematics, §5. Step 3: the naive assumption: independence that holds given the state. The assumption does not say that the two readings are independent on their own. They are not, as the robot’s own numbers show:
p(z_2 = \text{open}) = 0.6 \times 0.5 + 0.2 \times 0.5
= 0.4
p(z_2 = \text{open} \mid z_1 = \text{open})
= 0.6 \times 0.75 + 0.2 \times 0.25 = 0.5
A first “open” makes a second “open” more likely (0.5 instead of 0.4), because it makes an open door more likely. Only when the door is known does that link disappear.
Second reading, “sense open”. Same recipe, with 0.75 and 0.25 as the prior:
\text{open: } 0.6 \times 0.75 = 0.45
\text{closed: } 0.2 \times 0.25 = 0.05
\eta = 1 / (0.45 + 0.05) = 2
p(\text{open} \mid z_1, z_2) = 2 \times 0.45 = 0.9
p(\text{closed} \mid z_1, z_2) = 2 \times 0.05 = 0.1
Figure 2 plays both readings. For each one, watch the two bars shrink when multiplied by 0.6 and 0.2, then grow back when rescaled by \eta, one over their sum: the belief in an open door climbs from 0.5 to 0.75, then to 0.9.

Figure 2: Animation of the two readings. Each panel holds the belief in an open and a closed door (blue bars). For each reading, the bars of the belief before it are multiplied by p(z | x), the chance of “sense open” given the door: 0.6 for open, 0.2 for closed. The products turn grey: they add to 0.4 after the first reading and 0.5 after the second, not 1, so they are not yet probabilities. Then both are multiplied by η (eta), one over their sum (2.5, then 2), and grow back into blue bars that add to 1. The last frame shows the belief before any reading (0.5 for open), after the first sense open (0.75) and after the second (0.9)
The robot never went back to the first reading: it kept one number, 0.75, and reused it. That reuse is the whole idea of a filter. So far, though, nothing has changed the door between readings.
4. The Bayes filter: predict, then correct


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each step has two parts. Prediction: after the command, add up every way of reaching each state. Correction: after the reading, multiply by the measurement probability and rescale.


4.1 Why a moving world needs a second step
Section 3 kept only the last answer, but it assumed nothing changes the door. Once the robot pushes, the door may change between readings, and a robot that drives changes its own position. The belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the robot’s probability for each door state, must now follow two kinds of event: commands, which change the state and usually add doubt, and readings, which add knowledge (see the predicted belief (G-2436))Predicted belief: The belief after the latest command but before the latest reading, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t-1}, u_{1:t}); it separates the doubt a move adds from the knowledge a reading brings. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.5 The predicted belief: after the move, before the reading.
The direct way to know the belief is to recompute it from the whole history at every step (Figure 3, the archive row). Recomputing from the history is an archive, not a filter: after an hour at 10 readings a second, it holds 36,000 readings and keeps growing. The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. keeps only the last belief and updates it with the newest command and reading (Figure 3, the filter row). Updating a belief from the previous belief in this way is recursive state estimation (G-2450)Recursive state estimation: Estimating the state by updating the previous estimate with only the newest command and reading, instead of recomputing from the whole history; it keeps the work per step fixed however long the robot runs. Explained in §4.1 Why a moving world needs a second step. (PR §2.4).
Figure 3 runs both ways on the door for two steps (the numbers are worked out in Section 4.3). Watch the archive gain two entries at every step and read them all again, while the filter turns its one stored belief into the next and drops the command and reading it used: both reach the same 0.983, as Section 5 proves.

Archive row: every command u_t and reading z_t is stored (grey boxes), and the belief bel(x_t), the probability of each door state at time t, is recomputed from all of them. Filter row: only the last belief is stored (blue box); the newest command (purple) and reading (green) turn it into the new belief, and then the old belief, the command and the reading are dropped. Both give a belief in open of 0.5 at the start, 0.75 after step 1 (do nothing, sense open) and 0.983 after step 2 (push, sense open). The last frame shows any step t: the archive keeps growing, 36,000 readings after an hour at 10 a second, while the filter stores one belief
4.2 The prediction step
After the command, before the reading, the robot wants its predicted belief (G-2436)Predicted belief: The belief after the latest command but before the latest reading, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t-1}, u_{1:t}); it separates the doubt a move adds from the knowledge a reading brings. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.5 The predicted belief: after the move, before the reading \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t). The robot does not know the previous state, so it considers every previous state, asks how likely the command takes it to x_t, and weights that by how much it believed in that previous state. At step t:

x_{t-1} is the door before the command, open or closed;
x_t is the door after the command, open or closed;
u_t is the command, push at t = 2;
\text{bel}(x_{t-1}) is the belief before the command, a number from 0 to 1 (0.75 for open after t = 1);
p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}) is the state transition probability of Section 2, the chance that the command turns door x_{t-1} into door x_t (0.8 for a push that opens a closed door);
\sum_{x_{t-1}} adds over every possible previous state, here open and closed;
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) is the predicted belief, after the command and before the reading, a number from 0 to 1 (0.95 for open at t = 2).

Adding up every way of reaching x_t is the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview:
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum_{x_{t-1}} p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})
\times\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1})
The formula is the prediction step (G-2447)Prediction step (motion update): The Bayes-filter step after a command: for each state, add up the probability of reaching it from every previous state, weighted by the belief in that state, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1}); it moves the belief with the robot and usually widens it, because the motion is uncertain; a near-certain command, such as a push that opens a door, can make the belief sharper. Explained in §4.2 The prediction step., also called the motion update or time update (PR §2.4.1).
At t = 2, the command is “push”, and the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition after t = 1 is 0.75 open (Section 4.3 computes it). Figure 4 draws the four paths. Two of them end with the door open:
\overline{\text{bel}}(\text{open}) = 1 \times 0.75 + 0.8 \times 0.25
= 0.75 + 0.2 = 0.95
The other two end closed:
\overline{\text{bel}}(\text{closed}) = 0 \times 0.75 + 0.2 \times 0.25
= 0.05
In Figure 4, watch the bars as each path is taken: the 0.75 on open stays, and the closed bar’s 0.25 splits, 0.2 moving to open and 0.05 staying. The predicted belief is 0.95 for open and 0.05 for closed.

\overline{\text{bel}}(\text{closed}) = 0 \times 0.5 + 1 \times 0.5 = 0.5

z_t is the reading, “sense open” at t = 2;
p(z_t \mid x_t) is the measurement probability of Section 2, the chance of the reading given the door (0.6 for “sense open” at an open door);

\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition after the reading, a number from 0 to 1 (0.983 for open at t = 2).

The formula is the correction step (G-2448)Correction step (measurement update): The Bayes-filter step after a reading: multiply each state’s predicted belief by the measurement probability p(z_t \mid x_t) and rescale so the beliefs add to 1; it raises the states that explain the reading and sharpens the belief. Explained in §4.3 The correction step., also called the measurement update (PR §2.4.1). The step multiplies each state’s predicted belief by how well that state explains the reading, then rescales with \eta so the beliefs (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. At t = 2, the reading is again “sense open”:
\text{open: } 0.6 \times 0.95 = 0.57
\text{closed: } 0.2 \times 0.05 = 0.01

4.4 The algorithm
Together the two steps are the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. (PR §2.4.1). With the symbols listed in Section 4.2 and Section 4.3, for every possible state x_t:

Predict: \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum_{x_{t-1}} p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1}).
Correct: \text{bel}(x_t) = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_t)\ \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t).

Then return \text{bel}(x_t) and wait for the next command and reading.

Python: one step of the filter for a finite set of states.
import numpy as np
T_push = np.array([[1.0, 0.0],    # from open: to open, closed
                   [0.8, 0.2]])   # from closed
p_z = np.array([0.6, 0.2])        # p(sense open | open, closed)
bel = np.array([0.75, 0.25])      # belief after t = 1
bel_bar = bel @ T_push            # predict: [0.95, 0.05]
bel = p_z * bel_bar
bel = bel / bel.sum()             # correct: [0.983, 0.017]

Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition in open and in closed, (0.75, 0.25) after t = 1;
T_push is a 2 × 2 matrix of transition probabilities for a push: row i is the door before, column j the door after, so the closed row is (0.8, 0.2);
