5. Why the two steps give the exact belief


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Starting from the definition of the belief, five steps lead to the filter: Bayes’ rule, a Markov assumption for readings, the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview, a Markov assumption for motion, and the assumption that the newest command says nothing about the past.


The two steps threw the history away. Here we show that nothing was lost: they give exactly p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}), the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition as defined over the whole history, and we name every assumption on the way (PR §2.4.3). The state x_t, the command u_t, the reading z_t and the two probability tables are those of Section 2. The other symbols:

z_{1:t} is all readings z_1, \ldots, z_t, from time 1 to t, (“sense open”, “sense open”) at t = 2;
z_{1:t-1} is all readings before time t, only z_1 = “sense open” at t = 2;
u_{1:t} is all commands u_1, \ldots, u_t, (do nothing, push) at t = 2;
\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief, the probability of each state given all readings and commands, a number from 0 to 1 (0.983 for open at t = 2);
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) is the belief before the newest reading z_t, as in Section 4.2 (0.95 for open at t = 2);
\eta is the factor that rescales the beliefs so they add to 1 (1.724 at t = 2).

Line 0, the definition. Nothing is assumed:
\text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t},\ u_{1:t})
Line 1, Bayes’ rule with background knowledge. Split the newest reading z_t off from the rest; everything older is the background C of Section 3.2. The denominator does not depend on x_t, so it becomes the normaliser (G-2382)Normalizer \eta: The factor that rescales a set of numbers, or a density, so that they add up (or integrate) to 1; it is always one over the current total: the sum of the products in the Bayes filter (1/0.4 = 2.5 after a reading in the door world), the area under the cut curve in the beam model (1/0.655 = 1.53). Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §4.1 Measurement noise: a Gaussian around the expected range \eta:
\text{bel}(x_t) = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_t,\ z_{1:t-1},\ u_{1:t})
\times\ p(x_t \mid z_{1:t-1},\ u_{1:t})
This line is exact; it is a rule of probability.
Line 2, the Markov assumption for readings. If the state x_t is known, the past readings and commands tell nothing more about the current reading. The assumption is the same as for the door readings in Section 3.2, and the arrow structure of the dynamic Bayes network (G-2441)Dynamic Bayes network: A Bayesian network that repeats the same variables at every time step, such as states, commands and readings of a robot; it shows which variable depends on which over time, so a whole run’s probability splits into small factors. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §6.2 The robot as a dynamic Bayes network:
p(z_t \mid x_t,\ z_{1:t-1},\ u_{1:t}) = p(z_t \mid x_t)
The second factor of Line 1 is the predicted belief (G-2436)Predicted belief: The belief after the latest command but before the latest reading, \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t-1}, u_{1:t}); it separates the doubt a move adds from the knowledge a reading brings. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.5 The predicted belief: after the move, before the reading, by its definition. So:
\text{bel}(x_t) = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_t)\ \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t)
The result is the correction step (G-2448)Correction step (measurement update): The Bayes-filter step after a reading: multiply each state’s predicted belief by the measurement probability p(z_t \mid x_t) and rescale so the beliefs add to 1; it raises the states that explain the reading and sharpens the belief. Explained in §4.3 The correction step.. One assumption has paid for it: a history that grows forever dropped out of the measurement term.
Line 3, the law of total probability. We now unpack the predicted belief. We do not know where the robot was at t - 1, so we bring in every possible previous state and weight each by how likely it was. The sum brings in x_{t-1} on purpose, to reach the previous belief:
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum_{x_{t-1}} p(x_t \mid x_{t-1},\ z_{1:t-1},\ u_{1:t})
\times\ p(x_{t-1} \mid z_{1:t-1},\ u_{1:t})
This line is exact.
Line 4, the Markov assumption for motion. If we know the previous state, the older readings and commands tell nothing more about where the newest command takes the robot; only u_t still matters:
p(x_t \mid x_{t-1},\ z_{1:t-1},\ u_{1:t})
= p(x_t \mid u_t,\ x_{t-1})
Line 5, the newest command does not tell us the past. The last factor of Line 3 is the belief about x_{t-1}, except that it also knows u_t, the command given after time t - 1. We assume a command chosen now says nothing about where the robot was:

= p(x_{t-1} \mid z_{1:t-1},\ u_{1:t-1})
= \text{bel}(x_{t-1})
This assumption can fail. A robot with collision avoidance never commands “drive 20 cm forward” while standing in front of a wall, so that command does tell us the robot was not at the wall. In most cases the command carries no such hint, and we drop it (PR §2.4.3).
The result. Putting Lines 4 and 5 into Line 3:
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \sum_{x_{t-1}} p(x_t \mid u_t,\ x_{t-1})
\times\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1})

The derivation used three assumptions:

readings depend only on the current state (Line 2);
the next state depends only on the previous state and the newest command (Line 4);
the newest command does not tell us about the previous state (Line 5).

Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. is not an approximation; it gives the exact belief. 7. The belief is the probabilistic information state


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the robot’s probability for each state, can be updated from the previous belief, the newest command and the newest reading alone. So it carries everything the history knew, and the robot can throw the history away.


Why may the robot throw its history away? Because Section 5 showed that the new belief needs only the old belief, the newest command u_t and the newest reading z_t: whatever the history knew, the belief already holds. 8. One equation, many filters


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Every filter in the rest of this chapter is the Bayes filter with a particular way of storing the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the robot’s probability for each state.


The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in §4.4 The algorithm. keeps only the last belief, but it says what to compute, not how to store that belief over a continuous pose (position and heading), where the prediction sums over infinitely many previous states. Each practical filter answers that differently (PR §2.5):

grid filtersExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2. The histogram filter: chop the space into cells and keep one probability per cell, as in the hallway; the sum stays a sum;
particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step: keep a cloud of sample states; dense clouds mean high belief;
Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system: assume every belief is a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, a single bell-shaped curve, and keep only its mean and variance;
extended Kalman filter (G-2520)Extended Kalman filter (EKF): The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §4.1 The algorithm: the Kalman filter for motion and sensor models whose graphs are curves, not straight lines: nonlinear functions (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §1. Overview.

Each is a different bet about what shape the belief is allowed to have. Knowing the Bayes filter tells us what each of them is trying to compute, and what breaks when its bet is wrong.

What the normal distribution isAnother name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements.Particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by stepA Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors.Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian systemThe Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible.Extended Kalman filter (EKF) (G-2520)Extended Kalman filter (EKF): The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §4.1 The algorithmThe Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models.Nonlinear function (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §1. OverviewA function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-015-.title: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-015-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Chop the robot’s space into cells and keep one probability per cell: the Bayes filter then becomes plain arithmetic on a list of numbers. The same list of numbers also answers two questions about the past: where the robot most likely was, and which whole path it most likely took.



Figure 1: A hallway of 10 cells, numbered 0 to 9 and joined into a loop, with doors in front of cells 1, 3 and 7; a robot stands in cell 1 and does not know it
The robot can now update its belief from the newest command and reading alone, with the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm. What still breaks is its prediction step, a sum over every possible previous state. In the door worldExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §2. The door world that sum had 2 terms; a position along the hallway can be any number of metres, so the sum has infinitely many terms and cannot be done as written. This Note adds one number per cell, and answers: how does a computer run the Bayes filter, and what else can the same numbers tell us?
We go back to the hallway (Figure 1) on which the robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, its probability for every cell, was defined, with the same numbers:

10 cells of 1 m in a loop, with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7;
a door sensor that reads “door” with probability 0.6 at a door and 0.2 at a wall;
a command “move 2” that moves the robot 1, 2 or 3 cells with probability 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1.

The Note covers:

the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells.: one probability per cell, updated by multiplying (sensing) and sliding (moving) (Section 2);
how to cut a real, continuous space into cells: fixed cells or cells that adapt to the belief (Section 3);
the binary Bayes filter for a yes-or-no state that does not change, run in log odds (G-1116)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1, the logarithm of the yes-to-no odds (Section 4);
looking back: the smoothed belief at an earlier time, and the most likely whole path (Section 5).

2. The histogram filter


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Keep one probability per cell: sensing multiplies every cell by how well it explains the reading, then rescales. Moving slides the list along and blurs it with the motion probabilities.


2.1 Why cells
A continuous position, such as “3.42 m along the hallway”, can take infinitely many values, and a computer can only store a finite list. So we cut the hallway into cells, here 10 cells of 1 m, and keep one probability for each: the probability that the robot is somewhere in that cell. Cutting a range into cells is the same move as discretization (G-619)Discretization: Turning a continuous column into a discrete one by cutting its range into intervals (bins), such as ages 0–18, 18–60 and 60+; it turns endless values into a few groups that a model or a table can handle. Explained in: Binning and Binarization: Equal Width, Equal Frequency and k-means Binning, §1. Overview of a feature into bins, and the list of probabilities, drawn as bars, is a histogram (G-899)Histogram: A bar chart of how many values fall in each equal range (bin) of a numerical column; it shows the shape of a distribution at a glance: where values pile up, how far they spread and whether there are several peaks. Explained in: Univariate Analysis: Exploring One Column at a Time, §6. Histogram of the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition.
The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm run on such a list of cells is the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. (PR §4.1). When the states are finite to begin with, as in the door world, the same algorithm is called the discrete Bayes filter (Labbe ch.2). The sum of the prediction step now has only 10 terms, so it can be done exactly.
2.2 Sense: multiply, then rescale
The robot has no idea where it is, so each cell starts at 0.1. It reads “door”. Figure 2 runs the four stages in turn: watch each bar shrink as it is multiplied by its cell’s chance of a “door” reading, the 10 products stack up to 0.32, and the division by 0.32 grow them back until they add to 1, with each door cell now three times as tall as a wall cell.

Figure 2: The hallway’s 10 cells, with the doors at cells 1, 3 and 7 shaded. The bars start at 0.1, the prior. Each bar is multiplied by p(door | cell), the chance of reading door in that cell (0.6 at a door, 0.2 at a wall), and shrinks to 0.06 or 0.02. The 10 products stack one by one into the sum column, which reaches 0.32. Dividing every product by 0.32 grows them to 0.1875 at the doors and 0.0625 at the walls. Last frame: the new belief, with the prior 0.1 as a dashed line
Multiply each cell by the probability of the reading in that cell:
\text{door cell: } 0.1 \times 0.6 = 0.06
\text{wall cell: } 0.1 \times 0.2 = 0.02
Add the 10 products, 3 door cells and 7 wall cells:
3 \times 0.06 + 7 \times 0.02 = 0.32
Rescale by dividing every product by 0.32, so the cells add to 1 again:
\text{door cell: } 0.06 / 0.32 = 0.1875
\text{wall cell: } 0.02 / 0.32 = 0.0625
Multiplying and rescaling is the correction step of the Bayes filter, done cell by cell (Labbe ch.2). The robot reads “door” three times as often at a door as at a wall, and after the update each door cell holds three times the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition of a wall cell.
2.3 Move: shift, then blur
Next the robot moves 2 cells. If the move were exact, every probability would simply travel 2 cells to the right, wrapping round the loop (Figure 3, middle). But the move is 1 cell with probability 0.1 and 3 cells with probability 0.1, so some belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition also lands one cell short or one cell too far (Figure 3, right).
Make interactive
Figure 3: Left: the belief after reading door, 0.1875 at cells 1, 3 and 7. Middle: shifted exactly 2 cells, 0.1875 at cells 3, 5 and 9. Right: shifted and blurred by the 0.1/0.8/0.1 move, 0.1625 at cells 3, 5 and 9 and 0.0875 at cell 4
Which old cells can end in cell 3? Cell 2 (by moving 1), cell 1 (by moving 2) and cell 0 (by moving 3). Each contributes its old belief times the probability of that move:
\text{new cell 3} = 0.1 \times 0.0625
+\ 0.8 \times 0.1875
+\ 0.1 \times 0.0625
= 0.1625
Adding up the weighted old cells is the prediction step of the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm: the law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. Overview with three terms instead of ten, because only three old cells can reach each new one.
Every new cell is built the same way, with the same three weights, slid along the hallway. Figure 4 builds the whole predicted belief this way, one cell at a time.

Figure 4: Top: the old belief with the three cells that can reach the new cell highlighted and weighted 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1. Bottom: the new belief filled in cell by cell; new cell 3 = 0.1 x 0.0625 + 0.8 x 0.1875 + 0.1 x 0.0625 = 0.1625
The list of weights, here (0.1, 0.8, 0.1), is the motion kernel (G-2462)Motion kernel: The short list of move probabilities, such as (0.1, 0.8, 0.1) for one cell short, exact, one cell too far, slid along the belief in the prediction step; it spreads each cell’s belief over the cells the robot may have reached. Explained in §2.3 Move: shift, then blur.. Sliding a small list of weights along a longer list and adding the products at each position is a convolution (G-481)Convolution operation: Sliding a small filter over an input and, at each position, multiplying cell by cell and adding up, so the output (a feature map) is large where the input contains the filter’s pattern, such as an edge. Explained in: The Convolution Operation, §6. The convolution operation, the same operation a CNN filter performs on an image (Labbe ch.2). Convolution is valid here because the move’s error does not depend on where the robot is: the same kernel applies in every cell.
2.4 Moving without looking loses everything
What if the robot keeps moving and never reads its sensor? Figure 5 starts it sure that it is in cell 1 and repeats “move 2”.

Figure 5: After 1 move the highest cell holds 0.80, after 3 moves 0.56, after 10 moves 0.29, after 80 moves 0.11: the belief flattens towards 0.1 in every cell
Each move spreads the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition of every cell over three cells, so the highest cell’s belief shrinks:





















Moves without a reading0131080Highest cell1.000.800.560.290.11
The belief tends to 0.1 in every cell, where the robot started before it knew anything. A prediction can only lose information; only readings bring it back (Labbe ch.2).
2.5 Sense and move together
A real robot alternates: move, read, move, read. Figure 6 runs seven steps; t counts them from 1 to 7. The true robot starts in cell 1 and really moves 2 cells each time (cells 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 1, 3). Every reading is correct except at t = 5, where the sensor says “door” in front of the wall of cell 9.

Figure 6: Seven steps of the histogram filter: orange frames show the predicted belief after each move, blue frames the belief after each reading; the tallest bar follows the true cell except at t = 5, after the wrong reading, when it jumps to cell 3; at t = 6 and t = 7 it is back on the true cell
The tallest bar at each step:













































t1234567True cell1357913Tallest bar1, 3, 7 (tied)357313Its belief0.190.310.300.420.320.370.47
The wrong reading at t = 5 moves the tallest bar to cell 3, a door. But the true cell 9 keeps a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition of 0.24, because one reading never sets a cell to zero. Two correct readings later the filter is back on the true cell with 0.47. A filter that kept only one best guess would have been lost at t = 5 (Labbe ch.2).
2.6 The formal version
With the cells numbered 0 to 9, at time step t:

k is the number of a cell after the move, 0 to 9;
i is the number of a cell before the move, 0 to 9;
p_{i,t-1} is the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition in cell i one step earlier, a number from 0 to 1 (0.1875 for cell 1 after the first reading);
p(x_k \mid u_t,\ x_i) is the chance that the command u_t takes the robot from cell i to cell k (0.8 for “move 2” from cell 1 to cell 3);
\bar p_{k,t} is the predicted belief in cell k, after the move and before the reading (0.1625 for cell 3 at t = 2);
p(z_t \mid x_k) is the chance of the reading z_t when the robot is in cell k (0.6 for “door” at a door, 0.2 at a wall);
\eta is the factor that rescales the cells so they add to 1, one over the sum of the products (the sum is 0.32 after the first reading, Section 2.2);
p_{k,t} is the belief in cell k at time t, a number from 0 to 1 (0.3095 for cell 3 at t = 2).

The histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. is (PR §4.1.1):
\bar p_{k,t} = \sum_{i} p(x_k \mid u_t,\ x_i)\ p_{i,t-1}
p_{k,t} = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_k)\ \bar p_{k,t}
The first line is the prediction step with the sum over the old cells i; the second is the correction step. Both lines visit every cell, so one step costs a fixed amount of work per cell.

Python: the hallway filter, using np.roll to shift a list round the loop.
import numpy as np
door = np.isin(np.arange(10), [1, 3, 7])
def sense(bel, z):           # z = True: reads "door"
    p = np.where(door, 0.6, 0.2)
    if not z:
        p = 1 - p
    return p * bel / (p * bel).sum()
def move(bel):               # 1, 2 or 3 cells
    return (0.1 * np.roll(bel, 1)
            + 0.8 * np.roll(bel, 2)
            + 0.1 * np.roll(bel, 3))
bel = sense(np.full(10, 0.1), True)   # 0.1875 at doors
bel = sense(move(bel), True)          # 0.3095 at cell 3

The notebook RO-015-grid-filters.ipynb runs every example in this Note. Ten cells of 1 m make the sum exact on the hallway, but they place the robot only to the nearest metre.
3. Cutting a real space into cells


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Fine cells give an accurate belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the robot’s probability for each cell, but their number explodes with the size of the space and the number of state variables. A static decomposition fixes the cells in advance; an adaptive one makes cells small only where the belief needs them.


3.1 Why the number of cells explodes
Cells turned the sum over infinitely many positions into 10 terms, at a price: with cells of 1 m, the robot’s position is never known better than “somewhere in this metre”. Smaller cells give a sharper answer, but every cell costs memory and time, because both steps visit every cell. A real floor robot has a pose, its position and heading (see pose (G-2280))Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, so the grid has three directions. On a 30 m by 30 m floor (Fox 1999):

the position along the floor runs from 0 to 30 m in cells of 15 cm;
the position across the floor runs from 0 to 30 m in cells of 15 cm;
the heading, the direction the robot faces, runs from 0° to 360° in steps of 2°.

Counting the cells:
\frac{30}{0.15} = 200 \text{ cells along the floor}
\frac{30}{0.15} = 200 \text{ cells across the floor}
\frac{360}{2} = 180 \text{ headings}
200 \times 200 \times 180 = 7{,}200{,}000 \text{ cells}
Halving the cell size multiplies the count by 4 for the position alone, and each extra state variable, such as speed, multiplies it again by the number of its values (Labbe ch.2). Fox, Burgard and Thrun found that updating 7.2 million cells at every reading was too slow for the computers of 1999 (Fox 1999).
3.2 Static and adaptive decomposition
Most of those millions of cells hold a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition close to zero: the robot is not inside a wall or at the far end of the building. Two ways of cutting the space follow from that (PR §4.1.4):

A static decomposition (G-2464)Static decomposition: Cutting the state space into cells fixed before the robot starts, usually a regular grid such as 15 cm cells and 2° headings; simple, but it spends as much work on empty regions as where the robot is. Explained in §3.2 Static and adaptive decomposition. fixes the cells before the robot starts, whatever the belief turns out to be. A regular grid of equal cells is the usual choice (Fox 1999). A fixed grid is simple, and every cell is updated the same way, but it spends as much work on empty regions as on the region where the robot is.
An adaptive decomposition (G-2465)Adaptive (dynamic) decomposition: Cutting the state space into cells that change with the belief: small cells where the belief is high, large cells where it is near zero, as in a quadtree; it gives fine detail with far fewer cells. Explained in §3.2 Static and adaptive decomposition., also called a dynamic decomposition, changes the cells as the belief changes: small cells where the belief is high, large cells where it is near zero. A common way is a quadtree, which splits a square into four only where more detail is needed (ShanghaiTech slides; Fox 1999, §6).


Figure 7: Left: an 8 m by 8 m floor cut into 64 fixed 1 m cells, with the belief concentrated in one spot. Right: the same floor cut adaptively into 19 cells: 4 m cells where the belief is near zero, down to 0.5 m cells at the peak
Figure 7 compares the two on an 8 m by 8 m floor. The fixed grid uses 64 cells of 1 m. The adaptive one uses 19 cells, yet its smallest cells (0.5 m) are finer than the fixed grid’s where the belief peaks. The price is bookkeeping: cells must be split and merged as the belief moves. The smallest grid of all has just 2 cells.
4. The binary Bayes filter


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

For a yes-or-no state that never changes, each reading multiplies the odds by a fixed factor. In log odds (G-1116)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1, the logarithm of the odds, that becomes adding a fixed number, which is fast and does not round to 0 or 1.


4.1 A state that does not change
The smallest grid has 2 cells, open and closed. Go back to the door worldExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §2. The door world, but now nobody touches the door: it is open or closed, and it stays that way while the robot reads its sensor again and again. A state that the robot’s commands do not change is a static state (G-2467)Static state: A state that the robot’s commands do not change while it is being estimated, such as a door nobody touches; the prediction step then does nothing and only readings update the belief. Explained in §4.1 A state that does not change. (PR §4.2). With a static state the prediction step does nothing (the belief (G-2433), the robot’s probability for each door state, before a step equals the belief after it)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, so only the correction step is left.
The same situation appears in mapping: whether one small square of the floor is occupied by an obstacle is a yes-or-no question about something that does not move. A map built this way keeps one such filter per square (PR §4.2; Freiburg mapping slides).
4.2 Each reading multiplies the odds
The odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1 of the door being open compare the two possibilities. In symbols:

p(\text{open}) is the probability that the door is open, 0.5 at the start;
p(\text{closed}) is the probability that it is closed, 0.5 at the start.

The odds are their ratio:
\text{odds} = \frac{p(\text{open})}{p(\text{closed})}
Why does a reading multiply the odds? Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof gives each door state’s probability after a reading, with the same denominator for both: the overall chance of the reading. For one “sense open” from 0.5, the sensor reads it with chance 0.6 at an open door, 0.2 at a closed one and 0.4 overallExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §3.1 Why the robot needs Bayes’ theorem:
\text{open: } \frac{0.6 \times 0.5}{0.4} = 0.75
\text{closed: } \frac{0.2 \times 0.5}{0.4} = 0.25
\text{new odds} = \frac{0.75}{0.25}
= \frac{0.6 \times 0.5}{0.4} \div \frac{0.2 \times 0.5}{0.4}
= \frac{0.6 \times 0.5}{0.2 \times 0.5}
= \frac{0.6}{0.2} \times \frac{0.5}{0.5}
= 3 \times 1 = 3
The same steps for any reading:

z is the reading, “sense open” or “sense closed”;
p(z \mid \text{open}) is the chance of that reading when the door is open (0.6 for “sense open”);
p(z \mid \text{closed}) is the chance of that reading when the door is closed (0.2 for “sense open”);
p(z) is the overall chance of the reading, the same denominator in both lines (0.4 for “sense open”);
p(\text{open} \mid z) is the probability that the door is open after the reading (0.75 after one “sense open” from 0.5);
p(\text{closed} \mid z) is the probability that it is closed after the reading (0.25 after one “sense open” from 0.5).

p(\text{open} \mid z) = \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})\ p(\text{open})}{p(z)}
p(\text{closed} \mid z) = \frac{p(z \mid \text{closed})\ p(\text{closed})}{p(z)}
\text{new odds} = \frac{p(\text{open} \mid z)}{p(\text{closed} \mid z)}
= \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})\ p(\text{open})}{p(z)}
\div\ \frac{p(z \mid \text{closed})\ p(\text{closed})}{p(z)}
= \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})\ p(\text{open})}{p(z \mid \text{closed})\ p(\text{closed})}
= \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})}{p(z \mid \text{closed})} \times \frac{p(\text{open})}{p(\text{closed})}
The first fraction, the ratio of the two measurement probabilities, is the Bayes factor (G-2215)Bayes factor: A number that says how strongly the evidence favours yes over no: how many times more likely the evidence is if the answer is yes than if it is no, P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{yes}) / P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{no}). Multiplying the prior odds by it gives the posterior odds. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §6.1 The size of the update: the Bayes factor; the second is the old odds:
\text{new odds} = \text{old odds} \times \frac{p(z \mid \text{open})}{p(z \mid \text{closed})}
We never need p(z), whose inverse is the normaliser \eta of the correction step, which is why odds are convenient.
The factor is 3 for “sense open”, as above. For “sense closed” it is:
0.4 / 0.8 = 0.5
Starting from odds of 1 (that is, 0.5 against 0.5), two readings of “open” give:
1 \times 3 \times 3 = 9
Odds of 9 mean 9 parts open to 1 part closed:
p(\text{open}) = \frac{9}{9 + 1} = 0.9
the same 0.9 as in the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm.
4.3 Log odds turn the products into sums
Taking the logarithm turns a product into a sum. The natural log of the odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1 is the log odds (G-1116)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1. In symbols:

p is the probability that the door is open, a number from 0 to 1 (0.5 at the start);
1 - p is the probability that it is closed;
\ln is the natural logarithm;
l is the log odds, a number with no unit that can be any size (0 at the start).

Written out:
l = \ln \frac{p}{1 - p}
Figure 8 shows how probabilities map to log odds: 0.5 goes to 0, probabilities above 0.5 to positive numbers, below 0.5 to negative ones, and 0 and 1 are never reached.

This filter, a static binary state updated in log odds, is the binary Bayes filter (G-2466)Binary Bayes filter: The Bayes filter for a yes-or-no state that does not change, such as “door open” or “this map cell is occupied”, run in log odds: each reading adds the log of its Bayes factor. It is fast and does not round to 0 or 1. Explained in §4.3 Log odds turn the products into sums. (PR §4.2).
4.4 Why work in log odds
Two reasons:

Adding is cheaper than multiplying and rescaling. A map can hold millions of cells, each updated at every scan; one addition per cell is the cheapest update possible, and every cell can be updated at the same time (Freiburg mapping slides: the log odds (G-1116) update “only requires to compute sums”)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1.
Probabilities near 0 or 1 round off. Run 40 readings of “open” in ordinary probabilities. The odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1 become 3 to the power 40, about 12 billion billion, and the computer stores p(\text{open}) as exactly 1.0. After that, a reading of “closed” changes nothing, because 1.0 times anything, divided by itself, is still 1.0. In log odds the same run reaches 43.94, and a “closed” reading moves it to 43.25, as it should. The notebook shows both.

5. Looking back: smoothing and the most likely path


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Later readings also say where the robot was earlier. The forward-backward algorithm combines readings from before and after a time step into the smoothed belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, the probability of each cell at that earlier time; the Viterbi algorithm finds the single most likely path.


5.1 Three questions about a run
Now the second half of the opening question: what else the same cell probabilities tell us. Take the hallway robot’s run of three stepsExplained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §2.1 Why the true cell is out of reach, the run that first built its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, its probability for every cell: at time step t = 1 it stays and reads “door”; at t = 2 it moves 2 and reads “door”; at t = 3 it moves 2 and reads “wall”. Its true cells are 1, 3 and 5. The hidden Markov model (G-2439)Hidden Markov model (HMM): A Markov chain whose states cannot be seen, where each state produces an observation that can, such as hidden robot cells producing “door” or “wall” readings; it is the model behind robot state estimation, speech recognition and many trackers. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §6.3 Hidden Markov model of the robot, hidden cells that each produce a reading we can see, can answer three different questions (CS188 §8.2–8.3; J&M App. A):

Where is the robot now, given the readings so far? This is filtering (G-2469)Filtering (state estimation): Estimating the current state from the readings so far, p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}); what a robot needs while it drives, and what the Bayes filter computes. Explained in §5.1 Three questions about a run.; the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. of Section 2 does it.
Where was the robot at an earlier time, given all readings, including later ones? This is smoothing (G-2470)Smoothing: Estimating the state at an earlier time using all readings, including later ones, p(x_t \mid z_{1:T}); later readings often settle where the robot was, such as raising the true starting cell from 0.19 to 0.36. Explained in §5.1 Three questions about a run..
Which whole path of cells is most likely, given all readings? This is the most likely path (G-2476)Most likely path: The one sequence of hidden states with the highest probability given all readings, such as cells 1, 3, 5; one consistent answer for a whole run, found by the Viterbi algorithm. Explained in §5.1 Three questions about a run., found by the Viterbi algorithm (G-2474)Viterbi algorithm: The method that finds the single most likely sequence of hidden states in an HMM by keeping, for each state and time, only the best path ending there and where it came from, then tracing back; it costs states squared times steps instead of trying every path. Explained in §5.3 The most likely path: the Viterbi algorithm..

Filtering is what a robot needs while it drives. Smoothing and the most likely path are for looking back over a recorded run, for example to draw the path it took.
5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm
At t = 1 the filter knew only the first reading, so cells 1, 3 and 7 were equally likely (Figure 11, blue bars). Later readings settle it. A robot at cell 3 at t = 1 would be at cell 5 at t = 2, a wall, and would have read “door” there only 20 percent of the time. A robot at cell 1 would be at cell 3, a door. So the reading at t = 2 points back to cell 1.
The forward-backward algorithm (G-2471)Forward-backward algorithm: The method that computes smoothed beliefs in an HMM by multiplying a forward pass (evidence up to t) by a backward pass (evidence after t) and rescaling; it uses every reading of a recorded run for each time step. Explained in §5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm. makes this exact. The algorithm combines two quantities for every cell x and time t (J&M App. A):

the forward probability (G-2472)Forward probability \alpha_t: The probability of the readings up to time t together with being in state x at t; the histogram filter before rescaling, carrying the evidence from the past. Explained in §5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm. \alpha_t(x): the probability of the readings up to t and of being in cell x at t. It is the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. before rescaling; at t = 1 it is 0.06 at the doors and 0.02 at the walls (Section 2.2);
the backward probability (G-2473)Backward probability \beta_t: The probability of the readings after time t, given state x at t, computed from the last step backwards starting at 1; it carries the evidence from the future. Explained in §5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm. \beta_t(x): the probability of the readings after t, given cell x at t. It is computed from the end backwards, starting from 1 at the last step; for cell 1 at t = 1 it is 0.4144 (worked below).

Figure 11 computes both for the run, with one column of the 10 cells for each time step. Watch \alpha fill in from left to right and \beta from right to left, then the column t = 1 being multiplied and rescaled: the belief in cell 1 rises from 0.19 to 0.36.

Beta fills in from right to left: 1 at t = 3, 0.8 for cell 3 at t = 2, 0.4144 for cell 1 and 0.1072 for cell 3 at t = 1; coloured lines show the moves used. So \alpha carries the evidence from the past, \beta from the future. Their product, rescaled to add to 1, is the smoothed belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition. In symbols:

\eta is the factor that rescales the products so they add to 1, one over their total over all cells (the total is 0.06896);
\gamma_t(x) is the smoothed belief in cell x at time t, a number from 0 to 1 (0.36 for cell 1 at t = 1).

Written out:
\gamma_t(x) = \eta\ \alpha_t(x)\ \beta_t(x)
\beta for cell 1 at t = 1, worked backwards. At t = 3 there are no later readings, so \beta_3 = 1 everywhere. One step back, from cell 3 at t = 2 the robot reaches cell 4, 5 or 6 (all walls), and each reads “wall” with probability 0.8:
\beta_2(3) = 0.1 \times 0.8 + 0.8 \times 0.8
+\ 0.1 \times 0.8 = 0.8
Another step back, from cell 1 at t = 1 the robot reaches cell 2 (a wall), 3 (a door) or 4 (a wall), and must then read “door” and continue. \beta_2(2) is worked like \beta_2(3): from cell 2 the robot reaches cell 3 (a door, reads “wall” with probability 0.4), 4 or 5 (walls):
\beta_2(2) = 0.1 \times 0.4 + 0.8 \times 0.8
+\ 0.1 \times 0.8 = 0.76
\beta_2(4) = 0.76 the same way (notebook). Then:
\beta_1(1) = 0.1 \times 0.2 \times 0.76
+\ 0.8 \times 0.6 \times 0.8
+\ 0.1 \times 0.2 \times 0.76
= 0.4144
The same calculation for cell 3 gives only 0.1072, because a robot there would read “door” at a wall.
Why does a plain product work? The steps use two facts:

the Markov property (G-2316)Markov property: The property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.3 Complete state and the Markov property: once the cell at a time step is known, the earlier readings tell nothing more about the later ones;
the multiplication rule (G-2212)Multiplication rule: The chance that both A and B happen is the chance of B times the chance of A given B: P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) \times P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §5. The multiplication rule: the chance of one event times the chance of a second event given the first is the chance of both.

For cell 1 at t = 1:
\alpha_1(1)\ \beta_1(1) = 0.06 \times 0.4144
= 0.0249
The same steps for any cell and time step:

t is the time step, 1 above;
x is the cell, 1 above;
T is the last time step, 3 in our run;
z_{1:t} is the readings from time 1 to t, only “door” at t = 1;
z_{t+1:T} is the readings after t, (“door”, “wall”) at t = 1;
z_{1:T} is all readings of the run, (“door”, “door”, “wall”);
x_t = x means that the robot is in cell x at time t;
a comma inside p(\ldots) means “and”.

\alpha_t(x)\ \beta_t(x)
= p(z_{1:t},\ x_t = x)
\quad \times\ p(z_{t+1:T} \mid x_t = x)
= p(z_{1:t},\ x_t = x)
\quad \times\ p(z_{t+1:T} \mid x_t = x,\ z_{1:t})
= p(z_{1:T},\ x_t = x)
Cell 3 the same way:
\alpha_1(3)\ \beta_1(3) = 0.06 \times 0.1072 = 0.0064
The products over all 10 cells add to 0.06896, the probability of the three readings; it is the same at every t, which the notebook checks. Dividing each product by it gives the probability of its cell given all three readings, the smoothed belief (J&M App. A):
\gamma_1(1) = 0.0249 / 0.06896 = 0.36
\gamma_1(3) = 0.0064 / 0.06896 = 0.09

5.3 The most likely path: the Viterbi algorithm
Smoothing (G-2470)Smoothing: Estimating the state at an earlier time using all readings, including later ones, p(x_t \mid z_{1:T}); later readings often settle where the robot was, such as raising the true starting cell from 0.19 to 0.36. Explained in §5.1 Three questions about a run. gives a probability for each cell at each time. Sometimes we want one answer instead: the single path of cells that best explains all readings. Trying every path is hopeless for long runs: with 10 cells and T steps there are 10 to the power T paths, 1000 for our 3 steps but a 1 followed by 100 zeros for 100 steps (J&M App. A).
The Viterbi algorithm (G-2474)Viterbi algorithm: The method that finds the single most likely sequence of hidden states in an HMM by keeping, for each state and time, only the best path ending there and where it came from, then tracing back; it costs states squared times steps instead of trying every path. Explained in §5.3 The most likely path: the Viterbi algorithm. avoids this with one observation: the best path to a cell at time t must continue the best path to some cell at time t - 1. So for each cell it keeps only the probability of the best path ending there, and which cell that path came from, the back-pointer (G-2477)Back-pointer: The note the Viterbi algorithm keeps for each state and time of which earlier state the best path came from; following them backwards from the best end recovers the most likely path. Explained in §5.3 The most likely path: the Viterbi algorithm. (CS188 §8.3). For each cell x at time t:

x' is a cell at time t - 1, where the path may come from;
m_{t-1}(x') is the probability of the best path ending in cell x' at time t - 1 (0.06 at a door and 0.02 at a wall at t = 1);
p(x \mid u_t, x') is the chance that the command u_t takes the robot from cell x' to cell x (0.8 for “move 2” from cell 1 to cell 3);
\max_{x'} keeps the largest value over all cells x';
p(z_t \mid x) is the chance of the reading z_t in cell x (0.6 for “door” at cell 3);
m_t(x) is the probability of the best path ending in cell x at time t (0.0288 for cell 3 at t = 2).

The update is the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. of Section 2.6 without the rescaling, with the sum replaced by a maximum:
m_t(x) = p(z_t \mid x)
\times \max_{x'} p(x \mid u_t, x')\ m_{t-1}(x')
Storing each sub-answer once and reusing it is dynamic programming (G-652)Dynamic programming: Solving a problem by storing the answer to each overlapping sub-problem the first time it is computed and looking it up afterwards, so no work is repeated; memoization is one form of it. Explained in: Memoization in Backpropagation, §3.3 The memoized version.
At t = 2, cell 3. The best path into cell 3 comes from cell 1, cell 2 or cell 0, and m_1 is 0.06 at a door and 0.02 at a wall:
\text{from cell 1: } 0.8 \times 0.06 = 0.048
\text{from cell 2: } 0.1 \times 0.02 = 0.002
\text{from cell 0: } 0.1 \times 0.02 = 0.002
The best is from cell 1, so the back-pointer of cell 3 at t = 2 is cell 1, and:
m_2(3) = 0.6 \times 0.048 = 0.0288
This 0.0288 is the probability of the best path into cell 3, which is the robot’s true path: cell 1, then cell 3.
At t = 3, cell 5. The best way in is from cell 3 at t = 2:
m_3(5) = 0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.0288 = 0.0184

8. Key terms
Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.









































































































































TermMeaningHistogram filter (discrete Bayes filter) (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells.The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position.Motion kernel (G-2462)Motion kernel: The short list of move probabilities, such as (0.1, 0.8, 0.1) for one cell short, exact, one cell too far, slid along the belief in the prediction step; it spreads each cell’s belief over the cells the robot may have reached. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithmThe algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption.Belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definitionThe robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state.Log-odds (G-1116)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability.Discretization (G-619)Discretization: Turning a continuous column into a discrete one by cutting its range into intervals (bins), such as ages 0–18, 18–60 and 60+; it turns endless values into a few groups that a model or a table can handle. Explained in: Binning and Binarization: Equal Width, Equal Frequency and k-means Binning, §1. OverviewTurning a continuous column into a discrete one by cutting its range into intervals (bins), such as ages 0–18, 18–60 and 60+; it turns endless values into a few groups that a model or a table can handle.Histogram (G-899)Histogram: A bar chart of how many values fall in each equal range (bin) of a numerical column; it shows the shape of a distribution at a glance: where values pile up, how far they spread and whether there are several peaks. Explained in: Univariate Analysis: Exploring One Column at a Time, §6. HistogramA bar chart of how many values fall in each equal range (bin) of a numerical column; it shows the shape of a distribution at a glance: where values pile up, how far they spread and whether there are several peaks.Law of total probability (G-1053)Law of total probability: The rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §1. OverviewThe rule for the overall probability of an event: add its probability under each case, weighted by how likely that case is, P(B) = \sum_i P(B \mid A_i) P(A_i), when the cases A_i are mutually exclusive and cover every possibility.Convolution operation (G-481)Convolution operation: Sliding a small filter over an input and, at each position, multiplying cell by cell and adding up, so the output (a feature map) is large where the input contains the filter’s pattern, such as an edge. Explained in: The Convolution Operation, §6. The convolution operationSliding a small filter over an input and, at each position, multiplying cell by cell and adding up, so the output (a feature map) is large where the input contains the filter’s pattern, such as an edge.Pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the headingWhere a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading.Odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line.Bayes factor (G-2215)Bayes factor: A number that says how strongly the evidence favours yes over no: how many times more likely the evidence is if the answer is yes than if it is no, P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{yes}) / P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{no}). Multiplying the prior odds by it gives the posterior odds. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: A Bayes’ Theorem Problem, §6.1 The size of the update: the Bayes factorA number that says how strongly the evidence favours yes over no: how many times more likely the evidence is if the answer is yes than if it is no, P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{yes}) / P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{no}). Multiplying the prior odds by it gives the posterior odds.Sigmoid function (G-1798)Sigmoid function: An S-shaped function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z}); it turns a score into a probability, as in logistic regression. Explained in: Logistic Regression: The Sigmoid Function, §4. The sigmoid functionAn S-shaped function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, \sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z}); it turns a score into a probability, as in logistic regression.Hidden Markov model (HMM) (G-2439)Hidden Markov model (HMM): A Markov chain whose states cannot be seen, where each state produces an observation that can, such as hidden robot cells producing “door” or “wall” readings; it is the model behind robot state estimation, speech recognition and many trackers. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §6.3 Hidden Markov modelA Markov chain whose states cannot be seen, where each state produces an observation that can, such as hidden robot cells producing “door” or “wall” readings; it is the model behind robot state estimation, speech recognition and many trackers.Markov property (G-2316)Markov property: The property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.3 Complete state and the Markov propertyThe property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone.Dynamic programming (G-652)Dynamic programming: Solving a problem by storing the answer to each overlapping sub-problem the first time it is computed and looking it up afterwards, so no work is repeated; memoization is one form of it. Explained in: Memoization in Backpropagation, §3.3 The memoized versionSolving a problem by storing the answer to each overlapping sub-problem the first time it is computed and looking it up afterwards, so no work is repeated; memoization is one form of it.Particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian systemThe Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible.Gaussian distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-016-.title: Particle Filter
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-016-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A particle filter keeps the robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition as a cloud of guesses. Each reading reweighs the guesses, resampling keeps the good ones, and each move shifts them all; the cloud can take any shape, including several peaks at once.



Figure 1: A corridor that loops round a block, opened out from 0 to 10 m, with three doors set back into the right-hand wall; the robot at 2.1 m reads 1.46 m to the side. Below: the map, the reading expected at each position
So far the robot can run the Bayes filter with a histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2.1 Why cells: one probability per cell of the 10-cell hallway. The histogram filter breaks when the state grows: a floor robot’s pose (x, y, \theta), its position and heading, already needs 7.2 million cellsExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §3.1 Why the number of cells explodes. This Note keeps the belief as a cloud of samples instead, placed only where the robot may be.
A robot is somewhere in the corridor of Figure 1. It has a map of the corridor, but it does not know where it is. Its side sensor reads 1.46 m, which means “a door is beside me”. Three doors fit that reading, so the reading’s answer to “where am I?” is “at door 1, door 2 or door 3, about equally likely”: a belief with a peak at each door. These peaks are the belief’s three modes (G-1251)Mode: The value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, so the belief is multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode.
The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm gives the rule for updating such a belief. Two other ways of running it struggle here:

the grid filter, or histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2.1 Why cells, stores one number per cell, which is fine on a 10 m line but grows very fast with the number of state variables;
the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system stores the belief as a single bell-shaped curve, a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, and one Gaussian has only one mode (Section 3.1).

The particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in §4. The particle filter, step by step. stores the belief as a set of sample guesses instead. This Note builds it on the corridor of Figure 1:

why a cloud of samples can stand for a belief, and how accurate it is (Section 3);
the three steps, move, weigh and resample, worked by hand and then run on the corridor (Section 4);
the low-variance sampler (G-2499)Low-variance sampler (systematic resampling): A way to resample with one random start between 0 and 1/M and M pointers 1/M apart along the stacked weights; it keeps every particle with weight at least 1/M, adds little randomness and runs in time proportional to M. Explained in §4.3 Resample: copy the heavy particles, drop the light ones., the standard way to resample (Section 4.3);
what goes wrong with too few particles (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples., and the fixes (Section 5).

2. The running example and the Bayes filter in brief


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To tell the three doors apart, the robot has a map, a noisy side sensor and wheels that slip. The Bayes filter turns these into a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition with two steps per round: predict with the motion, update with the reading.


2.1 The corridor, the sensor and the motion
The corridor loops round a block and is 10 m around, so position 10 m is position 0 m again. The corridor is not the 10-cell hallwayExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2.1 Why cells of the grid filter: a particle (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. is a position, not a cell, so here the position is a continuous number of metres, and the doors are 1 m stretches of wall. Three doors are set 0.5 m back into the right-hand wall (Figure 1):

























DoorFrom (m)To (m)11.52.524.05.036.57.5
The map. The side sensor measures the distance to the right-hand wall. In symbols:

x is the robot’s position along the corridor, in m, from 0 to 10 m;
h(x) is the expected reading, what the side sensor should read at position x, in m.

The map tells us what it should read at each position:
h(x) = 1.5 \text{ m in front of a door}
h(x) = 1.0 \text{ m beside plain wall}
For example, h(2.0) = 1.5 m and h(3.0) = 1.0 m.
The sensor model. The sensor model, the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid x, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose x in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model of this corridor, gives the density of a reading at each position. The sensor is noisy: its error follows a Gaussian, also called a normal distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.15 m. In symbols:

z is the side sensor’s reading, in m (1.46 m at the first reading);
\sigma_z is the standard deviation of the sensor’s error, 0.15 m;
\mathcal{N}(z;\ h(x),\ \sigma_z^2) is the height at z of the Gaussian with mean h(x) and variance \sigma_z^2, the square of \sigma_z;
p(z \mid x) is the density of the reading z when the robot is at x, in probability per metre (2.567 for the reading 1.46 m at a door, Section 4.2).

So the reading z at position x has the density
p(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(z;\ h(x),\ \sigma_z^2)
a Gaussian centred on the expected reading. The beam model (G-2377)Beam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture explains why real range sensors need a richer curve; one Gaussian is enough for this Note.
The motion model. Each move is commanded as u = 2.5 m. The wheels slip, so the true move is 2.5 m plus a random slip with standard deviation \sigma_u = 0.15 m, a simple probabilistic motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density.
The run. The robot starts at 2.1 m, takes three readings and makes two moves:





























Reading 1Move 1Reading 2Move 2Reading 3True position (m)2.10+2.524.62+2.467.08Reading z (m)1.461.581.41
The filter never sees the true positions; they are there so we can check its answers.
2.2 The Bayes filter in brief
The robot’s belief \text{bel}(x_t) is a probability distribution over where it is at time t, given every command and reading so far (belief (G-2433))Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition. The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm updates it in two steps per round.
At step t:

x_t is the robot’s position at step t, in m (2.10 m at the first reading, which the filter never sees);
x_{t-1} is its position one step earlier, in m;
u_t is the command, a move of 2.5 m;
z_t is the side sensor’s reading, in m (1.46 m at the first reading);
\text{bel}(x_{t-1}) is the belief one step earlier, a density over positions, in probability per metre;
p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}) is the motion model, the density of the new position given the command and the old position, in probability per metre;
\int \ldots\ dx_{t-1} adds over every previous position x_{t-1};
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) (read “bel bar”) is the predicted belief, after the move and before the reading;
p(z_t \mid x_t) is the sensor model of Section 2.1, in probability per metre;
\eta is the number that makes the total 1;
\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief after the reading.

Predict with the command u_t: every place x_{t-1} the robot may have been sends probability to the places the move may take it.
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \int p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})
\qquad \times\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1})\ dx_{t-1}
Update with the reading z_t: multiply by how well each place explains the reading, then rescale so the total is 1.
\text{bel}(x_t) = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_t)\ \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t)
The update is Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof with the predicted belief as the prior.
The two formulas are exact, but they hold whole curves, and an integral over a curve cannot be computed for most maps and sensors (Labbe ch.12). Every Bayes-filter variant is a way of storing the curve so that the two steps become sums a computer can do.
