The idea. The reading is 1.46 m. A particle in front of a door expects 1.5 m: close, so it explains the reading well. A particle beside plain wall expects 1.0 m: 0.46 m off, more than three sensor standard deviations, so it explains the reading badly. The weight turns “explains well” into a number.
The weight. For particle m:

x^{[m]} is its position, in m (1.6 m for particle 2 below);
z is the reading, 1.46 m;
p(z \mid x^{[m]}) is the sensor model of Section 2.1, the density of the reading z at that position, in probability per metre (2.567 for particle 2);
w^{[m]} is the particle’s weight, the same number (2.567 for particle 2) until it is normalised below.

For each particle we ask the sensor model how likely the reading z is if the robot were where the particle says:
w^{[m]} = p(z \mid x^{[m]})

Python: the low-variance sampler in four lines.
def low_variance(w, rng):
    M = len(w)
    pointers = rng.uniform(0, 1 / M) + np.arange(M) / M
    return np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(w), pointers, side="right")
np.cumsum(w) gives the stretch ends; np.searchsorted(..., side="right") returns, for each pointer, the index of the first stretch that ends beyond it. x = x[low_variance(w, rng)] is the new particle set.

ReadingDoor 1: particles, exactDoor 2: particles, exactDoor 3: particles, exact1 (z = 1.46)0.33, 0.330.36, 0.330.29, 0.332 (z = 1.58)0.00, 0.010.49, 0.500.51, 0.503 (z = 1.41)0.00, 0.000.00, 0.010.96, 0.96
The cloud remembers the history without storing it: after reading 3, the only particles left are those whose whole path, door then door then door, fits every reading. The shares answer the opening’s “door 1, door 2 or door 3”: they start at about 0.33 each and end at 0.96 for door 3, where the robot is.
One answer from a cloud, and a trap. A controller usually wants one position. In symbols:

M is the number of particles, 100 here;
x^{[m]} is particle m‘s position, in m;
w^{[m]} is its weight, a number from 0 to 1, the weights adding up to 1;
\sum_{m=1}^{M} adds over all particles, from m = 1 to M;
\hat{x} is the single position the filter reports, in m (7.05 m after reading 3).

The usual choice is the weighted mean of the particles:
\hat{x} = \sum_{m=1}^{M} w^{[m]}\ x^{[m]}
After reading 3 it gives 7.05 m; the robot is at 7.08 m. After reading 2, the same formula gives 5.73 m, between the two clusters, in front of plain wall (the black diamond in frame 5 of Figure 8). The weighted mean is a good answer only when the cloud has one cluster; with several, report the heaviest cluster or keep the whole cloud (Labbe ch.12).
4.6 The algorithm
Putting the steps together gives the particle filter of Thrun Table 4.3, as also given in the Freiburg PF slides. Inputs: the particle (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. set \mathcal X_{t-1} from the last round, the command u_t and the reading z_t. The other symbols are listed in Section 2.2 and Section 3.3.

For each particle m = 1, \ldots, M:

move: sample x_t^{[m]} from p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}^{[m]});
weigh: set w_t^{[m]} = p(z_t \mid x_t^{[m]}).


Normalise the weights so they add up to 1.
Resample: draw M particles from the weighted set in proportion to the weights (low-variance sampler (G-2499))Low-variance sampler (systematic resampling): A way to resample with one random start between 0 and 1/M and M pointers 1/M apart along the stacked weights; it keeps every particle with weight at least 1/M, adds little randomness and runs in time proportional to M. Explained in §4.3 Resample: copy the heavy particles, drop the light ones.; they form \mathcal X_t, each with weight 1/M.

Every line uses the models only to draw a sample or to evaluate a density. No model needs to be linear, smooth or Gaussian: our map is a step, which a Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system could not use (Section 3.1). With 100 particles the loop found the right door; with fewer, it can fail.
5. Particle deprivation


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

If no particle (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. is near the true state, no step can create one there, and the filter settles on a wrong answer. More particles and fewer, smarter resamplings are the fixes.


5.1 Too few particles
The cloud can hold the three doors of Figure 1 only if some particles (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. sit at each of them. Resampling only copies particles that exist, and the move step only shifts them a little. So once every particle near the true position has been dropped, the filter has no way back. Losing the particles near the true state is particle deprivation (G-2501)Particle deprivation: The failure in which no particles are left near the true state, so the filter settles confidently on a wrong answer; caused by too few particles or unlucky resampling, and fought with more particles and fewer resamplings. Explained in §5.1 Too few particles. (Thrun §4.3).
With few particles it happens often. Figure 9 first runs 5 particles and 100 particles on the same three readings. Watch the 5: none starts at door 1, where the robot starts, so they follow the one particle at door 3 and end tight at door 1, the wrong door, while the 100 end at door 3. The last frame shows that this is not bad luck: we ran the corridor example 1000 times for each particle count and counted how often the filter ended at the right door.

Figure 9: Frames 1 to 8: 5 particles (top) and 100 particles (bottom, the run of Figure 8) get the same three readings; marker size grows with weight, the red triangle is the robot. The 5 start with none at door 1; the one at door 3 takes the weight of reading 1, and its copies go round the loop and end tight at door 1, the wrong door (0.99 of the weight); the 100 end at door 3 (0.96). Last frame: share of 1000 runs that end at the right door, 43.9 percent with 5 particles, 63.0 with 10, 87.8 with 20, 99.6 with 50, 100 with 100





















Particles M5102050100Runs at the right door (percent)43.963.087.899.6100.0
With 5 particles, the start often has no particle at door 1, the robot’s true door, or resampling drops the few there; the filter then follows whatever survived, with full confidence. Too few particles make the filter overconfident: it reports one tight cluster at the wrong door. The average share it gives door 3 shows the same bias: 0.432 with 5 particles against the exact 0.956 (notebook); a small particle set gives a biased belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition (Thrun §4.3).
The problem grows with the number of state variables. A cloud of 100 points covers a 10 m line densely, but spread over a room’s (x, y, \theta) the same 100 points leave wide gaps, so the number of particles needed grows very fast with the state’s dimension (Labbe ch.12).
5.2 Other fixes


More particles. The direct fix, paid for in computation (Labbe ch.12).


Resample less often. Each resampling throws away variety. One rule resamples only when the weights have become uneven: when the effective number of particles (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. falls below half of M, the number of particles (Labbe ch.12). In symbols:

w^{[m]} is the weight of particle m, a number from 0 to 1, the weights adding up to 1;
\sum_m adds over all M particles;
\hat N_{\text{eff}} is the effective number of particles, how many particles of equal weight the cloud is worth.

\hat N_{\text{eff}} = 1 / \textstyle\sum_m (w^{[m]})^2
With equal weights it equals M; with all weight on one particle it equals 1.


A very accurate sensor is a trap. If the sensor curve is much narrower than the gaps between particles, almost every particle gets a weight near zero and the cloud collapses onto one or two. Pretending the sensor is noisier than it is, or using more particles, keeps enough particles alive (Labbe ch.12).


6. Summary






























StepWhat it doesWhyStartspread M particles (100 here) evenly, weight 1/M eachthe robot knows nothing yetMoveeach particle moves by the command u plus its own slipsamples the predicted belief, no integral neededWeighweight w = sensor model p(z \mid x), then normaliseweighting by p(z \mid x) and rescaling turns the predicted cloud into the updated beliefResampledraw M new particles in proportion to weightputs the computation where the belief is

The robot of Figure 1, which saw a door and could be at any of three (about 0.33 each), ends after three readings and two moves with 0.96 of its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition at door 3, where it is, because the cloud held all three doors until the readings could tell them apart.
A cloud of samples can stand for any belief, because the share of samples in a region estimates its probability; the estimate’s standard deviation shrinks like one over the square root of the sample count M (0.030 at 100 particles (G-2491), 0.008 at 1000)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples..
One Gaussian cannot hold “door 2 or door 3”: its peak lands at 5.73 m, in front of wall, so a multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode belief needs a filter whose belief can take any shape, such as particles.
A particle’s weight is the height of the sensor curve at the reading (2.567 at a door, 0.024 at a wall), because weighting by the sensor model p(z \mid x) and normalising is the multiply-and-rescale of the update step.
Resampling (G-2498)Resampling (particle filter): Drawing a fresh set of M particles, with replacement, from the weighted set, each pick in proportion to weight, then giving all weight 1/M; heavy particles are copied and light ones dropped, so computation goes where the belief is. Explained in §4.3 Resample: copy the heavy particles, drop the light ones. with the low-variance sampler keeps every particle with weight at least 1/M, one over the number of particles, and halves the randomness of plain resampling, so good guesses are not lost by chance.
Each particle gets its own slip in the move step, so copies spread out and the cloud keeps covering the possible positions.
The weighted mean is a safe answer only for one cluster, because with two it averages them and can land between them, in front of a wall (5.73 m after reading 2).
Too few particles cause deprivation, because resampling only copies particles that exist, so a door left without particles is never recovered (43.9 percent right with 5 particles, 100 percent with 100).

The robot can now keep a belief of any shape, such as three doors at once. Still missing: every particle costs a motion step and a sensor check each round, and when the belief is a single Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, two numbers, a mean and a variance, carry all of it, which is the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-017-.title: Kalman Filter
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-017-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot has two noisy ways to know where it is: its commands, which drift, and its sensor, which jumps. The Kalman filter blends them with the weight that makes the result as certain as possible, and it does so one step at a time from two numbers.


Make interactive
Figure 1: Ten steps of a robot in a corridor: the true position, the jumpy beacon readings, the drifting estimate from the commands alone, and the Kalman filter estimate that follows the truth
The particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step lets the robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, its probability for each possible position, take any shape, but every particle must be moved and weighed every round. When the belief is a single bell-shaped curve, a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, two numbers carry all of it; this Note builds that filter, the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system.. It needs a new world. The three doors of the looped corridor give a belief with a peak at each door: three modes (G-1251)Mode: The value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, so the belief is multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, and one Gaussian cannot hold it. Here a ceiling beacon reports the position itself, so the belief has a single mode: it is unimodal (G-2528)Unimodal: Having a single mode (one peak); a unimodal belief can be held by one Gaussian, so the Kalman filter needs only its mean and variance. Explained in §1. Overview..
A delivery robot drives along a straight corridor. Every second it is commanded to move 0.5 m. A ceiling beacon system also reports its position once a second. Neither source is good enough on its own (Figure 1):

The commands give a smooth path, but they drift: each step’s error is the last step’s error plus a new wheel slip, so the error carries over and piles up. Over the ten steps of Figure 1, the commands alone miss the true position by 0.27 m on average (the root mean squared error (G-1705), RMSE)Root mean squared error (RMSE): The square root of the average squared error (MSE), so the error is back in the output’s units. Explained in: Regression Metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R² and Adjusted R², §4. Root mean squared error (RMSE).
The beacon jumps: each reading’s error is new, with no memory of the last one, so it never piles up, but it can swing from one side to the other between two seconds. Its readings miss by 0.51 m on average.

Figure 2 runs both sources for 60 steps from a known start. The commands’ error moves only a little each step, but the moves add up, and its band of two standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, twice the error’s typical size, widens with the number of steps (Section 2.4). With:

t is the number of steps since the start, from 1 to 60 in Figure 2;
0.1 m is the standard deviation of one step’s wheel slip.

The band reaches this far either side of zero, in m:
2 \times 0.1 \times \sqrt{t}
The beacon’s error lands somewhere new each step, but its band stays at ±0.8 m. After about 16 steps the commands are the worse source.

Figure 2: One simulated run of 60 steps from a known start, one frame per step. Top: the errors now, with an arrow from each last value; the commands’ error moves a little each step and wanders off, the beacon’s lands somewhere new each step, the Kalman filter’s stays near zero. Bottom: the errors so far; the commands’ band of two standard deviations widens, the beacon’s stays at ±0.8 m, the Kalman filter’s settles at ±0.38 m
Over the ten steps of Figure 1, the Kalman filter’s estimate misses by 0.17 m, better than either (notebook). In Figure 2 (blue), its error stays near zero, and its band settles at ±0.38 m, half the beacon’s, and does not widen. The filter gets there by asking, at every step, how far to trust each source, and the answer is a number we derive: the Kalman gain (G-2508)Kalman gain K: The weight the update gives to the reading, K = \bar{p}/(\bar{p} + R) in one dimension: the weight that makes the updated variance smallest, near 1 when the prediction is vague and near 0 when the reading is. 2.1 The Bayes filter in brief
The robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm updates it once a second, in rounds numbered by the step t. At step t:

x_t is the robot’s position, in m;
\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief, the probability distribution over the position x_t;
u_t is the command, 0.5 m forward;
z_t is the beacon’s reading, in m;

p(z_t \mid x_t) is the sensor model, the probability of each reading given the position.

Each round has two steps:

predict with the command u_t, spreading the belief by the motion model;
update with the reading z_t, multiplying by the sensor model and rescaling to a total of 1.

For a general belief these steps act on whole curves, which is costly: the particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. \text{Var}(y) = 4 \times 0.25 = 1
The shift b moves the Gaussian without widening it. That the result is still a Gaussian, not some other shape, is a property of the normal distribution (Freiburg KF slides; Labbe ch.4). The command is such a shift, but each step also adds a wheel slip, a second error.
2.4 Adding independent errors adds variances
The robot’s next position is its present position plus the commanded 0.5 m plus a random slip. The estimate moves by the same 0.5 m. The error is the true position minus the estimate. With:

x is the robot’s present true position, in m;
\hat{x} is the present estimate, in m;
w is the next step’s wheel slip, in m, with mean 0 and a standard deviation of 0.1 m;
e is the present error, the true position minus the estimate, in m.

The next error:
(x + 0.5 + w) - (\hat{x} + 0.5)
= x - \hat{x} + w
= e + w
The present error has mean 0, because the estimate is the mean, and variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable p, the estimate’s variance, 1 m² at the start (Section 2.2). The slip has mean 0 and does not depend on e, so the two errors are independent. Their variances add, where \text{Var} stands for the variance:
\text{Var}(e + w) = \text{Var}(e) + \text{Var}(w)
Why. Take a present error of 1 m or −1 m and a slip of 0.1 m or −0.1 m, all four pairs equally likely. Square each next error:
(1 + 0.1)^2 = 1 + 0.2 + 0.01
(1 - 0.1)^2 = 1 - 0.2 + 0.01
(-1 + 0.1)^2 = 1 - 0.2 + 0.01
(-1 - 0.1)^2 = 1 + 0.2 + 0.01
Average the four squares; each +0.2 cancels a −0.2:
\text{Var}(e + w) = 1 + 0.01
The same in symbols:
(e + w)^2 = e^2 + 2ew + w^2
Averaged, the 2ew parts cancel the same way: whatever e is, the slip is as often negative as positive.
\text{Var}(e + w) = \text{Var}(e) + \text{Var}(w)
So every slip adds its variance, and the commands’ drift grows step by step.

the reading is a linear function of the state, plus normal noise;
the first belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. x_t is the robot’s true position, in m;

6.1 Why a vector state: the hidden speed
So far the commands told the filter how far the robot moved, 0.5 m per step, drift and all. Suppose instead we do not know the robot’s speed, only that it drives roughly steadily: a person is pushing a trolley, or the odometry is unreliable. We still want the speed, for example because a speed controller needs it (Section 6.6), but nothing measures it.
We put the speed into the state. The state is now a vector (a list of numbers), written in bold:

\mathbf{x} is the state, a vector of 2 entries: the position, in m, on top, and the speed, in m/s, below.

6.2 The model as matrices
Motion. With steps of 1 s, the position grows by the speed and the speed stays as it is, plus noise. As a matrix times the state, at step t:

\mathbf x_t is the true state, a vector of 2 entries: position, in m, and speed, in m/s;
F is a 2 × 2 matrix that carries the state one step forward, given below;
\mathbf w_t is the process noise, a vector of 2 entries: the position slip, in m, and the speed change, in m/s, each with mean 0; their covariance matrix Q is given below.

\mathbf x_t = F\thinspace\mathbf x_{t-1} + \mathbf w_t
F = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \cr0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
The first row gives position plus speed; the second gives speed. F is the state transition matrix (G-2514)State transition matrix F: The matrix that carries the state one step forward in a linear model, such as F = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] for position and speed with 1 s steps (position plus speed, speed unchanged). Explained in §6.2 The model as matrices.; this choice of F is the constant-velocity model (Labbe ch.6). The noise \mathbf w_t has covariance Q, a 2 × 2 matrix: the variance of the position slip, in m², and of the speed change, in m²/s², on the diagonal, and 0 off it, as the two are not linked:
Q = \begin{bmatrix} 0.01 & 0 \cr0 & 0.001 \end{bmatrix}
a position slip of 0.1 m and a speed change of about 0.03 m/s per step (standard deviations).

z_t is the beacon’s reading, one number, in m;
H is a 1 × 2 matrix, a row of two numbers, that turns the state into the reading the sensor should give, given below;
v_t is the beacon’s error, normal with mean 0 and variance R, 0.16 m².

z_t = H\thinspace\mathbf x_t + v_t
H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}

Could we do the same with a speed sensor and no position sensor? No. Every position, shifted by the same amount, gives exactly the same speed readings, so no number of speed readings can tell where the robot is.
A system is observable (G-2517)Observability: Whether a system’s whole state can be worked out from its readings and commands over time; a filter needs it before it can pin down every state variable. Explained in §6.5 Observability: can the readings pin down the state?. if its whole state can be worked out from its readings (and commands) over time (FBS §8.1). 6.6 The state a controller needs: the filter as an observer
The speed estimate of Section 6.4 is what a controller needs. A controller that holds the robot at 0.5 m/s must know the speed; one that stops it at a door must know the position. Many controllers need the whole state, but sensors give only part of it (FBS §8.1). Something must rebuild the missing parts.
The obvious attempt is to run the model alone, with no readings: each step, multiply the last estimate by the state transition matrix F. Running the model alone is dead reckoning (G-2311)Dead reckoning: Working out a robot’s position from a known start by adding up its own moves, without looking at its surroundings; simple, but its error grows with every move, so it needs readings to correct it. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §2.1 Why counting moves is not enough: dead reckoning: any error in the start or in the model is never corrected. The fix is feedback: compare the reading with what the estimate predicts, and correct the estimate by a gain times the gap. With:

\bar{\mathbf{x}} is the estimate the model predicts, a vector of 2 entries: position, in m, and speed, in m/s;
z is the beacon’s reading, in m;
H is the measurement matrix of Section 6.2, the row (1, 0), which turns the state into the reading the sensor should give;
L is the observer’s gain, a vector of 2 entries: how far to correct the position and the speed per metre of gap; for the Kalman filter at step 1, 0.926 and 0.461;
\hat{\mathbf{x}} is the corrected estimate, a vector of 2 entries.

\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \bar{\mathbf{x}} + L\thinspace(z - H\bar{\mathbf{x}})
A model run alongside the real system and corrected this way is a state observer (G-2516)State observer: A model run alongside the real system and corrected by a gain times the gap between the measured and the predicted reading, so it rebuilds states no sensor measures for a controller to use; the Kalman filter is the observer with the best gain for the given noises. Explained in §6.6 The state a controller needs: the filter as an observer. (FBS §8.2). The size of the gain L is a trade-off: a large gain corrects errors fast but passes the sensor’s noise straight into the estimate (FBS §8.2). The Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system. is the observer whose gain, L = K, is the best compromise for the given noises (FBS §8.2). The controller then uses \hat{\mathbf{x}} in place of the true state (FBS §8.3), which is why the Kalman filter sits between the sensors and the controller in most robots. Every gain so far rested on two noise settings we were simply given: the slip’s variance Q and the beacon’s variance R.

\text{sample variance} = 0.134 \text{ m}^2
The datasheet value is 0.16 m². Sensor datasheets are the other source of R (kalmanfilter.net). The mean, 2.018 m, also shows no sizeable bias, which matters because the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system. assumes the noise has mean zero.
7.2 Q: tune the motion noise
The slip’s variance Q is harder: it covers everything the motion model leaves out (slips, pushes, a wheel radius slightly wrong), so there is no datasheet for it, and it is set by tuning against data (Labbe ch.8). Each wrong choice fails in its own way. We simulated 2000 runs of 50 steps in which the true slip variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable is 0.01, and ran three filters on them, each scored by its RMSE, the typical size of its error (Figure 10):





























Filter’s QGain it settles toError (RMSE, steps 11–50)What goes wrong0.0001 (too small)0.10 at step 10, falling0.305 mtrusts the commands, ignores readings, drifts with the slips0.01 (right)0.220.187 mnone1 (too big)0.880.353 mtrusts each reading, copies its noise
The readings alone give 0.399 m. Too small a Q trusts the commands and drifts like them; too large a Q follows every jump of the beacon (Labbe ch.4, “Incorrect process variance”; kalmanfilter.net, where a too-small Q causes a lag error). Figure 10 steps the three filters through one of these runs; watch each line against zero and each filter’s gain in the legend.

Figure 10: Error of three filters on one 50-step run, one step per frame, each set with a different slip variance Q; each legend entry gives the filter’s gain K at the current step and its RMSE over all 2000 runs. Q = 0.0001: gain 0.10 at step 10 and 0.03 at step 50, so its estimate lags below the truth for long stretches; Q = 1: gain 0.88, its estimate jumps with every reading; Q = 0.01: gain 0.22, its estimate stays closest to zero. The last frame shows all 50 steps
Only the ratio matters. Multiply the slip’s variance Q, the beacon’s variance R and the starting variance all by 10. The first predicted variance \bar{p}, the starting variance plus Q, is then 10 times larger too, and so is every later one. So every gain has a 10 on top and below:
K = \frac{10\thinspace\bar{p}}{10\thinspace\bar{p} + 10\thinspace R}
= \frac{\bar{p}}{\bar{p} + R}
The gains and the estimates are the same; the notebook finds a largest difference of exactly 0. What a filter designer really chooses is how much the model is trusted relative to the sensor.
How to tell when it is wrong without knowing the truth. On a real robot the truth is unknown, but the innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance., the gaps between each reading and its prediction, are not: a well-tuned filter’s innovations look like random noise of the size its own innovation variance S (Section 6.3) predicts. Testing them is the consistency checkExplained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §5. Consistency: is the filter telling the truth about itself? on the innovations.

The five lines of the one-dimensional filter, with:

In a linear Gaussian system the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition stays Gaussian, because a linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian and independent variances add, so a mean and a variance carry the whole belief.

Explained in §4.3 The best weight: the Kalman gain. is derived, not chosen: it is the weight on the reading that minimises the updated variance, and it equals the Bayes update of two multiplied Gaussians (0.776 m and 0.138 m² at step 1 either way).
The gain is high while the estimate is vague (0.863 at step 1) and settles near 0.22 once prediction and reading balance, so the beacon’s jumps are damped.
In matrix form the covariance links position and speed, so position readings estimate a speed nobody measures (0.421 m/s against a true 0.48 m/s).

R is measured from the sensor, Q is tuned because no datasheet covers what the motion model leaves out; too small a Q drifts like the commands, too large a Q follows every jump, and only the ratio matters.

The robot can now blend drifting commands and jumping readings with two numbers per step. RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-018-.title: Extended Kalman Filter
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-018-.content:
1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Most robot sensors and motions are nonlinear functions of the state, and a nonlinear function bends a Gaussian out of shape. The extended Kalman filter replaces each nonlinear function by its tangent line at the current estimate and then runs the ordinary Kalman filter; checking its innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance tells us whether its variance can be trusted.



Figure 1: Top: a radio beacon on the corridor wall at 6 m, 2 m to the side; the robot reads its straight-line distance to it. Bottom: that distance as a function of position, a curve with its lowest point at 2 m under the beacon; positions 4 m and 8 m both read 2.83 m
With the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system, the corridor robot blends its drifting commands and its jumping readings, and its estimate misses by 0.17 m, against 0.27 m for the commands alone and 0.51 m for the readings. The blend works because the belief stays a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, a bell-shaped curve set by a mean and a variance, and because the ceiling system reports the position itself plus noise, a linear function (G-2527)Linear function: A function y = ax + b: a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, whose graph is a straight line; passing a normal variable through it gives another normal variable, which is why the Kalman filter is exact for linear models. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian of the position, whose graph is a straight line. Now the robot has a new sensor in the same corridor: a radio beacon fixed on the wall at 6 m along the corridor, 2 m to the side, and it measures its straight-line distance to the beacon (Figure 1). Such range sensors are common: radio beacons, GPS ranges to satellites, a lidar’s range to a landmark.
The reading is no longer the position plus noise. Its graph against the position is a curve (Figure 1), so no fixed multiple of the position plus a constant gives it: the reading is a nonlinear function (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in §1. Overview. of the position:

far from the beacon, the distance changes almost one for one with position, nearly a straight line;
under the beacon, the distance stops changing: it bottoms out at 2 m;
past the beacon, it grows again, so 4 m and 8 m give the same reading.

The Kalman filter needs linear models (Section 2), so it cannot use this reading as it is. This Note adds the extended Kalman filter, which straightens the curve at the current estimate, and a check that tells when the result has gone wrong:

pushing a Gaussian through a nonlinear function, and the tangent-line fix (Section 3);
the extended Kalman filter, step by step on the corridor (Section 4);
its limits: one Gaussian can hold only one side (Section 4.4);
consistency, whether the filter’s variance matches its real errors: the innovation, its covariance, and the NIS and NEES tests (Section 5).

2. The Kalman filter in brief, and why nonlinear functions break it


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The Kalman filter is exact only because linear functions (G-2527)Linear function: A function y = ax + b: a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, whose graph is a straight line; passing a normal variable through it gives another normal variable, which is why the Kalman filter is exact for linear models. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian, whose graphs are straight lines, keep a Gaussian a Gaussian. A nonlinear function, such as the beacon distance, does not.


To see why the nonlinear beacon distance of Figure 1 breaks it, recall what the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system does. The Kalman filter keeps the belief as a mean \hat{x} and a variance p and runs two steps per round:

predict: move the mean by the command, 0.5 m, and add the process noise Q, the variance of each step’s wheel slip, 0.01 m², to the variance;
update: blend in the reading z with the Kalman gain (G-2508)Kalman gain K: The weight the update gives to the reading, K = \bar{p}/(\bar{p} + R) in one dimension: the weight that makes the updated variance smallest, near 1 when the prediction is vague and near 0 when the reading is. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.3 The best weight: the Kalman gain, which gives the reading the weight that makes the new variance smallest.

3.2 The tangent line: linearisation
Zoom in on any smooth curve and it looks straight. Near a point, the curve is close to its tangent line, the straight line that touches the curve there with the curve’s slope. 5. Consistency: is the filter telling the truth about itself?


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A filter is consistent when its real errors are as big as the variance it reports with its estimate: on average, error squared divided by variance comes to the number of variables. The innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance allow the check without knowing the truth.


5.1 Why we need a check
To tell when the result has gone wrong, the filter’s own variance is no help. The EKF’s variance comes from tangent lines and from the noise variances we chose, the slip’s Q and the sensor’s R, 0.01 m² each, so it can be wrong without any error message: the mirror filter of Figure 4 reported about 10 cm of uncertainty while 10 m off. A controller or a planner that trusts a variance needs to know whether that variance matches the real errors. A filter whose errors match its own variance is consistent (G-2524)Consistent filter: A filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner. Explained in §5.1 Why we need a check. (Chen et al. 2018; Labbe ch.8). On a real robot the true errors are unknown, but the innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance, the gaps between each reading and the reading the filter predicted, are not.
5.2 The innovation and its covariance
Every step, before it sees the reading, the filter predicts it. The filter also predicts how far off the reading will be. At step 1:

h(\bar{x}) is the reading the filter predicts, the beacon distance at \bar{x}, 5.852 m;
z is the reading, 5.61 m;

\bar{P} is the prediction’s covariance matrix, here one number, the variance 1.01 m²;
H^{\mathsf T} is the transpose of H, H flipped over its diagonal; for one number, H itself;
R is the sensor’s variance, 0.01 m²;
S is the innovation covariance, in m².

The innovation (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance z - h(\bar{x}) has two independent sources of error, the prediction’s and the sensor’s. The prediction’s error reaches the reading through the slope H, so its variance is multiplied by H^2 (variance times slope squaredExplained in: Kalman Filter, §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian); then the two independent variances addExplained in: Kalman Filter, §2.4 Adding independent errors adds variances:
S = H\bar{P}H^{\mathsf T} + R
This S is the innovation covariance (G-2523)Innovation covariance S: The variance the filter expects of its next innovation, S = H\bar{P}H^{\mathsf T} + R: prediction uncertainty seen through the sensor plus sensor noise; it scales the gain and is the yardstick for the NIS test. Explained in §5.2 The innovation and its covariance.: the variance the filter expects of its innovation (Labbe ch.8; Chen et al. 2018). At step 1, the innovation was −0.242 m with S = 0.902 m², a predicted standard deviation of:
\sqrt{S} = \sqrt{0.902} = 0.95 \text{ m}
So an innovation of 0.24 m was well within what the filter expected. Unlike the true error, the innovation is known on a real robot at every step, so it is the everyday test.
5.3 NIS: the innovation test, no truth needed
To turn each innovation (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance into one test number, divide its square by its predicted variance. At step 1:

y is the innovation, the reading minus the reading the filter predicted, −0.242 m;
S is its predicted variance, the innovation covariance, 0.902 m²;
\varepsilon_z is the test number, with no unit.

\varepsilon_z = y^2 / S
For several readings at once, y is a vector with one entry per reading, S is a matrix with one row and one column per reading, y^{\mathsf T} is y written as a row, and dividing by S becomes multiplying by its inverseExplained in: Multiple Linear Regression: The Normal Equation, §6. The normal equation S^{-1}:
\varepsilon_z = y^{\mathsf T} S^{-1} y
The number \varepsilon_z is the normalised innovation squared (NIS) (G-2526)NIS (normalised innovation squared): The squared innovation divided by its predicted covariance, y^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}y; for a consistent filter it follows chi-square with m degrees of freedom (one per reading) and averages m, so it tests consistency from readings alone, even on the robot. Explained in §5.3 NIS: the innovation test, no truth needed.. For step 1:
\varepsilon_z = 0.242^2 / 0.902 = 0.065
Why it should average 1. If the filter is consistent (G-2524)Consistent filter: A filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner. Explained in §5.1 Why we need a check., y follows a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, a bell-shaped curve, with mean 0 and variance S, so y / \sqrt{S} is a standard normal variable (mean 0, variance 1) and its square averages 1. A squared standard normal variable follows the chi-square distribution (G-378)Chi-square distribution: The shape the chi-square statistic \chi^2 follows when the null hypothesis H_0 is true: never negative, skewed to the right, with one parameter, the degrees of freedom. Explained in: Chi-square Tests, §3.1 Built from squared normal draws with 1 degree of freedom; with m readings at once, the NIS follows chi-square with m degrees of freedom and averages m (Chen et al. 2018). For one reading, 95 percent of a consistent filter’s NIS values lie below 3.84 (notebook), and an innovation two standard deviations out gives an NIS of 4.
On one run. Figure 5 plots 60 innovations with the band \pm 2\sqrt{S} the filter predicts. With the right sensor variance R, 0.01 m², 2 percent fall outside. A filter that assumes the sensor is twice as precise (R = 0.0025, a standard deviation of 0.05 m) predicts a narrower band, about ±0.24 m instead of ±0.32 m, and 13 percent fall outside: its innovations are bigger than its S allows (Labbe ch.8).
Make interactive
Figure 5: Innovations of one 60-step run with the band of two predicted standard deviations. With the right sensor variance R = 0.01 m², the band is about ±0.32 m and 2 percent fall outside; a filter that assumes R = 0.0025 m² predicts a band of about ±0.24 m, and 13 percent fall outside
5.4 NEES: the error test, when the truth is known
In a simulation, or with a much better reference sensor, the true state is known and we can test the error itself. Divide the squared error by the filter’s variance. At step 1:

x is the true position, 0.73 m;
\hat{x} is the filter’s estimate, 0.755 m;
p is the filter’s variance, 0.0112 m²;
\varepsilon_x is the test number, with no unit.

\varepsilon_x = (x - \hat{x})^2 / p
For a state of n numbers, the error \tilde{\mathbf{x}}, the true state minus the estimate, is a vector of n entries, P is the filter’s covariance matrix, n rows by n columns, and dividing by P becomes multiplying by its inverse P^{-1}:
\varepsilon_x = \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathsf T} P^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}
The number \varepsilon_x is the normalised estimation error squared (NEES) (G-2525)NEES (normalised estimation error squared): The squared estimation error divided by the filter’s variance, \tilde{x}^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}\tilde{x}; for a consistent filter it follows chi-square with n degrees of freedom and averages n, so its average over simulated runs tests consistency when the truth is known. Explained in §5.4 NEES: the error test, when the truth is known. (Labbe ch.8; Chen et al. 2018). By the same argument it follows chi-square with n degrees of freedom and averages n, here 1. For step 1:
\varepsilon_x = (0.73 - 0.755)^2 / 0.0112
= 0.056
One value says little; the test averages many. We simulated 500 runs of 16 steps, ran three EKFs on each, set with different slip variances Q and sensor variances R, and averaged NEES and NIS at each step (Figure 6). If the filter is consistent (G-2524)Consistent filter: A filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner. Explained in §5.1 Why we need a check., an average of 500 chi-square values with 1 degree of freedom lies between 0.88 and 1.13 in 95 percent of cases (notebook):





























FilterAverage NEESAverage NISVerdictright noises, Q = 0.01, R = 0.011.001.01consistentsensor trusted too much, R = 0.00253.252.41overconfidentmotion trusted too much, Q = 0.000115.95, rising to 32.92.12overconfident, getting worse
In Figure 6 the grey band marks 0.88 to 1.13: only the filter with the right noises stays inside it, the NEES of the filter that trusts its sensor too much sits near 3, and the NEES of the filter that trusts its motion too much climbs past 30.
Make interactive
Figure 6: Average NEES (left) and NIS (right) over 500 runs, per step, log scale. The filter with the right noises stays in the grey band around 1; trusting the sensor too much sits near 3; trusting the motion too much makes NEES climb past 30
5.5 Reading the results

Both near 1: the filter’s variances match its real errors; it can be trusted.
Both well above 1: the filter is overconfident. Increase the noise it assumes; which one is told by tuning experiments such as those of choosing Q and RExplained in: Kalman Filter, §7.2 Q: tune the motion noise.
NEES rising over time: errors pile up faster than the filter allows, the mark of too small a slip variance Q: the filter trusts its motion model and stops listening to readings.
Values well below 1: the filter is too timid; its noises are too large, and it wastes information.

The innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance should also look like random noise: centred on zero and with no slow trend. A trend means the model misses something, such as a bias or too little process noise (Labbe ch.8). NEES needs the truth, so it is a design-time test in simulation; NIS needs only the readings, so it can also run on the robot.
6. Summary



































IdeaWhat it doesWhyLinearisationreplace a nonlinear function by its tangent line at the estimatea linear function keeps a Gaussian a GaussianFirst-order propagationsd out ≈ slope × sd inthe tangent line’s slope stretches the GaussianEKFKalman filter with the motion Jacobian G and the measurement Jacobian H recomputed every stepnonlinear models with unimodal beliefsInnovation covariance Sthe variance the filter expects of its innovationa yardstick for each readingNIS, NEESsquared innovation or error over its predicted variance, average 1 per variabletests whether the filter is consistent

The beacon’s distance is a nonlinear function (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in §1. Overview. of the position (2 m at its lowest, 2.83 m at both 4 m and 8 m), yet the EKF still locates the robot from it, ending the 16 steps at 7.749 m against a true 7.86 m, because it straightens the curve at every prediction.
A nonlinear function bends a Gaussian: near the beacon the readings pile up against 2 m with skewness (G-1817)Skewness: A number for how lopsided a distribution is: 0 symmetric, positive right tail, negative left tail. Explained in: Univariate Analysis: Exploring One Column at a Time, §10. Skewness 1.89, so a mean and variance alone no longer describe them.
Linearising at the mean is almost exact where the curve is nearly straight across the Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is’s width (sd 0.46 both ways at 1 m) and too narrow where it bends (tangent-line sd 0.36 against the true 0.57 for a wide Gaussian at 5.5 m), so EKF accuracy depends on keeping the uncertainty small compared with the bends.
The EKF uses the nonlinear functions for the means and their slopes for the covariances, so with linear models it is exactly the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system.
The slope sets how much a reading tells, because the position is pinned only to the sensor’s standard deviation divided by the slope: at 0.94 that is 0.106 m; under the beacon the slope is near 0 and the filter coasts on its commands.
One Gaussian holds one hypothesis, so an EKF started on the wrong side follows the mirror path, 10.5 m off with tiny error bars; multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode beliefs need a particle filter.
A consistent filter (G-2524)Consistent filter: A filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner. Explained in §5.1 Why we need a check.’s NEES and NIS average 1 per variable (1.00 and 1.01 in our runs); values near 3 or a rising NEES flag noises set too small, and NIS works without the truth, so it can run on the robot.

So the robot can now locate itself with a sensor that measures a distance, not a position, and check with NIS whether it is consistent, as long as the belief is unimodal (G-2528)Unimodal: Having a single mode (one peak); a unimodal belief can be held by one Gaussian, so the Kalman filter needs only its mean and variance. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §1. Overview. Still missing is a close look at the sensors that give these readings and their noise, the subject of the next chapter, robot sensors.
